IMO no, this is essentially the same as the AddImage call in pkg/proc/linutil/dynamic.go, where we also discard the error. Dropping the error here keeps the behavior the same as it was before. An error loading the debug info here is going to show up in the `libraries` command.
You are right.

For the normal path the context is reset in `(*TargetGroup).Continue`. In our client ^C only calls CancelDownloads if we saw a download event, if the target is still running ^C won't cancel downloads.

3e4f098ee1b8126e97f0afcbacce128cc93766bb was trying to avoid calling debuginfod before we have a server running, can show a prompt to the user, give the option to cancel. At the point we can call `DownloadLibraryDebugInfo` it's fine to call debuginfod, it's infact what we should do (otherwise we'd never call it).

What clearing it here does is it stops the `if hadAttaching` loop in `(*TargetGroup).Continue` from running. That loop is there to try to load the debug info of all libraries that we skipped during the first attach. I put this there to avoid trying the download twice when the client is aware of this and has already sent a `DownloadLibraryDebugInfo(-1)`.

This is the correct behavior for our command line client (since it always sends the `DownloadLibraryDebugInfo(-1)` call) for a different client that sends `DownloadLibraryDebugInfo` only for specific libraries I'm not sure what would be the best thing to do. I think it's still fine, if the client is aware about this it can still send a call with `-1`.

Good point. I've changed the error message to have a count of how many libraries we tried to download and how many we succeeded. The individual errors aren't thrown away, they are stored in the loadErr of the library and can be see with the `libraries` command.

Somebody setting an events function needs to also fully drain the queue using GetEvents until they see `EventStopped` (for `Command`) or `EventDownloadLibraryDone` (for `DownloadLibraryDebugInfo`). Breakpoint materialization and process spawn can not happen between an `EventStopped` and the next `Command` call.

I'm going to document this explicitly.

The reason it's like this is that ListDynamicLibraries in rpc2/server.go skips Images[0] (because it isn't a library, it's the executable). The +1 in server.go is to make the indexes match with ListDynamicLibraries.

I didn't really intend to reserve 0 for download everything (you can see that I used -1 below for that), that `if n > 0` thing is mostly because we always load the main executable's debuginfo, we could change it to a `if n >= 0`.

As for the invalid indexes, they all quietly no-op. Maybe we should make them all error.
What's the motivation for rewriting this without the early returns? That some kernel could hypothetically pass weird options to XSAVE so that we have ZMM16 through 31 without having ZMM0 through 15?

issue.title: dlv trace hangs intermittently on FreeBSD (wait4 never returns)
issue.body:
What did you do

Ran dlv trace against the test fixtures in a loop on FreeBSD:

    cd _fixtures/buildtest
    dlv trace --output /tmp/x/__debug ../../_fixtures/goroutines-trace.go callme

What did you expect to see

It prints the trace and exits, as on Linux.

What did you see instead

Some runs never exit.  dlv sits in wait4 while the traced process is
already stopped, so nothing will wake it:

    ps -axwwo pid,ppid,stat,wchan,command
     17473 17437  I   uwait  dlvbin trace --output /tmp/tr1/__debug ...
     17481 17473  TX  -      /tmp/tr1/__debug

SIGQUIT on the hung dlv:

    golang.org/x/sys/unix.Wait4(...)
    pkg/proc/native.(*nativeProcess).wait
        pkg/proc/native/proc_freebsd.go:447
    pkg/proc/native.(*nativeProcess).trapWaitInternal
        pkg/proc/native/proc_freebsd.go:345
    pkg/proc/native.trapWait
        pkg/proc/native/proc_freebsd.go:327
    pkg/proc/native.(*processGroup).ContinueOnce
        pkg/proc/native/proc.go:295

    goroutine 1 is the trace command itself:
    pkg/terminal.(*Commands).cont      pkg/terminal/command.go:1374
    cmd/dlv/cmds.New.func8.traceCmd.1  cmd/dlv/cmds/commands.go:911

Trace output up to that point is normal, it just stops mid-stream.  The
hung pair is never reaped: after a few go test ./cmd/dlv runs there were
13 leftover dlv+__debug pairs on the machine.

How often

One test on its own, 30 iterations, idle bare-metal KVM, 6 vCPU:

    FreeBSD 15.1-RELEASE-p1 amd64   8/30 hung
    FreeBSD 14.4-RELEASE    amd64   6/30 hung

The rate is load dependent, so I would not read one probability off
those.  In whole-suite runs, 4 of 8 died on a trace test, and not always
the same one -- TestTraceMultipleGoroutines (goroutines-trace.go),
TestTrace2 (traceprog.go), TestTraceVerbosityLevel2 (traceverb.go).
Each ends as:

    panic: test timed out after 10m0s
        running tests:
            TestTrace2 (9m51s)
    FAIL github.com/go-delve/delve/cmd/dlv 600.045s

blocked in io.ReadAll on dlv's stderr, which never closes.

Not new

Same measurement at 8fc4acbd (2026-05-25, the last commit the Cirrus
FreeBSD job reported on): 4/30 on 15.1, 4/30 on 14.4.  At n=30 that is
not a significant difference from master, so I would not call it a
regression.  It also matches what Cirrus saw: of the last 145 commits it
reported on, 20 were not green.

Versions

    dlv built from master 3b775986, and from 8fc4acbd
    go1.26.6 freebsd/amd64 (pkg install -y go)
    FreeBSD 15.1-RELEASE-p1 amd64, FreeBSD 14.4-RELEASE amd64

AI disclosure, per Documentation/AI/AI_POLICY.md: I used Claude Code to
drive the FreeBSD VMs, collect the measurements above and draft this
text.  I reviewed and edited it; every number comes from a command run
on hardware I have.

issue.title: proc: fix infinite loop in mapIteratorSwiss.next
issue.body:
Fixes a bug found by the fuzzer in
https://github.com/go-delve/delve/actions/runs/32555989728.

If the table length is too large (because of memory corruption) the
multiplication between that value and the size of the group struct can
overflow. If the overflow is just right the resulting stride will be
zero, causing the loop in mapIteratorSwiss.next to never progress.

Also changes said loop to respect maxNumGroups even when we can't load
any tables but dirLen is large. This is unrelated to the fuzzer bug, it
was merely spotted during the investigation.

We might need some other mechanism to stop the search in mapAccess
early if the table is enormous, or appears to be because of memory
corruption, but doesn't cause an integer overflow. However there are no
obvious limits to impose there so leave it for now.

issue.title: fix(desktop): nest live workflow agents under their parent

issue.title: feat(desktop): add one-click Chats with persistent workspaces
issue.body:
Users can now start a standalone conversation with one click on the new **Chats → +** action. No folder picker or confirmation is needed. Chats appears above Projects, starts expanded, and lists the three most recent conversation titles with Show more for older chats. The active conversation remains visible even outside the recent three. Projects continues to list user-selected directories. Managed workspace folders are excluded from Projects and the new-chat project chooser; their conversations remain in Chats after reload.

Each creation allocates a persistent directory under `SeekMoon/workspaces` in macOS Application Support, Windows LocalAppData, or the Linux user data directory. Development builds use the same stable location independently of the checkout. Exclusive directory creation safely allocates `Unnamed workspace`, `Unnamed workspace 2`, etc., preserving existing files across concurrent requests. The host supplies the canonical managed root with workspace snapshots so classification follows directory ownership rather than display names.

Chat-storage resolution errors are carried separately from the project registry and displayed in the sidebar, so ordinary project operations remain usable. A newer project choice invalidates outstanding chat allocation results to prevent stale focus changes.

The frontend reuses the existing workspace registration and agent selection flow, blocks duplicate creation, ignores stale connection/request results, and allows retry after failure. OpenSeek and Codex conversations share the flat Chats section. The New Chat shortcut allocates another managed workspace when used from a managed chat. Allocated folders are retained if registration fails; there is no automatic deletion.

Validation:
- `moon info`, `moon fmt`, and generated interface review
- `just check`, `just test`, `just build`
- Host tests: concurrent allocation, existing-file preservation, storage failures, stable data path
- Frontend/protocol tests: one-click creation, duplicate/stale requests, failure recovery, flat grouping, similarly named user projects, snapshot ordering, Codex draft visibility, JSON metadata validation
- Chromium tests: direct creation and reload, failure/retry, user project classification, three-row preview and Show more, existing project picker
- Dark-mode Chats screenshot visually inspected
- Native desktop launched with `just desktop-dev`; startup verified from window/renderer logs. Native automated clicking is unavailable because the computer-use client/server versions differ; interactive coverage uses the browser build.

+  let (kind, message) = match terminal {
+    Finished(message) => ("finished", message)
+    ContextYield(message) => ("context_yield", message)
+    Aborted(message) => ("aborted", message)

**`GoalBaselineState` flattens its payload next to the discriminator while `GoalChange` nests its own — two encodings for one value, now frozen by a format version.**

Here `Captured` writes `{"kind":"captured","sha":…,"dirty":…}`, and `from_json` (line 282) recovers it by re-decoding the *same* object as a `GoalBaseline`, which only works because derived `FromJson` ignores the extra `kind` key. `GoalBaseline`'s own derived `ToJson` produces `{"sha":…,"dirty":…}`, so the struct has two on-wire shapes depending on who serializes it, and adding any field named `kind` to `GoalBaseline` silently corrupts the tagged one.

`GoalChange::to_json` two functions up already shows the shape that does not have this problem: `{"kind":"set","text":…,"baseline":<nested>}`. Nesting here too (`{"kind":"captured","baseline":{…}}`) makes the payload one value with one encoding. Worth settling before v2 records exist in the wild, since changing it later costs another format version.

**Altitude: the goal *state* is typed now, but this arm still decides what to render by string prefix — and it silently eats notices.**

`is_model_directed_notice` (`desktop/frontend/transcript/runtime_update.mbt:15`) is `content.has_prefix("[goal") || content.has_prefix("[plan reminder]")`. Any runtime notice whose text happens to start with `[goal` — a background-job completion quoting a goal, a tool result echoed into a notice — is dropped from the transcript with no card and no trace. That is the same defect class this PR set out to remove ("ordinary text resembling control markers cannot change state"), left standing one level down in the same `match` being rewritten here.

The deep fix is the same move applied to the remaining model-directed notices: give `[goal reminder]` / `[goal check]` / `[plan reminder]` a typed `SessionItem` (or a tagged `RuntimeNotice` kind) so "is this for the model or for the reader" is a field, not a prefix, and this predicate disappears.

**Reuse: `GoalMarker` is now a structural duplicate of `@openseek_protocol.GoalChange`, and this function is a 1:1 remap that only drops the baseline.**

The file header that justified the duplication — *"this js-only package cannot depend on that native package, so the marker shapes are duplicated here"* — was deleted in this same diff, because the package now imports `bobzhang/openseek_protocol` directly (see `desktop/frontend/transcript/moon.pkg`). With that reason gone, `GoalMarker` is four variants mirroring four variants, and `apply_goal_marker`, `SessionLoadView.goal_markers`, `Conversation.markers`, `GoalRequest::settled_by` and both `sessions.mbt` match sites all carry the shim.

Using `@protocol.GoalChange` throughout and matching `GoalSet(text, ..)` where the baseline is irrelevant deletes this type, this function, and the `Some(...)` wrapper in `model.mbt`.

**Dead parameter: `_content` is now unused but still threaded through both call sites.**

Every branch of this `match` reads only `origin` and `delegated`, yet `viz/view.mbt:2024` and `:2411` still compute and pass `message.content`. The underscore silences the warning rather than removing the argument. Drop the parameter and the two arguments.

**`wake` no longer has a production caller, and the one test that covers the behavior it existed for still fakes it.**

The only place that passed `wake=true` was serve's goal-marker path (`runtime.queue_steer(Notice(marker), wake=true)`), now `runtime.queue_steer(Goal(marker))`. Grepping the tree, `wake=true` survives only in `agent/job_wait_test.mbt:103` and `agent_runtime/input_wait_test.mbt:34,43,46`.

That first one matters: `agent/job_wait_test.mbt`'s `GoalChange` wake case is `runtime.queue_steer(Notice("NEW-GOAL"), wake=true)` — a shape serve no longer produces. So after this PR nothing verifies that a real `Goal(_)` steer interrupts a `job_wait`, which is the actual production path (`Goal(_) => true` two lines below). Switch that test to `queue_steer(Goal(GoalSet(...)))`; then decide whether `wake` still earns its place in the public API.

**Stale doc: this now returns a 3-tuple, and the doc still describes the 2-tuple.**

*"`("(no terminal)", "")` when the run recorded none"* — it is `("(no terminal)", "", false)` now, and nothing here says what the new `Bool` means or that `context_yield` is a status this can return.

`AttemptOutcome`'s doc at line 101 has the matching gap: *"`ok` is true only for a `finished` terminal; everything else (aborted/interrupted/failed/no terminal, or a thrown error) is a non-success"* — the new `context_yield` terminal belongs in that list by name, since it is precisely the case this PR was written to stop mis-scoring.

**`viz/README.mbt.md` still documents the text-matching rule this function just replaced — including the rationale for it.**

Line 38 of that README:

> The auto-continue text is matched against the constant the engine submits, so rewording that prompt stops the match instead of quietly captioning engine text as the user's.

and the classification table at line 34 keys the **Auto-continue** caption off `@agent_session.GoalContinuePrompt`. Both describe the mechanism this PR deleted; classification is now `origin is AutoContinue`, and rewording the prompt no longer affects it at all. The deleted test `"user cards name who actually wrote the message"` was the executable half of that contract, so nothing catches the drift.

`desktop/internal/engine/README.mbt.md:161` ("`goal_run` appends or steers a `[goal]` marker") and `protocol/README.mbt.md` (whose package table still lists only `Event, Usage, Command, SteerKind, to_json, parse`, and whose module description calls the module "the openseek run/serve stdout wire contract" though it now also owns the durable session schema) have the same problem.

**The doc directly above is now false, and the key order diverges from the native writer.**

Lines 378-380 still claim *"Omit an absent tag rather than writing `null`, matching what the store itself writes: an untagged prompt is byte for byte the line every record held before the field existed."* With `origin` unconditionally emitted, an untagged prompt is no longer byte-for-byte anything that was written before.

Separately, this writes `content` then `origin`, while `agent_session`'s derived `ToJson` for `UserMessage` (field order `origin, content, submission_id`) writes `{"origin":"human","content":...}` — as the updated fixtures in `agent_session/session_test.mbt`, `tests/cram/cli.md` and `desktop/internal/engine/follower.mbt` all show. comment.body:
**`openseek_protocol` gains a whole public API surface but `protocol/moon.mod` still says `version = "0.1.1"`.**

This file adds `SessionFormatVersion`, `InputOrigin`, `GoalBaseline`, `GoalBaselineState`, `GoalChange` and `TurnTerminal` as public API, and the root `moon.mod`, `desktop/moon.mod` and `cmd/viz_app/moon.mod` all still import `bobzhang/openseek_protocol@0.1.1`.

Inside `moon.work` the local member wins (the protocol README says so outright), so `just check` / `just test` / `just build` all pass while resolving the working tree. Any build that resolves from the registry instead — a publish tarball, `moonx bobzhang/openseek/cmd/openseek`, or an external consumer of `bobzhang/openseek@0.3.1` — gets the published 0.1.1, which has none of these symbols, and fails to compile.

This is the exact failure commit c3ebe5a72 ("release: publish openseek 0.3.1 and openseek_protocol 0.1.1 for wasm") was written to fix: *"`protocol/` had drifted from the published `openseek_protocol@0.1.0` without a version bump."* Bump protocol to 0.1.2 and follow both importers.

**A missing `origin` now silently deletes the user's prompt from the transcript.**

The doc comment 20 lines above this one warns against exactly this: *"Refusing there would drop a user's prompt out of the transcript over an annotation nothing renders, and the enclosing `SessionItem` decoder would swallow the refusal as `Unknown` rather than surface it."* The new `origin` branch raises, and `SessionItem::from_json` has `"user" => User(...) catch { _ => Unknown(json) }`, and `apply_session_item` ends with `Unknown(_) => ()`.

Scenario: a desktop frontend at this build talks to an older host (a remote `openseek` over the remote protocol, or a stale native host after a partial self-update). `session.load` / `session.load_archived` returns v1 user payloads with no `origin`. Every user prompt decodes to `Unknown` and vanishes; the transcript renders assistant turns answering nothing, with no error anywhere. `SessionDocument.version` is carried in the reply but the frontend never reads it (grep for `.version` under `desktop/frontend` finds only the file-editor's own counter), so the version bump this PR introduces buys no diagnosis on this path.

Either gate on `document.version` before projecting, or keep `origin` optional in the decoder with an explicit default so an old record degrades to a rendered prompt rather than a hole.

issue.title: math: pow special cases pow(1, NaN) and pow(±1, ±inf) return NaN, diverging from IEEE 754/C99 pow
issue.body:
## Behavior

On every backend (wasm-gc, wasm, js, native), the following all return `NaN`:

```moonbit
@math.pow(1.0, @double.not_a_number)   // NaN, IEEE 754 / C99 Annex F say 1.0
@math.pow(1.0, @double.infinity)       // NaN, IEEE 754 / C99 Annex F say 1.0
@math.pow(1.0, @double.neg_infinity)   // NaN, IEEE 754 / C99 Annex F say 1.0
@math.pow(-1.0, @double.infinity)      // NaN, IEEE 754 / C99 Annex F say 1.0
@math.pow(-1.0, @double.neg_infinity)  // NaN, IEEE 754 / C99 Annex F say 1.0
```

## Discussion

- IEEE 754-2019 (§9.2.1) and C99 Annex F (F.9.4.4) specify `pow(1, y) = 1` for **any** y, including NaN, and `pow(±1, ±∞) = 1` — the rationale being "1 to any power is 1".
- The current behavior follows the classic fdlibm ordering (NaN check first) and matches ECMAScript's `Math.pow` / `**`, so it is at least internally consistent and consistent across backends.
- However, the function's doc comment claims IEEE 754 semantics, so today either the docs or the behavior is wrong.

## Possible resolutions

1. Align behavior with IEEE 754/C99: special-case `x == 1.0` (and `|x| == 1.0` with infinite y) before the NaN check. This is what glibc/musl/Rust/Go do.
2. Keep JS-`Math.pow` behavior and fix the doc comment to say so explicitly.

Either way the divergence should stop being implicit. Found while adding QuickCheck special-value coverage in #4055 (the property suite currently pins the *actual* behavior, and can be flipped to the IEEE behavior if option 1 is chosen).

Reviewed 1b96df0. This is a worthwhile correctness fix, and I found no blocking issues.

The strongest reason for the change is consistency with the existing `powf` implementation: switching between Float and Double should not change these special-value results. The [ECMAScript specification](https://tc39.es/ecma262/multipage/ecmascript-data-types-and-values.html#sec-numeric-types-number-exponentiate) explicitly describes its differing NaN results as a historical compatibility choice.

The new guards are narrowly scoped, and the tests cover all five changed cases as well as `pow(-1, NaN)` and finite negative-base cases that must retain their behavior. I would be comfortable merging this, with one optional dead-code cleanup noted inline.

issue.title: fix(mbtx): avoid oversized sandbox arguments in review agents
issue.body:
Review and explore agents can fail every `mbtx` call, including `fn main { println(1) }`, with `OSError("@process.run(): Argument list too long")`. Their source-write sandbox profile grows with the repository and was passed inline to `sandbox-exec -p`, exhausting the OS argument limit before the compiler or snippet starts. Scanning nested agent worktrees amplified that growth. Changing the backend or execution directory does not avoid the wrapper.

The source-write sandbox now:

- Writes its profile to a caller-owned temporary file and launches with `sandbox-exec -f`. `mbtx` retains the file in its per-call build directory through compilation and background execution, then uses the existing cleanup. Write errors propagate instead of disabling protection.
- Appends a final deny rule protecting the canonical profile path, even inside a writable scratch lab. The availability probe exercises the same file-based mechanism.
- Skips `.worktrees` and `.claude/worktrees` during directory enumeration and mtime tracking. A workspace rooted inside either location is still scanned normally; ordinary source directories named `worktrees` are preserved. The source-file regex remains in force, and literal directory rules remain necessary to prevent moving source directories outside the workspace.
- Runs a dedicated macOS native CI job for the sandbox package and a reviewer print/read smoke test. `OPENSEEK_REQUIRE_SANDBOX_TESTS=1` makes unavailable enforcement fail the job rather than silently skipping the kernel tests. Portable tests also check the file-based argv contract and worktree exclusions on Linux/Wasm.

Regression coverage includes a profile exceeding 2 MB, successful reads with denied source writes, blocked profile overwrite/removal inside a writable lab, and a blocked source-directory escape. The bounded worker profile remains inline, with its different growth bound documented. Constructor and lifecycle documentation describe profile creation and loading explicitly.

Validation:

- Reproduced errno 7 / `Argument list too long` with the original inline-profile launch.
- `OPENSEEK_REQUIRE_SANDBOX_TESTS=1 moon test agent_tool/internal/sandbox --target native` — 26 passed, enforcement required.
- `moon test agent_tool/internal/sandbox --target wasm` — 26 passed, including portable transport and scan checks.
- `just check`
- `just test` — 3,068 native tests, 3,186 JS tests, 38 cram cases, CLI lifecycle checks, and offline workflow cases passed.
- `just build`
- `moon info && moon fmt`
- CI workflow YAML parsed successfully.

The separately reported missing `OPENSEEK_REFERENCES` environment variable is not addressed by this change.

| `.worktrees` (22 worktrees) | 6,607 | 30% |

The prune list needs both spellings. Between them they are 95% of the scan, which is the real reason the profile passed ARG_MAX.

The rest of finding (2) stands, and the tail is worth a look too — `.moonagent/eval_runs` (245), `desktop/target` (240), `desktop/dist` (161), `Desktop.app/Contents` (80), `.repos/*` vendored clones (~40). Those are build outputs and vendored copies carrying source that the source-write profile has no reason to protect; the genuine first-party tree is roughly 200 directories. That also strengthens the alternative I raised: if the per-directory literal denies are not load-bearing beyond the regex rule, dropping them makes the profile O(1) and none of this enumeration matters.

comment.body:
## Review

The fix is the right one and the mechanism is correct. Things I checked and they hold:

- `-f <path>` is the correct replacement for `-p <profile>`, and the path is `realpath`'d before it goes into argv, so a relative CWD at spawn time can't misresolve it.
- The availability probe still runs *before* the write, so off macOS `create_if_available` returns `None` without touching the filesystem — no new failure mode on Linux/Windows.
- A write failure raises instead of silently dropping enforcement, which is the same "misconfiguration cannot disable protection" discipline the existing input validation follows.
- `confine()` is called immediately before each of the two spawn sites (`build_snippet` for the wasm build phase, and the single-shot/staged run), so the file is always freshly written for the spawn that consumes it. The build phase is synchronous, so the run phase's `CreateOrTruncate` can't pull the profile out from under a live build.
- Cleanup checks out on both exit paths: `cleanup()` removes `dir`, and after background adoption `terminal_cleanup` removes `build_dir` (or `dir`) at terminal status. The PR body's "reclaimed by the existing cleanup" is accurate.

### 1. The regression test never runs in CI (medium–high)

Every test in `agent_tool/internal/sandbox` sits behind `guard sandbox_exec_available() else { return }`, and the `capability_test.mbt` argv-shape assertions early-return off macOS because `create_if_available` returns `None` there. No workflow runs `moon test` on macOS: `ci.yml` is `ubuntu-latest` × three targets, `desktop.yml` is windows + ubuntu, and the only `macos-latest` jobs are `editor.yml` and the release-gated `desktop-release.yml`.

So the new 2 MB-profile test, the `assert_eq(args[0], "-f")` assertion, and the `mbtx_test.mbt` read-only case all no-op in CI. A bug that broke *every* `mbtx` call for the review/explore roles is protected only by tests that run on developer machines — a revert to `-p` would go green.

Worth a narrow macOS job; `moon test agent_tool/internal/sandbox --target native` on `macos-latest` is a couple of minutes and would cover the whole sandbox package, not just this fix. If that's not wanted, please say so in the PR body so nobody reads green CI as coverage here.

There's also a platform-independent assertion available cheaply: "the profile never enters argv" is checkable on Linux if the argv construction is reachable without the availability probe (or by asserting on `source_write_readonly_profile_data` plus a pure argv builder). Right now nothing outside macOS can catch the regression.

### 2. Argv length was the only thing observing the profile's growth, and the growth is untouched (medium)

`source_write_readonly_profile_base` emits one `(deny file-write* (literal …))` per source-containing directory, and `should_prune_profile_scan_path` prunes `.git`, `.hg`, `.svn`, `.jj`, `node_modules` — but **not `.worktrees`**. This checkout has 22 worktrees, each a full copy of the repo, so the scan walks ~23× the tree and the profile carries ~23× the directory list. That is the dominant term behind the 2 MB+ profile this PR routes around.

After the fix, that cost is still paid, just silently: a multi-MB file written on every `mbtx` call, and `sandbox-exec` compiling a multi-MB SBPL profile on every spawn. The hard failure is gone; so is the signal. (Same root cause makes `cached_source_write_profile_valid` stat every scanned directory per call.)

Adding `".worktrees"` to the prune list is a one-word change and removes the dominant factor. It's arguably in scope here — it's the same defect, and this repo is the one that reported it.

Separately worth deciding out loud: the `(deny file-write* (regex …))` rule already covers every protected source *file* anywhere under the root, so the per-directory literal denies only add directory-level protection (creating/removing entries, `rm -rf` of a source dir). If that's the intent, a comment saying so keeps the next reader from deleting them as redundant. If it isn't, the list can go entirely and the profile becomes O(1) — which would make this whole class of bug unreachable rather than worked around.

### 3. The profile file lives inside the region the confined process may write (low, hardening)

`writable_subtree` is `dir` (or the enclosing lab), `build_dir = "{dir}/build"`, and the profile lands at `build_dir/source-write.sb`. So a read-only subagent's snippet can rewrite its own sandbox profile.

Not exploitable as written — `sandbox-exec` compiles the profile at exec time, and `confine()` rewrites it immediately before each spawn — but the safety rests on an invariant that is stated nowhere and enforced nowhere: *confine is called once per spawn, immediately before it*. A future retry, a re-spawn on transient failure, or a second phase that reuses a prepared `SandboxedCommand` would break it silently, and the failure mode is "the sandbox was disabled", which no test would notice.

Cheapest fix: SBPL is last-match-wins and the code already appends the lab allow last, so one more line after it — `(deny file-write* (literal "<profile_path>"))` — closes it permanently. Otherwise place the file outside `writable_subtree` while keeping it under the cleanup root.

### 4. `create_worker_if_available` still passes its profile inline (low)

It stays on `-p`. Its profile is bounded today — `(allow default)`, one deny per `deny_roots` entry, two allows and one deny — so there's no bug. But the two constructors now differ in launch mechanism for a reason that isn't visible from the worker call site, and anything that grows `deny_roots` reintroduces exactly this failure. Either move it to `-f` for uniformity, or leave a one-line comment there pointing at `create_if_available` for why the source-write profile can't use `-p`.

### 5. Smaller things

- `create_if_available` now writes a file and gained a raise path, but the name still reads as a pure probe. The doc comment covers it; `prepare_if_available` would carry it in the signature.
- "Keep the file unchanged until the command exits" is stronger than the actual contract — the profile is compiled into the kernel at `exec`, so it only has to be correct *until the spawn*. Nothing depends on the stronger wording (`build_dir` survives to terminal status in the background path anyway), and over-stating it makes the contract look harder to satisfy than it is.
- The tests and the README example put `profile_path` inside the workspace root being sandboxed (`"{dir}/profile.sb"`, `"{root}/profile.sb"`) — exactly what the new README text tells callers not to do ("a caller-owned file in an existing temporary directory"). Harmless (the profile is computed before the file is written) but it also perturbs the `watched_dirs` mtime cache for that root, and the examples are what people copy.
- `sandbox_exec_available()` still probes with `-p`, so the probe doesn't confirm that `-f` works on the host it just declared available. Fine in practice; noting it because the probe is the thing standing between "unavailable" and "enforced".

None of this blocks the fix — it addresses a real outage and does so in the right place. (1) is the one I'd want resolved before merge, since without it the fix has no guard; (2) is the underlying defect and is a one-word change away.

issue.title: fix(mbtx): avoid oversized sandbox arguments in review agents
issue.body:
Review and explore agents can fail every `mbtx` call, including `fn main { println(1) }`, with `OSError("@process.run(): Argument list too long")`. Their source-write sandbox profile grows with the repository and was passed inline to `sandbox-exec -p`, exhausting the OS argument limit before the compiler or snippet starts. Scanning nested agent worktrees amplified that growth. Changing the backend or execution directory does not avoid the wrapper.

The source-write sandbox now:

- Writes its profile to a caller-owned temporary file and launches with `sandbox-exec -f`. `mbtx` retains the file in its per-call build directory through compilation and background execution, then uses the existing cleanup. Write errors propagate instead of disabling protection.
- Appends a final deny rule protecting the canonical profile path, even inside a writable scratch lab. The availability probe exercises the same file-based mechanism.
- Skips `.worktrees` and `.claude/worktrees` during directory enumeration and mtime tracking. A workspace rooted inside either location is still scanned normally; ordinary source directories named `worktrees` are preserved. The source-file regex remains in force, and literal directory rules remain necessary to prevent moving source directories outside the workspace.
- Runs a dedicated macOS native CI job for the sandbox package and a reviewer print/read smoke test. `OPENSEEK_REQUIRE_SANDBOX_TESTS=1` makes unavailable enforcement fail the job rather than silently skipping the kernel tests. Portable tests also check the file-based argv contract and worktree exclusions on Linux/Wasm.

Regression coverage includes a profile exceeding 2 MB, successful reads with denied source writes, blocked profile overwrite/removal inside a writable lab, and a blocked source-directory escape. The bounded worker profile remains inline, with its different growth bound documented. Constructor and lifecycle documentation describe profile creation and loading explicitly.

Validation:

- Reproduced errno 7 / `Argument list too long` with the original inline-profile launch.
- `OPENSEEK_REQUIRE_SANDBOX_TESTS=1 moon test agent_tool/internal/sandbox --target native` — 26 passed, enforcement required.
- `moon test agent_tool/internal/sandbox --target wasm` — 26 passed, including portable transport and scan checks.
- `just check`
- `just test` — 3,068 native tests, 3,186 JS tests, 38 cram cases, CLI lifecycle checks, and offline workflow cases passed.
- `just build`
- `moon info && moon fmt`
- CI workflow YAML parsed successfully.

The separately reported missing `OPENSEEK_REFERENCES` environment variable is not addressed by this change.

issue.title: Visualize background jobs with live logs and browser coverage
issue.body:
Add a Jobs tab to the existing Desktop panel launcher. Users can inspect active and retained jobs, follow or pause output, copy a log path or tail command, reload the latest output, load older jobs, and stop the tracked execution.

The view polls only while visible, bounds reads and displayed text, preserves Unicode boundaries, and rejects stale replies after session or visibility changes. History refresh and storage failures remain visible even when output following is paused. UI review fixes and the complete browser regressions are included in this PR.

## Follow-up hardening

- Drain at most four 64 KiB pages per refresh cycle while following, display catching-up status, and defer a partial UTF-8 suffix when its cursor cannot advance.
- Serialize pause/resume and queued manual reload behind the outstanding selected-log read; cancel pending refresh intent when pausing or hiding the panel.
- Keep Stop available without an output path, keep the toolbar compact, and show readable stop reasons.
- Add state regressions and three production-browser scenarios: a large completed output burst, paused reload with a held response, and stopping a controllable job without a log path.

The existing opt-in Jobs launcher remains the product scope. A persistent conversation-level running-count entry and history-cache work are separate improvements.

## Validation

Current-head `c64c70dba` [CI](https://github.com/moonbitlang/openseek/actions/runs/34664735968) and [Desktop/Windows](https://github.com/moonbitlang/openseek/actions/runs/34664736056) passed. This PR remains one commit and is mergeable.

- Local combined-stack `moon info`, `moon fmt`, `just check`, `just test`, and `just build` passed. Final focused native regressions passed 262/262; Jobs state tests passed 8/8.
- Independent `openseek review` of the 13-file hardening delta found no blockers and two low-severity UI status issues. Both were fixed in #1469. The final four-file correction review returned **zero findings**. Runtime and host code needed no further review corrections.
- Final-head GitHub tests passed: **3,095 native, 3,198 JS, 2,345 Wasm**, 38 cram cases, and offline CLI/workflow integration.
- The rebuilt production browser passed **86/86 E2E tests without retries locally**, and **86/86 in GitHub CI**. All eight Jobs scenarios passed, including the final read-error/no-log assertions. Windows packaging and all **8 native job-host regressions** passed. Light/dark/narrow screenshots were inspected.
- Browser tests use production frontend code with a transport fixture backed by real subprocesses and retained files. Native host and real CLI tests cover the actual backend separately.

An earlier UI-head native attempt failed with process-spawn EAGAIN and a child-output assertion. Identical backend code passed runtime/host CI, and all 31 relevant tests passed locally. Its retry was superseded by the final UI-only correction. The final native run passed all 3,095 tests with no backend change or weakened test.

## Limits

The panel retains bounded recent output and exposes the complete retained file. Stop controls the tracked execution/direct child. Retention ends with session deletion; streaming does not fsync each chunk. Same-path external replacement with equal-or-larger content is outside the byte-cursor contract.

## Stack and review history

Plan #1465 is merged. Review and merge the implementation in this order: #1466 (runtime) → #1468 (host) → #1469 (UI).

The former lifecycle PR #1467 is absorbed into #1466. The corrections from #1470 are included in the layer they fix. This regrouping preserves the reviewed implementation and regression tests, retains newer main changes, and updates the delivery documentation. The original independent `openseek review` findings, resolutions, and aggregate validation remain available in #1470.

comment.body:
## Review — Jobs UI slice

The browser coverage here is the best part of the stack: a real subprocess writing to a real file behind the transport seam, with the production bundle in front of it. `background_jobs.spec.js` covers stdout/stderr interleaving, output with no trailing newline, multibyte text, pause → write → resume, manual-scroll auto-pause with a scrollTop assertion, clipboard for both path and tail command, stop with a `signalCode` check, a deliberately delayed obsolete `jobs.read` reply, conversation switching, page reload, and a selected job beyond the first 100 rows. The epoch/serial invalidation in `state.mbt` is correct and the tests actually prove it.

Also right: `subscriptions` returns `@sub.none` when the panel isn't active, so there is no hidden-view polling; the 262,144-UTF-16-unit buffer cap with the trailing-surrogate guard; and `tail_command`'s quoting — `'\''` for POSIX and `''` for PowerShell are both correct, and the UNC/drive-letter detection is reasonable.

### 1. Stop, Pause and Reload are nested inside `if view.output_path is Some(path)` (medium)

In `view.mbt` the whole `jobs-toolbar` — Copy path, Copy tail command, Pause/Follow, Reload tail **and Stop job** — lives inside that branch. A job whose record has `output_file: None` therefore has no Stop button at all, and no way to pause or reload. That is reachable: memory-only retention, and any job whose log creation failed but which still registered.

Only Copy path and Copy tail command actually depend on the path. Split the toolbar so the lifecycle controls render unconditionally.

### 2. `page.more` is never read — no burst continuation, no final drain (low–medium)

`more` is returned by `jobs.read` and never consulted anywhere in `desktop/frontend`. Following therefore advances at most one 64 KiB page per 1 s tick, while the note above the pane says "Following output". A job writing faster than ~64 KiB/s falls permanently behind and the UI doesn't say so. The plan called for "a continuation for bursts and a final drain after terminal status".

Minimal fix: when a page comes back with `more: true` and `follow` is on, immediately issue the next read instead of waiting for the tick (bounded by a small per-tick page budget so it can't become a tight loop), and show "catching up" while `more` holds.

### 3. Every `Poll` re-lists from disk, and `job_changed` already tells you when to (low)

`Poll` fires `request_list(offset=0)` *and* `request_read` every second, and `JobsChanged` dispatches another `Poll`. Since the event is the exact signal, the timer only needs to be a backstop. Listing is the expensive side — see #1468 (4), where each list walks every generation directory. Suggest keeping the read at 1 s and dropping the list to a 5–10 s backstop, letting `job_changed` drive it otherwise. That also removes the list request from the steady state where nothing is happening.

### 4. Raw reason identifiers reach the user (low)

`status_label` special-cases `user` and `session_ended`, then falls through to `"Stopped · \{reason}"`. So the failure reasons the runtime actually produces render as **Stopped · output_limit**, **Stopped · time_limit**, **Stopped · capture_failed**. `status_class` already enumerates exactly those three — give `status_label` the same arms with sentences ("Stopped · hit the output cap", "Stopped · hit the 30-minute limit", "Stopped · output capture failed"). The plan asked to "display the reason when they stop a job", which I read as prose, not the wire token.

### 5. The plan's persistent `Jobs · N running` conversation entry isn't here (product decision)

The plan's UX section opens with it, and it's the thing that makes the feature ambient rather than opt-in. What shipped puts "N active · M loaded" inside the panel, so a user with a job running sees nothing until they open the Jobs tab — and the tab is reachable only through the launcher row. The doc update in this PR records the change, but I'd flag it as a decision to take explicitly rather than absorb: right now a backgrounded `mbtx` is still discovered the old way, through the model's prose handoff.

### 6. Nits

- `tail -n 100` / `-Tail 100`; the plan said 200. Pick one and make the doc match.
- `Pause` sets `reading: false` while a read may still be outstanding, so `ToggleFollow` can put a second read in flight. `read_serial` makes this correct, but it breaks the plan's "one request in flight". Leave `reading` alone and let the serial guard drop the reply.
- `state.warnings` renders one `jobs-error` div per host error with no cap; with #1468's unbounded `errors` array a directory with many unreadable entries becomes a wall of alerts above the list.
- `Elapsed Ns` / `Last output Ns ago` are computed from `@interop.now_ms()` at render time, so they freeze whenever polling stops (panel hidden, disconnected, paused list). Fine, but the "Disconnected" banner is the only hint that the numbers are stale.
- The `jobs.read` UTF-8 windowing is reimplemented in `background_jobs_harness.js`, so a divergence from `job_utf8_window` wouldn't surface in the browser suite. The native tests cover the real one — worth a comment in the harness saying the two must be kept in step.
- This PR is where the plan doc flips to "implemented". #1466 and #1468 each merge carrying a plan that still says "Status: proposed … No runtime or UI changes implemented". Moving the status line and the decisions section to #1466 would make each PR self-consistent.

(1) is the one I'd fix before merge; (2) and (3) are worth doing while the code is fresh; (5) is a call for you rather than a defect.

issue.title: Expose retained job history and bounded Desktop controls
issue.body:
Desktop can list retained background jobs, read bounded log slices, and stop a live job through scoped host commands. The host overlays generation-specific live state on retained history, allowing controls to work independently of the model turn.

The PR includes ownership and recovery rules, 100-record history pages, 64 KiB UTF-8-safe byte reads, explicit missing/truncated/storage errors, and preservation of live jobs when metadata or directories are damaged. POSIX, Windows, and UNC path handling and all related review fixes live in this layer.

## Follow-up hardening

- Separate Stop delivery (5 s) from settlement (30 s). A settlement timeout explicitly reports unconfirmed completion; delivery alone never becomes Stopped.
- Consume correlated snapshot/stop replies after routing, including late replies, instead of broadcasting them to every browser.
- Distinguish a failed live refresh from an external owner while preserving generation-specific control checks.
- Add actual stream-consumer isolation and settlement-timeout tests, and extend owner diagnostics coverage.

The review's proposed clamp to persisted output_bytes is not applied: metadata changes on lifecycle events and would freeze reads of growing logs. The runtime already hard-cancels the direct process. Empty-generation cleanup belongs in #1466; generation caching and scan quotas remain separate optimizations.

## Validation

Current-head `4b254ce31` [CI](https://github.com/moonbitlang/openseek/actions/runs/34663737032) and [Desktop/Windows](https://github.com/moonbitlang/openseek/actions/runs/34663737041) passed. This PR remains one commit and is mergeable.

- Local combined-stack `moon info`, `moon fmt`, `just check`, `just test`, and `just build` passed. Final focused native regressions passed 262/262; Jobs state tests passed 8/8.
- Independent `openseek review` of the 13-file hardening delta found no blockers and two low-severity UI status issues. Both were fixed in #1469. The final four-file correction review returned **zero findings**. Runtime and host code needed no further review corrections.
- The complete final stack also passed 86 browser E2E scenarios and eight Windows job-host regressions; final aggregate evidence is recorded in #1469.

## Stack and review history

Plan #1465 is merged. Review and merge the implementation in this order: #1466 (runtime) → #1468 (host) → #1469 (UI).

The former lifecycle PR #1467 is absorbed into #1466. The corrections from #1470 are included in the layer they fix. This regrouping preserves the reviewed implementation and regression tests, retains newer main changes, and updates the delivery documentation. The original independent `openseek review` findings, resolutions, and aggregate validation remain available in #1470.

comment.body:
## Review — host slice (list / read / stop bridge)

The byte-cursor work is the strongest part of the stack. `job_utf8_window` correctly skips continuation bytes only on a genuine mid-file tail, rejects a cursor that isn't on a boundary, trims an incomplete trailing sequence by lead-byte width, and validates lead bytes (`0xc2..0xf4`, so overlongs and `0xf5+` are refused). `read_job_record` checks that the decoded record's `generation`/`id` match the directory it came from. `jobs_store_path` normalizing both sides of the ownership comparison, and the Windows CI job that exercises it, are the right amount of paranoia. The `owner.lock` `try_lock` projection to `Interrupted` is exactly the plan's owner-verification contract.

### 1. The 5 s `job_request` timeout is applied to `JobStop`, whose reply arrives only after the process settles (medium–high)

`job_request` wraps `reply.get()` in `@async.with_timeout(5000, …)`. On the engine side, `JobStopResult` is emitted only after `jobs.stop(job_id)` returns, and that awaits `exec.wait()` (process actually terminal) plus `wait_any` (completion published). `request_stop` sends one cancel to the direct child; there is no SIGTERM→SIGKILL escalation anywhere, so the ceiling is the 30-minute reaper.

Consequence: any process that doesn't die within ~5 s of the cancel makes `jobs.stop` raise `EngineError`, which #1469 renders as an error under the Stop button and clears `stopping`. Meanwhile the stop is genuinely in flight and `defer self.job_requests.remove(request_id)` has already torn down the waiter, so the real `JobStopResult` is dropped on arrival. The UI only recovers a second later via the next `jobs.list` poll, if the process died by then. A well-behaved process with a large final drain can hit this too.

Two ways out, either is fine:
- Split the timeouts — keep 5 s on the `ack` (delivery really should be fast) and give the reply a much longer budget, or none, relying on the request's own cancellation.
- Or change the contract: have the engine reply `Stopped` as soon as the stop is *requested* and let `job_changed` report settlement. That also matches "keep stopping asynchronous relative to command intake" better than the current blocking `BgJobRuntime::stop`.

Either way, a `Stopping`/`StopTimedOut` outcome would let the UI say "stop requested, still running" instead of showing a transport error.

### 2. `read_job_page` reads to `file.size()`, ignoring the record's committed `output_bytes` (medium)

#1466 goes to some trouble never to advance `file_bytes` past a failed write, precisely so that a committed cursor exists. The reader then ignores it and uses the raw `file.size()`. So bytes from a torn/partial write are inside the page, and `job_utf8_window` will raise `invalid UTF-8 in job output` for the whole read rather than returning the committed prefix — turning a degraded log into an unreadable one. The same applies to a mid-`write_at` tail observed while the writer is active (the width trim handles a truncated-but-valid sequence; it hard-fails on an invalid lead).

Suggest clamping `size` to `min(file.size(), job.output_bytes)` when `job.output_bytes > 0`, and reporting the gap as log health rather than as a read failure. The record already carries `output_error` for the "log is incomplete" story.

### 3. A failed or slow live snapshot mislabels a live job as owned elsewhere (medium)

In `list_jobs`, if `job_request(JobsSnapshot)` raises (including the 5 s timeout, or `session_root is None`, or the directory-mismatch guard), the page is built from disk with `live = false`. For a still-running record that sends `job_view` down the owner-lock path, where `try_lock` fails *because this very engine holds the lock* — so the row reports:

> The owner is running outside this Desktop connection; controls are unavailable.

and `controllable: live && …` is false, disabling Stop. That's the wrong diagnosis for the most likely cause. Worth distinguishing "we know the live engine for this scope exists but the refresh failed" (keep the row controllable, show the refresh error) from "no live engine claims this scope" (current message).

### 4. History listing cost is proportional to session age, not to job count (medium, given #1469's 1 Hz poll)

`job_history_page` does `readdir(jobs/)`, then per generation `@fs.kind` + `@fs.mtime(owner.lock)` + `readdir(jobs/<gen>)`, accumulating ids until `offset + 100` — every call. #1469 calls it once per second while the panel is visible, and also on every `job_changed`. Combined with #1466's unpruned empty generation directories (one per engine run that executed anything), that is unbounded growth in per-second syscalls for a long-lived conversation. Deep paging also re-scans from zero each time, so `Load older jobs` is O(n²) in pages.

Fixing the prune in #1466 removes most of this. Beyond that, caching the generation list keyed on the `jobs/` directory mtime would make the steady-state poll nearly free.

### 5. Correlated replies are also broadcast to every client (low–medium)

`ServeEngine::consume` routes `JobsSnapshot`/`JobStopResult` to `job_requests[request_id]` but does not consume them — they continue to the sink and reach every attached browser, where `decode_engine_event` returns `None` and discards them. So every `jobs.list` poll (1/s) pushes the full `JobRecord` array to all clients for nothing. Suppress these two after routing, or route them out of band.

### 6. The host re-derives the store layout instead of using `SessionStore::job_logs_dir` (low)

The plan asked for "a session-store artifact-path API rather than duplicating private path construction across packages". #1466 added `SessionStore::job_logs_dir`, `cmd/openseek` uses it — and then `jobs_store_path` here rebuilds `root/sessions/<id>/jobs` by hand, in two functions, with the `ArchivedStore` variant on top. I understand why (the host works from `@pathx.Absolute` roots, not a `SessionStore`), but the layout now lives in two places and a change to one breaks the other silently. Either expose a path-level helper from the store package that the host can call, or add a test that pins the two constructions to the same string.

### 7. Nits

- `job_utf8_window` ends with `ignore(@utf8.decode(bytes[start:end]))` and `read_job_page` then decodes the same slice again. Return the decoded string from the window function.
- `errors : Array[String]` is unbounded — one entry per unreadable generation or job. #1469 renders each as its own alert div. Cap it and add an "and N more" tail.
- `read_job_record`'s 1 MiB metadata cap and `read_job_page`'s `limit` bounds are good; consider the same explicit cap on the number of generations scanned per call, so a pathological directory can't make one request unbounded.

(1) and (2) are the two I'd want fixed before merge; (3) is a small conditional; the rest can follow.

issue.title: Retain background job logs and durable lifecycle controls
issue.body:
Background commands now expose a retained output file before their handoff or Started event. Output produced before background adoption is seeded into the same file, and subsequent output remains available for external tailing and later inspection. Small foreground commands remain memory-first.

This PR includes the complete runtime contract: generation-scoped metadata and ownership, structured lifecycle events, correlated snapshot/stop commands outside model turns, and retention with the owning session. Storage failures remain explicit. Failure to create required scratch/log storage stops setup or adoption with an error; production does not silently degrade to memory-only retention. Runtime review fixes and real CLI regressions are included here, so correctness does not depend on a later hardening PR.

Two small Desktop exhaustive-match adaptations accompany the new wire variants so this PR builds on its own. Desktop job access and the Jobs panel follow in #1468 and #1469.

## Follow-up hardening

- Remove an unused generation after foreground-only execution, only when no job was adopted and no unexpected files remain. Missing metadata is never a reason to delete a retained log.
- Snapshot the committed output prefix under the sink mutex and read the file outside the writer lock. Preserve the captured memory head after a failed initial seed while retaining the partial path for inspection.
- Add foreground-only cleanup, failed-metadata retention, concurrent append/read, and failed-seed regressions.

The review's proposed cleanup based only on absent JSON was narrowed to protect logs after metadata failure. The suggested terminal-event race was not established under the existing cooperative scheduling and serialized publication; no speculative ordering rewrite is included.

## Validation

Current-head `47543fb72` [CI](https://github.com/moonbitlang/openseek/actions/runs/34663737012) and [Desktop/Windows](https://github.com/moonbitlang/openseek/actions/runs/34663737043) passed. This PR remains one commit and is mergeable.

- Local combined-stack `moon info`, `moon fmt`, `just check`, `just test`, and `just build` passed. Final focused native regressions passed 262/262; Jobs state tests passed 8/8.
- Independent `openseek review` of the 13-file hardening delta found no blockers and two low-severity UI status issues. Both were fixed in #1469. The final four-file correction review returned **zero findings**. Runtime and host code needed no further review corrections.
- The complete final stack also passed 86 browser E2E scenarios and eight Windows job-host regressions; final aggregate evidence is recorded in #1469.

## Stack and review history

Plan #1465 is merged. Review and merge the implementation in this order: #1466 (runtime) → #1468 (host) → #1469 (UI).

The former lifecycle PR #1467 is absorbed into #1466. The corrections from #1470 are included in the layer they fix. This regrouping preserves the reviewed implementation and regression tests, retains newer main changes, and updates the delivery documentation. The original independent `openseek review` findings, resolutions, and aggregate validation remain available in #1470.

comment.body:
## Review — runtime slice (retained logs, durable records, controls)

Design is sound and matches the plan closely. The things I checked and found correct:

- `open_spill`/`append_locked` no longer swallow I/O errors, and `file_bytes` is not advanced past a failed write — the committed-vs-observed distinction the plan asked for is real.
- Adoption is serialized against the pipe reader through the sink mutex, and `materialize()` seeds the file before `register` publishes, so the `output_file` in a `job_changed(started)` always exists. `turn_finish.py` asserts exactly that, including the pre-adoption UTF-8 prefix.
- `register` publishes `Started` under `protect_from_cancel` before spawning the watcher, so a process that exits during adoption still gets `Started` then one terminal event. Group defers run FILO and `with_task_group` asserts `children.is_empty()` before running them, so `finalize()` cannot race the watcher's `finish_job` and the `scratch` rmdir cannot outrun `finalize`. Ordering is right.
- Lazy `prepare_output` is a good call — it is why an idle restart allocates no generation directory, which the integration test also checks.
- `owner.lock` under a `CreateNew` in an exclusively-created directory is the right ownership primitive.

### 1. Nothing ever prunes an empty generation directory (medium)

`spawn_foreground_retained` calls `prepare_output()`, so **any** engine run that executes a single snippet allocates `<session>/jobs/<generation>/` plus `owner.lock` — even when no job is ever adopted and `discard()` removes the `fg-N.out`. `finalize()` writes metadata but never removes a generation that ended up with no `*.json`.

A conversation reopened N times accumulates N directories containing nothing but a lock file, forever. #1468's `job_history_page` then does `kind()` + `mtime(owner.lock)` + `readdir()` on every one of them, and #1469 calls it once per second while the panel is open. The two multiply.

Suggest: at the end of `finalize()`, under `protect_from_cancel`, `rmdir` the generation directory if it contains no `*.json` (after closing/removing `owner.lock`). Cheap, and it keeps the listing cost proportional to jobs rather than to session age.

### 2. `read_all` now holds the sink mutex across a full-file read (medium)

`read_all` acquires `self.lock`, then opens the log and reads `file_bytes` in one shot. `append_chunk` needs the same lock. So a `job_output` call with an `offset` (which goes through `read_output` → `read_all`) blocks the execution's pipe reader for the entire read+`decode_lossy` of up to `hard_cap` = 20,000,000 characters — ~80 MB worst case. The child's pipe fills and the child stalls.

This is new: before this PR `read_all` touched `self.file` without a lock. The plan's "network slowness must never backpressure the execution's pipe reader" applies to a local reader too.

The lock is only needed for the cursor. Suggest snapshotting `file_bytes` (and the head) under the lock, releasing, then opening and reading outside it — `read_tail` is already bounded and fine either way.

### 3. `stop` can publish `Updated` after the watcher published `Finished` (low)

```
job.requested_stop = true
job.exec.request_stop()
self.publish(id, Updated)
```

`publish` contends on `publish_lock` with the watcher's `finish_job`. If the child dies immediately, `finish_job` can win the lock, emit `Finished` at revision 2, and then this `Updated` lands at revision 3 carrying a terminal state — so `Updated` is the last event for a terminal job, with the highest revision.

Harmless today because #1469 discards event payloads and re-polls, but it breaks the "one terminal event, last" property the `register` comment is careful to establish. Skip the `Updated` publish when the job is already terminal, or publish it before `request_stop()`.

### 4. A failed seed write hides output that was already captured (low)

`open_spill` sets `self.file_created = true` *before* `file.write_at(seed, position=0)`. If the seed write fails, `file_created` stays true and `file_bytes` stays 0, so `spill_path()` returns `Some` and `read_all` reads zero bytes — returning `""` rather than the head that is sitting in memory. The field comment says the path is retained "for inspecting partial output", but the read path can't reach the memory copy any more.

`failure` is set and the execution is killed, so this is narrow. Still, honest reporting would be to fall back to the head when `file_bytes == 0 && failure is Some(_)`, or to set `file_created` only after the seed succeeds and keep a separate `path_exists` flag if the path really needs retaining.

### 5. Smaller things

- `ShellExecution::output_bytes` falls back to `@utf8.encode(self.head()).length()` when no file was created. For a memory-only sink whose output passed `inline_cap`, that understates the real total (the head is capped). Fine for the no-spill-path case where the rest is dropped; worth a comment saying so, since the value is surfaced as "N B" in the UI.
- `generation: "memory-\{@env.now()}"` collides for two memory-only runtimes constructed in the same millisecond. Not persisted, so cosmetic, but a counter would cost nothing.
- `sync_job_directories` fsyncs `dir`, `dir/..` and `dir/../..` on **every** publish. Only the first publish in a generation needs the parent-directory syncs; subsequent ones only need `dir` (the rename target). Three opens + three fsyncs per lifecycle event is more than the plan's "match the session store's best-effort policy" implies.
- `@fs.tmpdir` failure is now a hard `fail` out of `build_tools` rather than a silent memory-only degrade. That is what the plan asked for ("not a silent production fallback") and the error text is actionable — but it changes the engine's startup failure mode, so it belongs in the PR description.
- `start` now calls `exec.background()`, which also clears `kill_when_full`. `spawn_exec` doesn't set that flag, so this is a no-op today; the state change `Running → Backgrounded` is the real effect. Worth a one-line comment on why `start` needs it, since `adopt`'s reason (the foreground waiter) doesn't apply.

Nothing here blocks. (1) and (2) are the two I'd fix before merge; (3) and (4) are cheap; the rest are notes.

issue.title: Plan durable background job logs and Desktop visibility
issue.body:
Background jobs previously exposed lifecycle mainly through prose, created output files only above an inline limit, and removed those files at session teardown. This plan defines files available before background handoff, durable lifecycle metadata and structured control, bounded host reads, and a Desktop Jobs panel.

The six-part implementation is complete. The document preserves the reviewed proposal and records final scope decisions and limits. Independent `openseek review` found no blocking/design issue; three citation nits were corrected. This slice changes no executable behavior; its GitHub checks pass.

Stack: #1465 → #1466 → #1467 → #1468 → #1469 → #1470. Review and merge in this order; aggregate validation and review disposition are recorded in #1470.

comment.body:
## Architecture review of this plan, read against the implementation in #1466 → #1468 → #1469

Verdict: **the architecture is solid and the stack should proceed.** This is a better-than-usual plan — it does the two things that decide whether an observability feature survives contact with reality, and it does them before any code:

- It names the **identity tuple** `(store, session, runtime_generation, job_id)` and explicitly forbids deriving a log path from a displayed `bg-N`. That single decision is why a restarted engine can't overwrite an old log and why two sessions with a `bg-1` stay separate. The implementation honours it end to end (`JobRecord.generation`, `valid_job_component`, `WrongRuntime`).
- It separates **committed** from **observed** bytes and insists on honest I/O failure instead of the previous swallow-and-advance. `sink.mbt` now refuses to advance `file_bytes` after a failed write and propagates the failure into a `capture_failed` terminal state. That is the right invariant and it is the one most implementations get wrong.

Other choices that hold up: scratch/log ownership split (`@fs.tmpdir` for snippets, session store for logs), relative artifact references resolved at serve time so archive/unarchive works, `owner.lock` as the ownership primitive rather than a PID, and byte cursors with explicit UTF-8 boundary handling. The phased gates were real gates — the integration fixture in `turn_finish.py` and the native host tests in `jobs_wbtest.mbt` actually test the things the gates named.

### Four places where the plan itself has gaps, each of which produced a finding downstream

1. **`stop` has no time bound and no escalation.** The plan says "keep stopping asynchronous relative to command intake" and "emit its final result when the tracked execution settles", but never says how long settling may take or what to do when it doesn't. It also states plainly that cancellation reaches only the direct child. The implementation took this literally: the engine emits `JobStopResult` only after the process is terminal, and #1468 wraps that reply in a 5 s timeout. A process that ignores SIGTERM therefore reports a *failed* stop while the stop is in fact still pending, with the 30-minute reaper as the only backstop. The contract needed a typed third outcome (`Stopping`/`StopTimedOut`) or a SIGTERM→SIGKILL escalation; details in #1468.

2. **Revision-based merging was specified, then quietly replaced.** The plan asks for "merge the snapshot with incoming events by identity and revision, so a late snapshot cannot roll back an exit". The implementation instead makes disk authoritative and re-lists on every `job_changed` plus a 1 Hz timer; the event's `job` payload is discarded and `JobRecord.revision` has no consumer anywhere in `desktop/`. The simpler scheme is defensible — but then `revision` and the event payload are dead protocol surface, and the freshness ordering now depends on poll timing rather than a stated rule. Pick one: use the revision, or drop it and shrink the event to an identity ping.

3. **The generation directory has no lifecycle.** "Age/quota cleanup can follow with an explicit policy" covers *log* growth. It doesn't cover the fact that a directory-per-runtime scheme creates a directory unconditionally — `spawn_foreground_retained` calls `prepare_output`, so any engine run that executes a single snippet allocates `jobs/<generation>/owner.lock` even when no job is ever adopted, and nothing ever removes an empty one. #1468 then readdir/stats every one of them on every list. That's a design hole, not an implementation nit.

4. **The headline UX affordance was dropped.** "Provide a persistent `Jobs · 2 running` entry in the conversation UI" is the sentence that makes this feature discoverable; the shipped UI puts the count inside the panel, so a running job is invisible unless the user already knows to open the tab. #1469's doc update acknowledges the change, but it converts the feature from ambient to opt-in. Worth an explicit decision rather than a footnote.

Also: the plan's own numbers drifted in implementation without being restated — 500 ms polling became 1 s, `tail -n 200` became `tail -n 100`. Harmless, but the plan is the spec people will read later.

None of the four is a reason to hold the stack. (1) is a real bug to fix in #1468, (3) wants a four-line prune, (2) and (4) are decisions to record. Per-PR reviews follow on #1466, #1468 and #1469.

issue.title: sync: Map.Store crashes on Windows with concurrent first-use (HashTrieMap.expand corrupts type hash pointer)

labels.name: NeedsInvestigation
labels.description: Someone must examine and confirm this is a valid issue and not a duplicate of an existing one.

labels.name: compiler/runtime
labels.description: Issues related to the Go compiler and/or runtime.

issue.body:
**Go version:** go1.26.6 windows/amd64
**OS:** Windows Server

When multiple goroutines concurrently call `sync.Map.Store` for the first time
on an empty map, the process crashes with:

    unexpected fault address 0xffffffffffffffff
    fatal error: fault

    aeshashbody()                         asm_amd64.s:1547
    runtime.typehash()                    alg.go:237
    runtime.nilinterhash()                alg.go:190
    internal/sync.(*HashTrieMap).expand() hashtriemap.go:169
    internal/sync.(*HashTrieMap).Swap()   hashtriemap.go:272
    sync.(*Map).Store()                   map.go:53

**Minimal reproducer:**
```go
package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "runtime"
    "sync"
)

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "runtime"
    "sync"
)

func main() {
    var m sync.Map
    m.Store("", struct{}{}) // initial element 
    m.Clear()               // reset to empty

    var wg sync.WaitGroup
    for i := 0; i < runtime.NumCPU()*4; i++ {
        wg.Add(1)
        go func(n int) {
            defer wg.Done()
            m.Store(fmt.Sprintf("key%d", n), n)
        }(i)
    }
    wg.Wait()
}


or with this 
root node of map is not allocated

func main() {
    var m sync.Map
    var wg sync.WaitGroup
    for i := 0; i < runtime.NumCPU()*4; i++ {
        wg.Add(1)
        go func(n int) {
            defer wg.Done()
            m.Store(fmt.Sprintf("key%d", n), n)
        }(i)
    }
    wg.Wait()
}

Root cause: HashTrieMap.expand() calls nilinterhash() to hash the key,
which reads the type descriptor's hash function pointer (alg.hash). Under
concurrent expansion of the same empty trie node, two goroutines race to write
children — one reads a partially-written type descriptor with a nil alg.hash
pointer → fault at 0xffffffffffffffff.

Expected: no crash — sync.Map is documented as safe for concurrent use.

Platform: Windows only. Linux misses the race window due to scheduler
differences.

comment.body:
I don't understand the description of the race. If two nodes are being expanded into, that's serialized by a lock on the node. For concurrent reads (and writes, walking down the tree) there's a commit point here: https://cs.opensource.google/go/go/+/master:src/internal/sync/hashtriemap.go;l=272;drc=603439a1c6f2d37c7f02e246342847056ed04c21

If the problem is whether the map is initialized, that's also fully serialized by a lock. Furthermore, goroutine can proceed until they observe `inited` set to 1, at which point it is safe to continue (seeing it set to one is the synchronization edge required).

I believe you that there's a bug here (I haven't reproduced it myself), but the explanation either needs to be more specific, or it's wrong. What's odd is that we also definitely have tests that swap on a fresh map with string keys (https://cs.opensource.google/go/go/+/master:src/internal/sync/hashtriemap_test.go), and these run on Windows. I don't think we've seen this crash pop up before. I'll note though that one difference from those tests seems to be that `sync.Map` is really a `sync.HashTrieMap[any, any]` which is relevant to this particular crash.

release.name: v0.1.0
release.body:
First published release. `npm install --global agentlive`

AgentLive broadcasts and replays coding-agent sessions — Claude Code, Codex, Kimi Code and OpenCode — from one stable URL, capturing structured events rather than screen video.

Try it without a server or an agent:

```sh
npm install --global agentlive
curl -LO https://raw.githubusercontent.com/bojieli/agentlive/main/docs/sample/agentlive-sample.agentlive
agentlive replay --source agentlive-sample.agentlive --interactive
```

**Pre-release.** `0.x` makes no production-readiness claim. 807 offline tests pass on Linux and macOS in CI, and the release was verified against the installed tarball, a container image, an HTTPS reverse proxy and headless Chrome. It has not had outside testers, and several limits are [measured and published](https://github.com/bojieli/agentlive/blob/main/docs/limits.md) rather than solved — see [implementation status](https://github.com/bojieli/agentlive/blob/main/IMPLEMENTATION_STATUS.md).

This artifact was published from a workstation and therefore carries **no provenance attestation**. Trusted publishing (OIDC) is now configured, so later releases will.

The full list of changes is in the [changelog](https://github.com/bojieli/agentlive/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md#010--2026-09-12).

issue.title: Prototype: Astro homepage and Chapter 1 reader
issue.body:
Following up on #1069, this draft adds an Astro prototype of the homepage and complete Chapter 1 for feedback on the reading experience before extending it to the rest of the book.

The prototype lives in `web-astro/` and reads the existing Markdown and figures directly. MkDocs, the book sources, and the PDF pipeline are unchanged; other chapter links open the existing site.

- Redesigned homepage with an animated agent loop.
- Chapter navigation, light/dark themes, text sizing, and focus mode.
- Browser-saved highlights and notes, with backup export/import.
- English, Simplified Chinese, and Traditional Chinese editions.

@bojieli, does this look like a direction you’d like me to continue? I’d appreciate feedback on the visual design and reading tools before expanding beyond Chapter 1.

### Screenshots

| Homepage | Chapter 1 |
| --- | --- |
| ![Astro homepage](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/whanyu1212/ai-agent-book/b0f1327b909142c6f38cf251b641a86fc9b01d2b/web-astro/review/homepage.png) | ![Chapter 1 reader](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/whanyu1212/ai-agent-book/b0f1327b909142c6f38cf251b641a86fc9b01d2b/web-astro/review/chapter-1.png) |

### Try locally

Requires Node.js 22.12 or newer:

```sh
cd web-astro
npm ci
npm run dev
```

Open `http://127.0.0.1:4321/` and use the header language switcher. No hosted preview is configured.

Validation: `npm run check`, `npm run build`, and all 12 tests pass. Browser checks covered language switching and note persistence across editions.

issue.title: fix(pedo/eval): let the timeout handler run in execute_test_case
issue.body:
`chapter5/permission-embedded-data-objects/pedo/eval/benchmark_spec_errors_v2.py` guards each generated test case with a 5-second `SIGALRM`, whose handler raises the module's own `TimeoutError`:

```python
class TimeoutError(Exception):
    pass

def _timeout_handler(signum, frame):
    raise TimeoutError("timed out")
```

But in `execute_test_case` the broad handler is listed first:

```python
    except (ValueError, PermissionError, Exception) as e:
        ...
        if expected == "reject":
            return {"status": "pass", "result": f"rejected via exception: {err[:80]}"}
        else:
            return {"status": "fail", "result": f"should allow but raised: {err[:80]}"}
    except TimeoutError:
        return {"status": "timeout", "error": "timed out"}
```

`TimeoutError` subclasses `Exception`, so the tuple already caught it and the timeout handler never ran. Two consequences:

- A generated function that hangs on an `expected: "reject"` case scored **pass** — `"rejected via exception: timed out"`. An infinite loop counted as a correct rejection.
- `print_spec_v2_results` computes its "Error" column as `sum(1 for t in tests if t["status"] in ("compile_error", "timeout"))`, so that column could only ever count compile errors.

Moving the handler above the broad one is enough. `benchmark_final_comprehensive.py`, in the same `eval/` directory, already has the working shape — `except (ValueError, PermissionError)` (no `Exception`) followed by `except TimeoutError` — which is what the ordering here was meant to be.

### Verification

`TimeoutError`, `_timeout_handler` and `execute_test_case` were lifted out of the file by line range (nothing retyped) and exercised on Linux with a real `SIGALRM`, using a test expression that sleeps past the 5-second alarm:

| case | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| times out, `expected: allow` | `{'status': 'fail', 'result': 'should allow but raised: timed out'}` | `{'status': 'timeout', 'error': 'timed out'}` |
| times out, `expected: reject` | `{'status': 'pass', 'result': 'rejected via exception: timed out'}` | `{'status': 'timeout', 'error': 'timed out'}` |
| returns `True`, `expected: allow` | `pass` | unchanged |
| returns a string, `expected: reject` | `pass` | unchanged |
| raises `PermissionError`, `expected: reject` | `pass` | unchanged |
| raises `PermissionError`, `expected: allow` | `fail` | unchanged |
