issue.title: fix: harden PKCS#11 session and token concurrency
issue.body:
## Summary

This PR hardens the PKCS#11 3.2 implementation for concurrent sessions, token-wide authorization, managed Windows integration, complete PIV algorithm coverage, and real-card validation.

## Review Fixes

- Remove global-session/per-session lock inversions during close, object enumeration, token info, and session creation.
- Protect Digest, Sign, Verify, Encrypt, and Decrypt state against concurrent cancellation and close.
- Reserve token-wide USER/SO and protected-management-key transitions atomically.
- Immediately zeroize and free session secret keys.
- Funnel management-key authentication through one cleanup path.
- Give combined-hash Sign and Verify independent hash contexts.
- Preserve stable reader slot IDs and queue PnP events correctly.
- Roll back USER login established by a failed PIN-managed composite login.
- Keep managed binding cleanup retryable and support rotated Windows card handles and per-context allocators.

## PIV Algorithms And Extensions

- Discover key and certificate metadata across all 24 PIV key slots.
- Support RSA-2048/3072/4096 generation, import, sign/verify, encrypt/decrypt.
- Support P-256, P-384, P-521, and secp256k1 generation, import, ECDSA sign/verify, and ECDH.
- Expose Ed25519 as `CKK_EC_EDWARDS` and X25519 as `CKK_EC_MONTGOMERY` with RFC 8410 parameters and their PIV operations.
- Expose the correct SM2 curve identity without pretending it is ECDSA.
- Support ML-DSA-65 and ML-KEM-768 generation/import and PKCS#11 3.2 operations.
- Expose firmware 6.0+ random generation through `C_GenerateRandom`.
- Add `C_CNK_GetPivMetadataDirectory()` for one-call, version-gated firmware 5.7+ PIV directory discovery. The API is read-only, call-local, two-stage, and retains no card or cache state.

`CKM_EDDSA` truthfully advertises card-side signing only. Host verification is implemented where the bundled provider supports it.

## Authentication And Object Model

- Implement token-wide USER/SO and context-specific PIN semantics.
- Support PIV PIN change, PUK unblock, protected management-key login, and explicit PIN-managed finalization.
- Support PIV certificates and data objects through PKCS#11 object APIs.
- Honor per-key PIN and touch policies for generated and imported keys.
- Keep PIV token objects non-copyable/non-destroyable while supporting secure session-secret lifecycle.

## Validation

- Ubuntu latest and macOS latest builds with unit tests.
- Windows Server ClangCL builds for the supported workflows.
- Standalone and real-card suites, including RSA, ECDSA, ECDH, P-521, Ed25519, X25519, ML-DSA, ML-KEM, PIN management, concurrency, and failure cleanup.
- Development-card Windows signing and ECDH tests pass after the batched metadata-directory optimization.

The current development card has an EC key in `9D`, so RSA key-exchange decrypt is intentionally a documented precondition failure until an RSA `9D` key is provisioned.

## Compatibility And Scope

- Managed mode is process-wide for one physical card and supports multiple contexts for that same card.
- Firmware gates are explicit: PIV 5.7+ metadata directory, PIV 6.0+ RNG, and APDU feature probes for algorithm extensions and legacy management-key algorithms.
- PIV metadata and operation transactions select PIV before dependent APDUs and complete the logical operation within one card transaction.

issue.title: feat: complete writable CanoKey Windows minidriver
issue.body:
## Summary

This PR turns the original read-only prototype into a usable Windows Smart Card Minidriver backed by `canokey-pkcs11`. It covers live card discovery, certificate enumeration, authentication, signing, key exchange, provisioning, and hardware-backed testing.

Windows-specific policy remains in the minidriver. PIV APDUs, cryptographic operation state, PIN-policy enforcement, and sensitive management-key handling remain in the statically linked PKCS#11 layer.

## Windows Surface

- Stable `cardid`/`CP_CARD_GUID`, `cardcf`, `mscp/cmapfile`, certificate files, file enumeration, and Base CSP/KSP read-only plumbing.
- Six stable Windows containers: indexes `0..5` map to PIV objects `9A`, `9C`, `9D`, `9E`, `82`, and `83`.
- RSA and NIST P-256/P-384/P-521 ECDSA signing through CAPI and CNG.
- RSA PKCS#1 and OAEP decryption for an RSA `9D` key-exchange container.
- P-256/P-384/P-521 ECDH with `BCRYPT_KDF_RAW_SECRET` byte ordering.
- RSA and NIST EC container generation and private-key import through `CardCreateContainerEx`.
- Certificate writes with live metadata refresh after card mutations.
- User PIN changes, PUK-based unblock/reset, protected management-key login, and per-key PIN/touch policies.

P-521 is supported when provisioned in one of the six mapped containers. A P-521 key in retired PIV slot `84` (object ID 7), as well as Ed25519, X25519, and PQC slots, remains PKCS#11-only by policy.

## Metadata And Cache

- The minidriver uses the read-only `C_CNK_GetPivMetadataDirectory()` extension when available. This sends the firmware 5.7+ metadata-directory APDU once per inventory refresh and avoids repeated `FindObjects` probes.
- Older firmware falls back to the existing `C_FindObjects` path.
- The first cache read reuses the acquisition snapshot; later cache and certificate reads refresh live metadata at most once per configured `RefreshWindow` (60 seconds by default). External PKCS#11/PIV changes therefore become visible within a bounded interval without rescanning the card for every Windows query.
- `cardcf` and `cmapfile` remain cache-coherency views. Live PKCS#11 metadata is authoritative, and container GUIDs remain stable across key replacement.

## PKCS#11 Integration

- Process-wide managed mode reuses the Windows-owned PC/SC context and card handle for one physical card.
- Each minidriver context owns one PKCS#11 session and closes it before finalization.
- Session lifecycle, slot events, signing, verification, encryption, decryption, ECDH derivation, key generation/import, and token random generation are covered by the integrated path.
- PKCS#11 supports all 24 PIV object IDs internally. Windows exposure remains limited to the six containers represented by the current CPDK contract.

## Post-Quantum Boundary

The bundled PKCS#11 3.2 interface supports ML-DSA-65 and ML-KEM-768, including generation/import and the corresponding PKCS#11 operations. Current Windows `cardmod.h` headers do not define compatible key types, properties, or callbacks, so the minidriver does not invent a private ABI or expose PQC containers to Base CSP/KSP.

## Verification

- Windows ClangCL Debug build and registry-only debug deployment passed.
- Windows Server 2022 / Visual Studio 2022 and Windows Server 2025 / Visual Studio 2026 builds passed for x86, x64, ARM64, and Arm64X in Debug and Release.
- PKCS#11 Ubuntu and macOS builds passed.
- PKCS#11 unit and ASan/UBSan suites passed with leak detection enabled.
- Real development-card CNG signing passed for RSA, P-256, P-384, and all discovered Windows containers.
- Real development-card ECDH raw-secret derivation passed for all discovered P-256/P-384 containers.
- The RSA decrypt test is skipped when the card has no RSA `9D` key-exchange container, as required by the documented slot policy.
- The standalone public-cache path was verified with cached metadata and certificate reads; managed mode continues to bypass it.

The metadata-directory and direct-handle discovery path reduced the focused Windows signing test from about 14 seconds to 7.9 seconds and the ECDH test from about 16 seconds to 5.7 seconds on the development card.

## Known Limitations

- This remains a development minidriver; release packaging, catalog signing, and INF installation need dedicated validation.
- ECDH supports `BCRYPT_KDF_RAW_SECRET` / `CKD_NULL` only.
- PIN-always ECDH creation is rejected because `C_DeriveKey` has no context-specific authentication boundary. Signing and RSA decryption have one-shot context-PIN retries.
- KSP cannot select PIV 9D by container name; RSA key-exchange provisioning requires an explicit slot-aware path.
- PUK changes and challenge/response PIN authentication are not exposed.
- Hardware-dependent tests require the corresponding keys and certificates to be provisioned on the development token.

issue.title: fix: harden PKCS#11 session and token concurrency
issue.body:
## Summary

This PR hardens the PKCS#11 3.2 implementation for concurrent sessions, token-wide authorization, managed Windows integration, complete PIV algorithm coverage, and real-card validation.

## Review Fixes

- Remove global-session/per-session lock inversions during close, object enumeration, token info, and session creation.
- Protect Digest, Sign, Verify, Encrypt, and Decrypt state against concurrent cancellation and close.
- Reserve token-wide USER/SO and protected-management-key transitions atomically.
- Immediately zeroize and free session secret keys.
- Funnel management-key authentication through one cleanup path.
- Give combined-hash Sign and Verify independent hash contexts.
- Preserve stable reader slot IDs and queue PnP events correctly.
- Roll back USER login established by a failed PIN-managed composite login.
- Keep managed binding cleanup retryable and support rotated Windows card handles and per-context allocators.

## PIV Algorithms And Extensions

- Discover key and certificate metadata across all 24 PIV key slots.
- Support RSA-2048/3072/4096 generation, import, sign/verify, encrypt/decrypt.
- Support P-256, P-384, P-521, and secp256k1 generation, import, ECDSA sign/verify, and ECDH.
- Expose Ed25519 as `CKK_EC_EDWARDS` and X25519 as `CKK_EC_MONTGOMERY` with RFC 8410 parameters and their PIV operations.
- Expose the correct SM2 curve identity without pretending it is ECDSA.
- Support ML-DSA-65 and ML-KEM-768 generation/import and PKCS#11 3.2 operations.
- Expose firmware 6.0+ random generation through `C_GenerateRandom`.
- Add `C_CNK_GetPivMetadataDirectory()` for one-call, version-gated firmware 5.7+ PIV directory discovery. The API is read-only, call-local, two-stage, and retains no card or cache state.

`CKM_EDDSA` truthfully advertises card-side signing only. Host verification is implemented where the bundled provider supports it.

## Authentication And Object Model

- Implement token-wide USER/SO and context-specific PIN semantics.
- Support PIV PIN change, PUK unblock, protected management-key login, and explicit PIN-managed finalization.
- Support PIV certificates and data objects through PKCS#11 object APIs.
- Honor per-key PIN and touch policies for generated and imported keys.
- Keep PIV token objects non-copyable/non-destroyable while supporting secure session-secret lifecycle.

## Validation

- Ubuntu latest and macOS latest builds with unit tests.
- Windows Server ClangCL builds for the supported workflows.
- Standalone and real-card suites, including RSA, ECDSA, ECDH, P-521, Ed25519, X25519, ML-DSA, ML-KEM, PIN management, concurrency, and failure cleanup.
- Development-card Windows signing and ECDH tests pass after the batched metadata-directory optimization.

The current development card has an EC key in `9D`, so RSA key-exchange decrypt is intentionally a documented precondition failure until an RSA `9D` key is provisioned.

## Compatibility And Scope

- Managed mode is process-wide for one physical card and supports multiple contexts for that same card.
- Firmware gates are explicit: PIV 5.7+ metadata directory, PIV 6.0+ RNG, and APDU feature probes for algorithm extensions and legacy management-key algorithms.
- PIV metadata and operation transactions select PIV before dependent APDUs and complete the logical operation within one card transaction.

issue.title: feat: complete writable CanoKey Windows minidriver
issue.body:
## Summary

This PR turns the original read-only prototype into a usable Windows Smart Card Minidriver backed by `canokey-pkcs11`. It covers live card discovery, certificate enumeration, authentication, signing, key exchange, provisioning, and hardware-backed testing.

Windows-specific policy remains in the minidriver. PIV APDUs, cryptographic operation state, PIN-policy enforcement, and sensitive management-key handling remain in the statically linked PKCS#11 layer.

## Windows Surface

- Stable `cardid`/`CP_CARD_GUID`, `cardcf`, `mscp/cmapfile`, certificate files, file enumeration, and Base CSP/KSP read-only plumbing.
- Six stable Windows containers: indexes `0..5` map to PIV objects `9A`, `9C`, `9D`, `9E`, `82`, and `83`.
- RSA and NIST P-256/P-384/P-521 ECDSA signing through CAPI and CNG.
- RSA PKCS#1 and OAEP decryption for an RSA `9D` key-exchange container.
- P-256/P-384/P-521 ECDH with `BCRYPT_KDF_RAW_SECRET` byte ordering.
- RSA and NIST EC container generation and private-key import through `CardCreateContainerEx`.
- Certificate writes with live metadata refresh after card mutations.
- User PIN changes, PUK-based unblock/reset, protected management-key login, and per-key PIN/touch policies.

P-521 is supported when provisioned in one of the six mapped containers. A P-521 key in retired PIV slot `84` (object ID 7), as well as Ed25519, X25519, and PQC slots, remains PKCS#11-only by policy.

## Metadata And Cache

- The minidriver uses the read-only `C_CNK_GetPivMetadataDirectory()` extension when available. This sends the firmware 5.7+ metadata-directory APDU once per inventory refresh and avoids repeated `FindObjects` probes.
- Older firmware falls back to the existing `C_FindObjects` path.
- The first cache read reuses the acquisition snapshot; later cache and certificate reads refresh live metadata at most once per configured `RefreshWindow` (60 seconds by default). External PKCS#11/PIV changes therefore become visible within a bounded interval without rescanning the card for every Windows query.
- `cardcf` and `cmapfile` remain cache-coherency views. Live PKCS#11 metadata is authoritative, and container GUIDs remain stable across key replacement.

## PKCS#11 Integration

- Process-wide managed mode reuses the Windows-owned PC/SC context and card handle for one physical card.
- Each minidriver context owns one PKCS#11 session and closes it before finalization.
- Session lifecycle, slot events, signing, verification, encryption, decryption, ECDH derivation, key generation/import, and token random generation are covered by the integrated path.
- PKCS#11 supports all 24 PIV object IDs internally. Windows exposure remains limited to the six containers represented by the current CPDK contract.

## Post-Quantum Boundary

The bundled PKCS#11 3.2 interface supports ML-DSA-65 and ML-KEM-768, including generation/import and the corresponding PKCS#11 operations. Current Windows `cardmod.h` headers do not define compatible key types, properties, or callbacks, so the minidriver does not invent a private ABI or expose PQC containers to Base CSP/KSP.

## Verification

- Windows ClangCL Debug build and registry-only debug deployment passed.
- Windows Server 2022 / Visual Studio 2022 and Windows Server 2025 / Visual Studio 2026 builds passed for x86, x64, ARM64, and Arm64X in Debug and Release.
- PKCS#11 Ubuntu and macOS builds passed.
- PKCS#11 unit and ASan/UBSan suites passed with leak detection enabled.
- Real development-card CNG signing passed for RSA, P-256, P-384, and all discovered Windows containers.
- Real development-card ECDH raw-secret derivation passed for all discovered P-256/P-384 containers.
- The RSA decrypt test is skipped when the card has no RSA `9D` key-exchange container, as required by the documented slot policy.
- The standalone public-cache path was verified with cached metadata and certificate reads; managed mode continues to bypass it.

The metadata-directory and direct-handle discovery path reduced the focused Windows signing test from about 14 seconds to 7.9 seconds and the ECDH test from about 16 seconds to 5.7 seconds on the development card.

## Known Limitations

- This remains a development minidriver; release packaging, catalog signing, and INF installation need dedicated validation.
- ECDH supports `BCRYPT_KDF_RAW_SECRET` / `CKD_NULL` only.
- PIN-always ECDH creation is rejected because `C_DeriveKey` has no context-specific authentication boundary. Signing and RSA decryption have one-shot context-PIN retries.
- KSP cannot select PIV 9D by container name; RSA key-exchange provisioning requires an explicit slot-aware path.
- PUK changes and challenge/response PIN authentication are not exposed.
- Hardware-dependent tests require the corresponding keys and certificates to be provisioned on the development token.

issue.body:
## Summary

This PR turns the original read-only prototype into a usable Windows Smart Card Minidriver backed by `canokey-pkcs11`. It covers live card discovery, certificate enumeration, authentication, signing, key exchange, provisioning, and hardware-backed testing.

Windows-specific policy remains in the minidriver. PIV APDUs, cryptographic operation state, PIN-policy enforcement, and sensitive management-key handling remain in the statically linked PKCS#11 layer.

## Windows Surface

- Stable `cardid`/`CP_CARD_GUID`, `cardcf`, `mscp/cmapfile`, certificate files, file enumeration, and Base CSP/KSP read-only plumbing.
- Six stable Windows containers: indexes `0..5` map to PIV objects `9A`, `9C`, `9D`, `9E`, `82`, and `83`.
- RSA and NIST P-256/P-384/P-521 ECDSA signing through CAPI and CNG.
- RSA PKCS#1 and OAEP decryption for an RSA `9D` key-exchange container.
- P-256/P-384/P-521 ECDH with `BCRYPT_KDF_RAW_SECRET` byte ordering.
- RSA and NIST EC container generation and private-key import through `CardCreateContainerEx`.
- Certificate writes with live metadata refresh after card mutations.
- User PIN changes, PUK-based unblock/reset, protected management-key login, and per-key PIN/touch policies.

P-521 is supported when provisioned in one of the six mapped containers. A P-521 key in retired PIV slot `84` (object ID 7), as well as Ed25519, X25519, and PQC slots, remains PKCS#11-only by policy.

## Metadata And Cache

- The minidriver uses the read-only `C_CNK_GetPivMetadataDirectory()` extension when available. This sends the firmware 5.7+ metadata-directory APDU once per inventory refresh and avoids repeated `FindObjects` probes.
- Older firmware falls back to the existing `C_FindObjects` path.
- The first cache read reuses the acquisition snapshot; later cache and certificate reads refresh live metadata at most once per configured `RefreshWindow` (60 seconds by default). External PKCS#11/PIV changes therefore become visible within a bounded interval without rescanning the card for every Windows query.
- `cardcf` and `cmapfile` remain cache-coherency views. Live PKCS#11 metadata is authoritative, and container GUIDs remain stable across key replacement.

## PKCS#11 Integration

- Process-wide managed mode reuses the Windows-owned PC/SC context and card handle for one physical card.
- Each minidriver context owns one PKCS#11 session and closes it before finalization.
- Session lifecycle, slot events, signing, verification, encryption, decryption, ECDH derivation, key generation/import, and token random generation are covered by the integrated path.
- PKCS#11 supports all 24 PIV object IDs internally. Windows exposure remains limited to the six containers represented by the current CPDK contract.

## Post-Quantum Boundary

The bundled PKCS#11 3.2 interface supports ML-DSA-65 and ML-KEM-768, including generation/import and the corresponding PKCS#11 operations. Current Windows `cardmod.h` headers do not define compatible key types, properties, or callbacks, so the minidriver does not invent a private ABI or expose PQC containers to Base CSP/KSP.

## Verification

- Windows ClangCL Debug build and registry-only debug deployment passed.
- Windows Server 2022 / Visual Studio 2022 and Windows Server 2025 / Visual Studio 2026 builds passed for x86, x64, ARM64, and Arm64X in Debug and Release.
- PKCS#11 Ubuntu and macOS builds passed.
- PKCS#11 unit and ASan/UBSan suites passed with leak detection enabled.
- Real development-card CNG signing passed for RSA, P-256, P-384, and all discovered Windows containers.
- Real development-card ECDH raw-secret derivation passed for all discovered P-256/P-384 containers.
- The RSA decrypt test is skipped when the card has no RSA `9D` key-exchange container, as required by the documented slot policy.
- The standalone public-cache path was verified with cached metadata and certificate reads; managed mode continues to bypass it.

The metadata-directory and direct-handle discovery path reduced the focused Windows signing test from about 14 seconds to 7.9 seconds and the ECDH test from about 16 seconds to 5.7 seconds on the development card.

## Known Limitations

- This remains a development minidriver; release packaging, catalog signing, and INF installation need dedicated validation.
- ECDH supports `BCRYPT_KDF_RAW_SECRET` / `CKD_NULL` only.
- PIN-always ECDH creation is rejected because `C_DeriveKey` has no context-specific authentication boundary. Signing and RSA decryption have one-shot context-PIN retries.
- KSP cannot select PIV 9D by container name; RSA key-exchange provisioning requires an explicit slot-aware path.
- PUK changes and challenge/response PIN authentication are not exposed.
- Hardware-dependent tests require the corresponding keys and certificates to be provisioned on the development token.

issue.title: feat: complete writable CanoKey Windows minidriver
issue.body:
## Summary

This PR turns the original read-only prototype into a usable Windows Smart Card Minidriver backed by `canokey-pkcs11`. It covers live card discovery, certificate enumeration, authentication, signing, key exchange, provisioning, and hardware-backed testing.

Windows-specific policy remains in the minidriver. PIV APDUs, cryptographic operation state, PIN-policy enforcement, and sensitive management-key handling remain in the statically linked PKCS#11 layer.

## Windows Surface

- Stable `cardid`/`CP_CARD_GUID`, `cardcf`, `mscp/cmapfile`, certificate files, file enumeration, and Base CSP/KSP read-only plumbing.
- Six stable Windows containers: indexes `0..5` map to PIV objects `9A`, `9C`, `9D`, `9E`, `82`, and `83`.
- RSA and NIST P-256/P-384/P-521 ECDSA signing through CAPI and CNG.
- RSA PKCS#1 and OAEP decryption for an RSA `9D` key-exchange container.
- P-256/P-384/P-521 ECDH with `BCRYPT_KDF_RAW_SECRET` byte ordering.
- RSA and NIST EC container generation and private-key import through `CardCreateContainerEx`.
- Certificate writes with live metadata refresh after card mutations.
- User PIN changes, PUK-based unblock/reset, protected management-key login, and per-key PIN/touch policies.

P-521 is supported when provisioned in one of the six mapped containers. A P-521 key in retired PIV slot `84` (object ID 7), as well as Ed25519, X25519, and PQC slots, remains PKCS#11-only by policy.

## Metadata And Cache

- The minidriver uses the read-only `C_CNK_GetPivMetadataDirectory()` extension when available. This sends the firmware 5.7+ metadata-directory APDU once per inventory refresh and avoids repeated `FindObjects` probes.
- Older firmware falls back to the existing `C_FindObjects` path.
- The first cache read reuses the acquisition snapshot; later cache and certificate reads refresh live metadata at most once per configured `RefreshWindow` (60 seconds by default). External PKCS#11/PIV changes therefore become visible within a bounded interval without rescanning the card for every Windows query.
- `cardcf` and `cmapfile` remain cache-coherency views. Live PKCS#11 metadata is authoritative, and container GUIDs remain stable across key replacement.

## PKCS#11 Integration

- Process-wide managed mode reuses the Windows-owned PC/SC context and card handle for one physical card.
- Each minidriver context owns one PKCS#11 session and closes it before finalization.
- Session lifecycle, slot events, signing, verification, encryption, decryption, ECDH derivation, key generation/import, and token random generation are covered by the integrated path.
- PKCS#11 supports all 24 PIV object IDs internally. Windows exposure remains limited to the six containers represented by the current CPDK contract.

## Post-Quantum Boundary

The bundled PKCS#11 3.2 interface supports ML-DSA-65 and ML-KEM-768, including generation/import and the corresponding PKCS#11 operations. Current Windows `cardmod.h` headers do not define compatible key types, properties, or callbacks, so the minidriver does not invent a private ABI or expose PQC containers to Base CSP/KSP.

## Verification

- Windows ClangCL Debug build and registry-only debug deployment passed.
- Windows Server 2022 / Visual Studio 2022 and Windows Server 2025 / Visual Studio 2026 builds passed for x86, x64, ARM64, and Arm64X in Debug and Release.
- PKCS#11 Ubuntu and macOS builds passed.
- PKCS#11 unit and ASan/UBSan suites passed with leak detection enabled.
- Real development-card CNG signing passed for RSA, P-256, P-384, and all discovered Windows containers.
- Real development-card ECDH raw-secret derivation passed for all discovered P-256/P-384 containers.
- The RSA decrypt test is skipped when the card has no RSA `9D` key-exchange container, as required by the documented slot policy.
- The standalone public-cache path was verified with cached metadata and certificate reads; managed mode continues to bypass it.

The metadata-directory and direct-handle discovery path reduced the focused Windows signing test from about 14 seconds to 7.9 seconds and the ECDH test from about 16 seconds to 5.7 seconds on the development card.

## Known Limitations

- This remains a development minidriver; release packaging, catalog signing, and INF installation need dedicated validation.
- ECDH supports `BCRYPT_KDF_RAW_SECRET` / `CKD_NULL` only.
- PIN-always ECDH creation is rejected because `C_DeriveKey` has no context-specific authentication boundary. Signing and RSA decryption have one-shot context-PIN retries.
- KSP cannot select PIV 9D by container name; RSA key-exchange provisioning requires an explicit slot-aware path.
- PUK changes and challenge/response PIN authentication are not exposed.
- Hardware-dependent tests require the corresponding keys and certificates to be provisioned on the development token.

issue.title: [Bugfix][SM120] Enable CUTLASS grouped GEMM (MoE) for SM_120/SM_121 consumer Blackwell

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

issue.body:
## Summary

Fixes two bugs that silently disabled the CUTLASS FP8 grouped GEMM path for all SM_120/SM_121 hardware (RTX 5090/5080/5070, DGX Spark GB10), causing every MoE expert dispatch to fall back to the Triton backend.

Fixes #43507.

---

## What changed

### Bug 1 — Python gate (`vllm/_custom_ops.py`)

\`\`\`python
# Before (wrong):
if cuda_device_capability < 90 or cuda_device_capability >= 110:
    return False

# After (correct):
if cuda_device_capability < 90 or cuda_device_capability >= 130:
    return False
\`\`\`

\`cuda_device_capability\` is an integer: \`121 >= 110\` is \`True\`, so this gate always returned \`False\` for SM121, routing every call through Triton. \`>= 130\` is correct — it reserves the exit clause for genuinely unsupported future architectures beyond SM12x.

### Bug 2 — Missing SM120 grouped GEMM kernel

Added \`csrc/libtorch_stable/quantization/w8a8/cutlass/moe/grouped_mm_c3x_sm120.cu\`, the SM120 analog of \`grouped_mm_c3x_sm100.cu\`. Configuration:

- **Schedule**: \`KernelPtrArrayTmaWarpSpecializedCooperativeSm120<2>\` (cooperative, 4×2 UMMA atom layout)
- **Tile shape**: \`128×128×128\` (same as SM100 default)
- **Cluster shape**: \`1×1×1\` (no programmatic multicast on consumer Blackwell)
- **Epilogue**: \`EpilogueScheduleAuto\` (auto-selects per-tensor/per-token scaling in the epilogue, matching the FP8-Dynamic quantization scheme)
- **Arch tag**: \`Sm120\` (runs on SM_121 as well per CUDA arch compatibility)

Added dispatch block in \`scaled_mm_entry.cu\` for \`version_num >= 120 && version_num < 130\`.
Added the \`.cu\` file to the existing SM12x build block in \`CMakeLists.txt\` (under \`FP4_ARCHS\`, which already sets \`ENABLE_CUTLASS_MOE_SM120=1\`).

---

## CUTLASS dependency

\`KernelPtrArrayTmaWarpSpecializedCooperativeSm120<2>\` requires the \`MainloopSm120ArrayTmaWarpSpecialized\` collective specialization, which is **not yet in CUTLASS 4.5**. It has been contributed upstream via [NVIDIA/cutlass#3280](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cutlass/pull/3280) (currently in review). This vLLM PR will compile correctly once vLLM's pinned CUTLASS revision includes that change.

---

## Why not duplicate

- \`gh pr list --repo vllm-project/vllm --state open --search "SM121 cuda_device_capability"\` — no results
- \`gh pr list --repo vllm-project/vllm --state open --search "grouped_mm_c3x_sm120"\` — no results
- Existing SM120 PRs (#43477, #41738, #42856) address different subsystems (FlashInfer, NVFP4, sparse-MLA), not the FP8 grouped GEMM path

---

## Hardware validation

Validated on **SM_121 hardware** (NVIDIA DGX Spark, GB10, 128 GB LPDDR5X unified memory):

- **Container**: vLLM source build, CUDA 13.0.2, \`TORCH_CUDA_ARCH_LIST=12.0a;12.1a;12.1+PTX\`, patched CUTLASS (includes NVIDIA/cutlass#3280 changes)
- **Model**: \`RedHatAI/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-FP8-Dynamic\` (Gemma 4 MoE, 26B total / 4B active, FP8-Dynamic quantization)

**Result**: SM120 CUTLASS grouped GEMM collective activates and produces correct outputs. Previously fell back to Triton for every MoE dispatch.

### Throughput comparison (wall-clock, single-stream, MTP speculative decoding, 3 iterations)

| Prompt size | Baseline (Triton fallback) | This fix (SM120 CUTLASS) | Delta |
|---|---|---|---|
| Short (128 tok output) | 76.3 tok/s | 81.9 tok/s | **+7.3%** |
| Medium (512 tok output) | 89.8 tok/s | 89.8 tok/s | ≈0% (within noise) |
| Long (1024 tok output) | 87.6 tok/s | 85.5 tok/s | -2.4% (within noise) |

Short-sequence improvement is the clearest signal (decode-dominated, grouped GEMM runs every forward pass). Medium/long variance is dominated by speculative decoding accept-rate noise over 3 iterations.

---

## Update — rebased onto main (2026-06-20)

Rebased cleanly onto current \`main\` (post-v0.23.0). No conflicts. The two changed hunks (\`_custom_ops.py\` gate fix and \`scaled_mm_entry.cu\` dispatch block) applied without modification.

**Relevant context from v0.23.0**: #40923 (Marlin MoE SM 12.x native cubins) and #42027 (gelu_tanh CUTLASS/WNA16 MoE) both landed in v0.23.0, covering adjacent SM12x infrastructure. This PR addresses the remaining gap: the FP8 grouped GEMM Python gate and the missing SM120 CUTLASS kernel.

---

## AI assistance disclosure

This fix was developed with Claude (Anthropic) AI assistance, including root cause analysis of the gate condition, derivation of the SM120 kernel configuration from the SM100 analog, and iterative compile debugging (four full Docker builds on real SM_121 hardware). All changed lines have been reviewed by the human submitter (Tyler Merritt). Build and inference validation ran on physical DGX Spark hardware.

Related CUTLASS upstream PR: [NVIDIA/cutlass#3280](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cutlass/pull/3280)

Fixed in `f116174`. When PC/SC rollback fails, initialization now records both PC/SC and backend cleanup as pending, preserving the required PC/SC-before-backend retry order.

Completed in `47c80dc`. CardDeleteContext now retries pending managed cleanup by re-entering C_Initialize/C_Finalize before releasing the CARD_DATA context, so a failed acquire can make progress without an unrelated future acquisition.
Addressed in `89e88f4`. Windows provisioning rejects `NewKeyPinPolicy=3` until a per-operation context-PIN bridge exists.
Fixed in `a52675d`. Known `ROLE_ADMIN` is rejected with `SCARD_W_SECURITY_VIOLATION`; only unknown PIN identifiers return `SCARD_E_INVALID_PARAMETER`.
Fixed in `a52675d`. `CardAcquireContext` now holds the exclusive context lock across managed binding, PKCS#11 initialization, session creation, and context publication.

The managed PKCS#11 backend already reference-counts `C_Initialize`/`C_Finalize` for each active `CARD_DATA`; acquisition and deletion are serialized by the context lock. A second compatible context therefore does not finalize the first context.
Fixed in `a52675d`. The key-generation script now requires the explicit PIN-protected-management-key flow and authenticates USER before invoking container creation.

Fixed in `ee27bae`. Initialization rollback now preserves backend mutex state when a destroy callback fails; each mutex has an independent initialized marker so a later retry only invokes callbacks for resources that still exist.
Fixed in `ee27bae`. Finalization returns before resetting the allocator, mode, or backend descriptors when cleanup fails, and `C_Initialize` can retry the retained backend cleanup.
Fixed in 13b2c82. CardCreateContainer and CardCreateContainerEx require ROLE_USER, and CardCreateContainerEx rejects ROLE_ADMIN explicitly, matching the documented Windows provisioning policy.

> There is no pointer value p.

The issue here is with pointers. Let's say that the pointer value is `p`. `p` is a single memory word. The pointer also points to other memory. I am calling that memory `*p` because that is it is accessed. The values of `p` (the pointer itself) and `*p` (the memory that the pointer points to) are changed by different instructions at different times, and without explicit synchronization different CPUs can fail to agree on the order in which `p` and `*p` are written.

comment.body: That's now how modern processors work. Returning a pointer does not imply that a different processor will see the data to which that pointers points. ```

### What did you do?

### What version of Go are you using?

go version go1.25.x

### Does this issue reproduce with the latest release?

Yes.

### What did you do?

The built-in Go fuzzer currently supports stopping after a fixed duration using `-fuzztime`.

In practice, during long-running fuzzing campaigns, coverage often reaches a plateau long before the configured timeout expires.

For example:

- coverage grows during the first several minutes;
- afterwards no new interesting inputs or coverage are found for tens of minutes or even hours;
- the fuzzer continues consuming CPU until `-fuzztime` expires.

This is especially noticeable in CI and Kubernetes-based fuzzing infrastructure where CPU time is limited.

This is not a new fuzzing concept. AFL++ provides a similar mechanism through the `AFL_EXIT_ON_TIME` environment variable:

> `AFL_EXIT_ON_TIME` causes afl-fuzz to terminate if no new paths were found within a specified period of time (in seconds). May be convenient for some types of automated jobs.

Reference:
https://aflplus.plus/docs/env_variables/#settings-for-afl-fuzz

### What did you expect to see?

It would be useful to have a stopping condition based on coverage progress rather than only elapsed time.

For example:

```text
go test -fuzz=FuzzFoo -fuzzplateau=10m
```

where the fuzzer exits if no new coverage has been discovered for 10 minutes.

Alternatively, exposing coverage progress or "new coverage discovered" events through an API or statistics would allow external orchestrators to implement their own stopping policy without introducing a new command-line flag.

### What did you see instead?

Currently the only built-in stopping condition is elapsed time (`-fuzztime`), so fuzzing continues even when coverage has not changed for a long period.

### What did you see happen?

The built-in Go fuzzer currently supports stopping only after a fixed duration using `-fuzztime`.

In practice, coverage often reaches a plateau long before the configured timeout expires. After that point, the fuzzer may continue running for tens of minutes or even hours without discovering new coverage while continuing to consume CPU resources.

This is especially noticeable in CI pipelines and Kubernetes-based fuzzing infrastructure where compute resources are limited.

A similar concept already exists in AFL++ through the `AFL_EXIT_ON_TIME` environment variable:

> `AFL_EXIT_ON_TIME` causes afl-fuzz to terminate if no new paths were found within a specified period of time (in seconds). May be convenient for some types of automated jobs.

Reference:
https://aflplus.plus/docs/env_variables/#settings-for-afl-fuzz

### What did you expect to see?

It would be useful to provide a way to stop fuzzing after no new coverage has been discovered for a configurable period of time.

For example:

```text
go test -fuzz=FuzzFoo -fuzzplateau=10m
```

Alternatively, exposing coverage progress or notifications about newly discovered coverage would allow external tools to implement the same policy without introducing a dedicated command-line flag.

issue.title: proposal: sum types as a non-interface union type

milestone.description:
Proposals that are pending (not yet accepted/rejected).
See https://go.dev/s/proposal-process.

issue.body:
This is an issue to discuss yet another form of sum type to Go. This is not a full proposal, and not a language change that I expect will be adopted in the near future. I am filing this issue as a point of reference to discuss this particular approach.

A sum type, tagged union, variant, variant record, choice type, discriminated union, disjoint union, or coproduct is a type which can hold a value of one of a fixed set of types. (Thanks [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tagged_union) for the list.) Rust calls these enums, which means that when someone says Go should support "enums" they might be asking for a C-style enumeration of integers or a Rust-style enumeration of types.

I posit that most people who want this feature in Go are looking for something along the lines of a Rust enum: https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch06-01-defining-an-enum.html

To guide what follows, I'm going to also propose a few motivating examples which any design should support well.

1. A Direction type holding one of four cardinal directions: North, South, East, and West.
2. A Maybe type which either holds a value of some type or nothing.
3. An IP type holding either a `[4]byte` IPv4 address or a `[16]byte` IPv6 address.

### A digression: Can we just use interfaces?

Many proposals for sum types in Go aim to extend interface types to cover this case. Since interfaces already support listing a set of type variants for use in type constraints, it's tempting to say that we could just permit something like this:

```go
type IPv4 [4]byte
type IPv6 [16]byte
type IP interface { IPv4 | IPv6 }
```

I think that while this is tempting, it's the wrong approach.

First, this doesn't support the Direction case well at all. Do we need to define types for North/South/East/West?

The zero value of an interface is nil. Do we require that sum types all have an additional zero-value case that users need to handle, even if they don't actually want a zero value?

You need to define top-level symbols (types) for every variant. That's not so bad in the IPv4/IPv6 case, but it's not difficult to imagine types where this is a problem.

The syntax doesn't scale to lots of variants.

I just don't like this approach; I think it's trying to force two similar but different concepts (interfaces and sum types) together in a way that doesn't work well.

### Digression over, proposal

Go structs are a "product type" in the terminology of type theory. Let's define a sum type using similar syntax to our product types. We'll call a sum type a "union" in the following, but I'm not wedded to the name:

```go
type Direction union {
	North, South, East, West atom
}

type Maybe[T any] union {
	Unset atom
	Set   T
}

type IP union {
	IPv4 [4]byte
	IPv6 [16]byte
}
```

This is exactly the struct syntax, except instead of fields we'll have "variants".

I've also introduced a new predeclared type here, called "atom". (Again, I'm not wedded to the name. "unit" might also work.) An atom is a `struct{}`, just like an any is an `interface{}`:

```
type atom = struct{}
```

We use atoms to indicate variants that have no data. The new identifier is introduced because it looks weird and hacky to write `struct{}` all over the place and `struct{}{}` is worse.

A value of a union type always contains exactly one of the type variants. The zero value of a union is the zero value of the first variant, so for our above examples: North, Unset, and 0.0.0.0. Yes, this means the order of the variants in the declaration is important. So is the order of values if you use iota to define an enum with something like `const ( North = Direction(iota); South; East; West )`. It's fine.

#### Selectors on variant types: T.Variant

Variants of a union may be named with a selector expression on the type like `T.Variant`. This is going to be ambiguous with method selectors, but selectors are already ambiguous on fields and methods so I think that's fine.

For a variant of type atom, the selector expression evaluates to a value of the union type with that variant. So for example:

```go
d := Direction.North // d is a Direction with variant North

if d == Direction.North {
}

switch d {
case Direction.North:
case Direction.South:
case Direction.East:
case Direction.West:
}
```

For a non-atom variant, evaluating the selector expression is an error.

```go
m = Maybe[int].Set // error: evaluating non-atom union selector
```

#### Selectors on variant values: v.Variant

As with structs, a selector expression may be used on a value of a union type.

In an assignment statement, a selector expression sets the value of a union to that variant.

```go
// Set m to the "Set" variant with value 42.
var m Maybe[int]
m.Set = 42
m.Unset = atom{} // but m = Maybe.Unset is probably clearer

// Set ip to 127.0.0.1
var ip IP
IP.IPv4 = [4]byte{127, 0, 0, 1}
```

When evaluated, a selector expression on a non-atom variant yields two values: The value of the variant and an untyped bool indicating whether that is the currently set variant.

A selector expression on an atom variant yields only one value: An untyped bool indicating whether that is the currently set variant.

```go
var m Maybe[int]

if v, ok := m.Set; ok {
	// v is the value of the Maybe
}

if m.Unset {
	// the Maybe is not set
}
```

To avoid accidents, it is an error to assign a atom variant to two values, or a non-atom variant to a single value.

```go
v := m.Set       // error: this must be v, ok := m.Set
v, ok := m.Unset // error: this must be just v := m.Unset
```

#### Composite literals

Composite literals of union type must contain at most one keyed element. They may not contain elements without a key.

```go
d := Direction{North: atom{}} // same as d := Direction.North
m := Maybe[int]{Set: 42}

m := Maybe[int]{42} // error: elements must be keyed
ip := IP{IPv4: [4]byte{...}, IPv6: [16]byte{...}} // error: too many elements
```

#### Union switches

We add a new form of switch statement, the "union switch". This behaves much the same as a type switch, but over the variants of a union.

```
switch d.(union) {
case North:
case South:
case East:
case West:
}

var m Maybe[int]
switch v := m.(union) {
case Unset:
	// v is not in scope here.
case Set:
	// v has type int
}
```

Union switches must be exhaustive. You can include a default case if you want a non-exhaustive switch.

```
// Error: Failed to handle all cases.
switch d.(union) {
case North:
}

// This is fine.
switch d.(union) {
case North:
default:
}
```

#### Addressability

Union variants are not addressable. (But you can put a pointer to something addressable in a variant if you want.)

#### Comparability

Unions are comparable if all their variants are comparable.

### FAQ

Q: Do we need this atom type? We could just omit the type from the union definition for the "has no value case".

That works, but it looks a lot like an embedded type:

```go
type Maybe[T any] union {
	Unset // looks like an embedded Unset type
	Set T
}
```

Also, atoms are pretty nice for non-union uses, like `map[string]atom` or `chan atom`.

Q: How about just `Direction{North}`? `Direction{North: atom{}}` is weird.

This works, but `Direction{North}` looks like an unkeyed composite literal and we're going to interpret North as a key. Maybe that's okay. But you can just write `Direction.North`, which is simpler.

Q: How about `m := Maybe[int].Set(42)`, as opposed to `Maybe[int]{Set: 42}`?

I considered extending type conversion syntax for creating a union variant in this fashion. I don't like it, though, because it makes the variant look like a type. One of my notions in this design is that while in programming language theory each variant may be a type, expressing those types in the Go type system just adds confusion.

Q: What if I write `x := someMaybe.Set`?

Evaluating a selector for a non-atom variant always yields two values, and it is an error to assign the selector to a single value. This isn't like map access where the second ", ok" value is optional.

If we allowed a selector like this to evaluate to a single value, we'd have two choices:

It could evaluate to the value of the variant, and panic if that isn't the current variant. People hate panics. If you're really certain of the currently selected variant, you can write `x, _ := someMaybe.Set` and discard the bool.

Alternatively, it could evaluate to a bool indicating whether the variant is selected, so you could write `if someMaybe.Set { … }`. However, this invites incredibly confusing errors if the value of the variant is a bool:

```go
m := Maybe[bool]{Set: false}
if m.Set {
	// This executes, because Set is the selected variant,
	// even though the *value* of set if false...
}
```

So, no, selectors on non-atom variants always yield two values.

Q: I really don't want adding a new variant to my exported union to be a breaking API change, but the exhaustive type switch requirement makes it one.

Add a blank case to your union:

```go
type Extendable union {
	_ atom // default case

	North, South, East, West
	// new directions to be added as science discovers them
}
```

Now type switches all need to contain a "default:" clause. Also, your zero value is now distinct from any of the defined variants.

Q: Can I have methods on a union type?

Of course, it's just a type.

```go
type IP union {
	IPv4 [4]byte
	IPv6 [16]byte
}

func (ip IP) String() string { ... }
```

Q: Do you think we should add this (or some form of sum type)?

I don't know.

The argument in favor is that this is one of the most common language feature requests (usually phrased as a request for "enums", which may indicate that this often comes from frustrated Rust programmers).  Some form of union or sum type is a conventional language feature, and it's perhaps a bit strange that Go doesn't have one. I think the above design also fits fairly nicely into the language; I don't think we'd have regretted it if it had been present in Go 1.0.

issue.title: cmd/link: linkerFlagSupported drops trailing arguments from multi-word CC when probing linker flags

labels.name: NeedsInvestigation
labels.description: Someone must examine and confirm this is a valid issue and not a duplicate of an existing one.

labels.name: compiler/runtime
labels.description: Issues related to the Go compiler and/or runtime.

issue.body:
### Go version

go version go1.28-devel_2117d7cf9f Wed Aug 26 21:30:33 2026 -0700 linux/ppc64le

### Output of `go env` in your module/workspace:

```shell
GOARCH='ppc64le'
GOHOSTARCH='ppc64le'
GOOS='linux'
CGO_ENABLED='1'
CC='gcc'
CXX='g++'
GOPPC64='power10'
GOVERSION='go1.28-devel_2117d7cf9f Wed Aug 26 21:30:33 2026 -0700'
GOEXPERIMENT=''
GOFLAGS=''
GOTOOLCHAIN='local'
clang version 21.1.8 (Red Hat, Inc. 21.1.8-2.el9)
Target: ppc64le-redhat-linux-gnu
```

### What did you do?

**_This was first observed in the Go CI/CD builder on ppc64le POWER10, and I then reproduced it locally on a POWER10 system using current Go master._** [Link](https://ci.chromium.org/ui/p/golang/builders/ci/gotip-linux-ppc64le_power10/b8672343691901487009/overview)

On a ppc64le POWER10 system, I checked out current Go master and ran the full test suite with `GOPPC64=power10`.

The failure reproduces locally in:

```text
TestScript/cgo_path_space_quote
```

I then reproduced the test directly with:

```bash
GOPPC64=power10 ./bin/go test cmd/go \
    -run='TestScript/cgo_path_space_quote' \
    -count=1 -v
```

The test sets `CC` to a wrapper executable whose path contains spaces, followed by `clang`, for example:

```text
"/tmp/.../program files/which cc" clang
```

I also verified independently that the compiler supports the Power10 flag:

```bash
clang -m64 -mcpu=power10 /tmp/p10.c -o /tmp/p10
echo $?
```

which returns:

```text
0
```


### What did you see happen?

`TestScript/cgo_path_space_quote` fails during `go run .` with:

```text
# test
.../pkg/tool/linux_ppc64le/link: The external toolchain does not support -mcpu=power10. This is required to externally link GOPPC64 >= power10
```

The test itself successfully preserves the multi-word `CC` value:

```text
"/tmp/.../program files/which cc" clang
```

To inspect the Power10 capability probe, I temporarily instrumented `linkerFlagSupported`. The failing probe executed:

```text
DEBUG linkerFlagSupported: flag="-mcpu=power10"
cmd=["/tmp/.../program files/which cc"
     "-m64"
     "-o" "..."
     "-mcpu=power10"
     ".../trivial.c"]
```

The trailing `clang` argument from `CC` is missing.

The corresponding call site passes only `argv[0]`:

```go
linkerFlagSupported(ctxt.Arch, argv[0], "", "-mcpu=power10")
```

while `linkerFlagSupported` later executes:

```go
exec.Command(linker, flags...)
```

As a result, the wrapper is invoked without the trailing compiler argument, causing the flag probe to return false.

The compiler itself does support the flag:

```text
$ clang -m64 -mcpu=power10 /tmp/p10.c -o /tmp/p10
$ echo $?
0
```


### What did you expect to see?

`TestScript/cgo_path_space_quote` should pass when `CC` contains a quoted executable path followed by additional arguments.

In this case, the external linker command is effectively:

```text
"/tmp/.../program files/which cc" clang
```

Flag probing should preserve the complete external linker command, including the trailing `clang` argument.

The Power10 capability probe should therefore invoke the wrapper with `clang` before `-mcpu=power10`, detect that the compiler supports the flag, and allow `go run .` to complete successfully.

comment.body: There is a problem with my earlier suggestion of `type S select { ... }`. In general a type can appear at the start of a statement. Using one of these sum types would start with `select { ... }`. But of course that is also how a `select` statement starts. So we would have a parsing ambiguity. It's not too bad for a non-empty `select` as for that the next token must be the keyword `case` or the keyword `default`. But `select{}` would be both a valid statement and a valid sum type. I believe this problem can be resolved, but it does exist.

comment.body:
It's worth noting that because individual elements of a sum types are not addressable, you can't call pointer methods on them. That is, given something like

```Go
type Locker union {
    mu   sync.Mutex
    rwmu sync.RWMutex
}

var lock Locker
```

you can't write `lock.mu.Lock()`. That would require `lock.mu` to be addressable, but in general it can't be. Of course it would be permitted to write

```Go
type Locker union
    mu *sync.Mutex
    rwmu *sync.RWMutex
}

var lock Locker
```

and then write `lock.mu.Lock()`. But the zero value of this type would not be useful.

### Proposal Details

<details>

<summary>Filled out language-change form, collapsed</summary>

**Would you consider yourself a novice, intermediate, or experienced Go programmer?**

Experienced.

**What other languages do you have experience with?**

Numerous; relevantly here, Haskell, Typescript, a wide suite of dynamically-typed languages.

**Would this change make Go easier or harder to learn, and why?**

Minimally harder.

**Has this idea, or one like it, been proposed before? If so, how does this proposal differ?**

Several sum type proposals. I have read them all. This one differs in that rather than being a brand new feature it is a minor extension of an existing one.

**Who does this proposal help, and why?**

It does provide a blessed and cleaned-up mechanism for handling situations in the expression problem when some particular bit of code needs to focus on adding operations in external packages.

**What is the proposed change? Please describe as precisely as possible the change to the language. What would change in the language spec? Please also describe the change informally, as in a class teaching Go.**

See all that below.

**Is this change backward compatible? Breaking the Go 1 compatibility guarantee is a large cost and requires a large benefit.**

Yes.

**Show example code before and after the change.**

See below.

**What is the cost of this proposal? (Every language change has a cost).**

Fairly minimal.

**How many tools (such as vet, gopls, gofmt, goimports, etc.) would be affected?**

There would be some sort of new keyword that would need to be added or some other syntax change. However it is nearly identical to existing constructs; many such tools could just alias the new keyword as a new spelling of `interface` and continue providing the same services as before.

**What is the compile time cost?**

Verifying that an embedding chain (to coin a term) doesn't terminate in a sum-type interface is a negligible cost.

**What is the run time cost?**

Already paid in existing techniques.

**Can you describe a possible implementation?**

See below.

**Do you have a prototype? (This is not required.) How would the language spec change? Orthogonality: how does this change interact or overlap with existing features?**

See below.

**Is the goal of this change a performance improvement? Does this affect error handling? Is this about generics?**

No, no, and no.

</details>

# Overview

In my opinion, a lot of sum type discussion on the internet (not necessarily any given proposal here) has taken it as read that in order to have "sum types", they must look and act exactly as they do in other languages, or they aren't "real" sum types.

But I think far more important is to look at sum types, look at how they are used, extract from them the capabilities we are looking for, then look at how we put those capabilities in Go in the most harmonious manner, rather than potentially introducing long-term warts into Go.

The capabilities one might want from a sum type:

* A set of typed product values that can be used as a single type in a type declaration.
* This set is closed; external packages can not add to it.
* Since it is closed, exhaustiveness checking is possible, whether in a compiler or a linter like `go vet`.
* The ability to do some sort of type switch on the components of the sum type.
* Compiler optimization to take advantage of the closed nature of the type to pack it more efficiently in RAM is at least possible.

  I don't intend that as part of this proposal, but I think this can be used as a metric for measuring it; it should be _possible_ for a compiler to implement this based on the proposal, even though I would not consider implementing that as part of this proposal. I believe this is the case but if anyone can show otherwise I would consider that a substantial criticism.

Thus, the correct question is not "how can we _transliterate_ sum types into Go?" but "how can we _translate_ the features sum types provide into Go?"

It is well-known that you can get close to meeting all of the above criteria in current Go simply by declaring an unexported method in an interface:

```
type MySumType interface {
    Name() string
    isMySumType()
}

type Red struct {}
func (r Red) isMySumType() {}
func (r Red) Name() string { return "red" }

func DoSomething(val MySumType) {
    switch v := val.(type) {
    case Red:
        // etc.
    }
}

```

But this does not quite get there, because there is a hole in the system, plenty large enough to ruin these use cases in practice. A struct in an external package can embed the interface representing the sum type. This struct then automatically conforms to the interface. This causes two problems:

1. Instances of this new struct can be passed to `DoSomething`, but it is impossible for the type switch to match it and do anything useful with it. So `DoSomething` can't count on the guarantee of receiving only a bounded set of types known at the time it was written.
2. This struct can also override any exported methods, which means those aren't available for the sum type to make any guarantees about, as the overriding implementation can break those guarantees with impunity. This may be somewhat less Go-like, but it is very similar to the desire to know the function can receive only a constrained set of types, and in particular the constrained methods that would be on those types.

See [this example](https://go.dev/play/p/DohbnLxFWMY) on the Go Playground for concrete code.

If it weren't for this particular issue, this would largely, and I believe entirely, meet the criteria above.

# Proposal

Therefore, my proposal is that rather than trying to build a complicated new feature, we simply fix the problem that embedding interface types creates. Allow an interface to declare that it can't be embedded by a struct, which we can call `sum_interface`:

```
package somepackage

type MySumType sum_interface {
    Name() string
    isMySumType()
}

// Red and other elements of MySumType as above
```

It would then be a compiler error for an **external** package to embed this interface value into a struct, by any amount of embedding recursion or type aliasing. The package that offers the `sum_interface` can do it, because any code that switches on the types could account for its own internal type, but external packages would be forbidden to embed it.

It is not necessary to block embedding into an interface. All an external interface declaration can do is further narrow the interface, if the sum type-providing package exports the parts of the sum types and if those types have methods that may allow further distinguishing of the components. Type assertion can be used like normal to test if a member of a sum interface is or is not also a member of some narrowed interface.

A `sum_interface` must include a non-exported method or the compiler should error. The compiler imposes no constraints beyond "some unexported method". I'm using verbose `isThisType()` methods as an example, but any unexported method will do. As a matter of style rather than requirement, if there is a sensible method to put on the `sum_interface` that perform some actual task, so much the better. Empty tag methods are only required when there is no useful method otherwise. In the event this proposal was to be accepted I would advise documentation to treat tagging with a useful method as the primary case, and mention in the prose that you can create a do-nothing "tag" method as well, lest people think that the tag methods are mandatory because that's what the docs show.

I am not passionate about this syntax, though I would observe I don't think `type MySumType sum interface` is a good idea since that makes it look like there could be other modifiers. I weakly recommend some single token, and recommend against a pragma. This is the most bikesheddable portion of this entire proposal and I doubt anything I can put here will prevent it from happening anyhow, so I will deliberately harness it instead of fighting it.

## Interface Semantics Retained

A type can implement multiple sum type interfaces at once, because it can implement multiple interfaces at once and there is no reason to exclude this possibility. This differs from most sum types in most languages, but I personally do not consider this a requirement for sum types. I see no reason why it is _mandatory_ for the individual components of a sum type to be fully disjoint at the type level from the components of other sum types. There may be pros and cons to each possibility, and other languages may build further structure on top of the choice they make, but I do not see it as integral to the concept, nor do I see it as integral that it _must_ be impossible to use the type system to specify just some particular component of the sum type.

This requires no additional semantic specifications beyond it being a compile error to embed an unembedable interface, as interfaces are already fully specified in Go. For instance, it is obvious how this works with generic interfaces, because a "generic sum type" _is_ just a generic interface, including usage in constraints: It works exactly as it would today without the `sum_interface` annotation.  It is also clear how to use a sum interface as a generic constraint, for the same reason. Further it should be future-proof; any future work on interfaces should automatically apply to sum types and extend them appropriately.

I would personally propose leaving exhaustiveness checking to external linters that interested users can easily integrate into their compilation process and in most cases directly into their development environment. This prevents the Go project itself from having to take a stance on whether a "complete" type switch includes `nil` or not, which is situational. This is also fairly bikesheddable, although in this case I think the divergences in opinions are fundamental, and that shifting them out into a linter is not just punting, but actually the correct decision for Go.

## `reflect` Implications

`reflect.StructOf` should panic if a user attempts to embed a `sum_interface` as an anonymous field. As it stands now [it looks like this is already implemented because `StructOf` already panics on attempts to embed an interface with unexported methods](https://cs.opensource.google/go/go/+/refs/tags/go1.26.4:src/reflect/type.go;l=2397), which references [a 2016 issue #15924](https://github.com/golang/go/issues/15924). Implementing this proposal complicates ever fixing that issue, though it shouldn't make it impossible. 

I can't find a reason this would need to be a separate `reflect.Kind`. I can't even find a concrete reason at the moment that a method to indicate something like `CanEmbedInStruct() bool` would need to be added. The utility of such a method to prevent panics from misusing `reflect.StructOf` is apparently already not enough to make it worth including in the `reflect` package today.

I did a [search for reflect.StructOf](https://github.com/search?q=language%3Ago+reflect.StructOf&type=code) on GitHub and it turned up 167 distinct uses as of my search. (It initially says many thousands but if you click through it dedupes and consolidates and the number drops dramatically.) Perusing those it seems to be mostly cases like constructing structs for use with reflect-based serializers, database interaction, and other cases where it doesn't seem likely that the users have any use for an anonymous field, especially since it is currently impossible to embed an interface with an unexported field into a struct anyhow.

I would also observe that any sum type proposal that involves adding a new `reflect.Kind` is arguably a violation of the Go 1.0 compatibility promise. Introducing a new `reflect.Kind` into the set of possibilities could break a lot of code.

# Standard Library Prior Art

There is an example of this in the standard library, modulo the use of the `sum_interface` type to enforce it.

The [standard library `ast` package]((https://pkg.go.dev/go/ast)) nearly implements this proposal. It has four disjoint sum types, [`Expr`, `Stmt`, `Decl`](https://cs.opensource.google/go/go/+/refs/tags/go1.26.4:src/go/ast/ast.go;l=42), and [Spec](https://cs.opensource.google/go/go/+/refs/tags/go1.26.4:src/go/ast/ast.go;l=903), each with a corresponding `exprNode()` or similar unexported method.

It turns out they also provide a standard-library example of the utility of the ability to build on these using the standard Go tools for interfaces. The [`Node` type](https://pkg.go.dev/go/ast#Node) is an interface that also joins all the AST node types into one unifying type. This type includes all the types that implement `Expr`, `Stmt`, etc., directly, without creating a wrapper type for `Expr` that has to be deconstructed itself. `Node` technically is not a sum type, as it has only exported methods, but it incorporates all the node types in the previous paragraph. But a function like [`Unparen`](https://pkg.go.dev/go/ast#Unparen) nails down the argument it takes to just the `Expr` type, which if you consider `Node` as a _de facto_ sum type demonstrates composing together multiple sum types, and/or narrowing broad sum types, already in the standard library. `Node` also includes types that aren't any of those four things. Not all languages that implement sum types have an analog to this flexibility.

(If an external package tries to create new types that implements `Node`, while it is technically possible, it's walking into a minefield, because of things like the [Walk function panicking on unknown `Node` members](https://cs.opensource.google/go/go/+/refs/tags/go1.26.4:src/go/ast/walk.go;l=351).  I think it's reasonable for me to cite this as an example of four sum types that are then composed cleanly into one overarching sum type, even if `Node` does not contain an unexported method.)

# Weakness

## Sum Types Always Have A `nil`

Sum types in this proposal always end up with `nil` as a valid value and there is no type-based way to get rid of that.

I have seen at least one other sum type proposal some work on trying to figure out how to define a "zero value" for the sum type to avoid this. I believe this should be treated orthogonally to the question of sum types in general. If it is desirable to work out how to avoid a `nil` getting forcibly adjoined to sum types by creating some sort of declaration of what a "zero value" is for the type, it is equally desirable for the several other types that have the same problem. A "solution" to that problem that works only for sum types only makes the foreignness of such a solution to the rest of Go even worse. E.g., people declaring a "sum type" with only one component type like an int so that they can get a default value of "100" just to get the defaulting behavior would be quite the wart.

If it is desirable to solve this problem it should be solved for Go as a whole, not just for sum types.

As it stands for the purposes of this proposal, a `nil` is a perfectly normal thing in Go and it is well beyond the scope of this proposal to try to change something so fundamental.

## Sum Types Have Methods

A lot of people associate sum types with functional programming, which tends to eschew methods. Some critics may claim that sum types that have methods aren't "real sum types".

However, both Zig and Nim have sum types that can have methods defined on them. Given that their sum types can also be of types that have methods on them themselves, they even have the equivalent of the ability to assert some aspect of the sum type is of some type that can have methods called on it, and then call methods on it.

One could argue this puts Go closer to the cutting edge in what sum types are doing in the latest languages, rather than necessarily being "wrong".

It's hard to know every language. An AI search suggests that there may not be any other major languages that allow methods on their official sum type implementation anyhow, suggesting that the behavior of methods on sum types is not something the community at large has strong opinions about yet.

## Methods Can't Change The Underlying Type

However, one thing Zig's and Nim's methods can do that Go would not under this proposal is [have a method on a sum type change the "branch" the sum type is in](https://codapi.org/embed/?sandbox=zig&code=data%3A%3Bbase64%2CfZDNaoQwFIX3PsXBlQ4SmZ8Wqgh9h5auCkPUWEP1ZjAxwyBuu%2B4z9klKokMZWppdcu93Ts6pFGkDbWoUeJT9SQ0mCrWpwzgPgsoPX3iHAiNJRZGgsY8xBQAgyWSQ%2B13ib02nuMnQ3B%2BSwD8s8JPoGif93EodxTmANMXXxydMKzWkhmkF3sUFnSSxgKexREPQwhyNOnrdSIuuybBxagmst4lhlazXv7jjdtgGBdgE5jEUsJhX0340vOwu0GdpqlZolAOnqvX4%2FJezpN%2B%2Bcr%2F731fS1XUVnvMgWHV7Lim6wS0fnOrS8A9%2B2F15y25q2LPtYXv3EC%2FDNIV1FZI632Ret66ptKlZLcrxjZ0GlymcOF3mVwoTsMnOcR7M3w%3D%3D). The linked example shows a Zig union of an `int32` and a `float64` (in Go type terms) and shows methods that mutate a value of that type populated by one of the constituent types and flip it to the other type.

Go would not be able to do this. No method declared in the sum interface can mutate to another type because no method can mutate the concrete type of what it is called on. Since this proposal doesn't propose to tie types to belong to specific sum interfaces, and specific types may participate in more than one of them, the implementation of a method couldn't know what other types would be valid, a necessary prerequisite to any "solution" to this.

A function could implement this behavior by taking a pointer to the sum interface value. Taking a pointer to an interface is generally considered "weird" in Go. I think it would continue to be so. This seems like an edge case most people aren't interested in as sum types are generally associated with a style of programming that would just return a new value instead. I think this provides good enough coverage of what is already an edge-case that there's no need to try to cover this use case in the main proposal.

## Interface Unmarshaling

An interface-based sum type inherits the problems with the common reflect-based approaches to unmarshaling into interface values; that is not new. What is new to this proposal is that it also blocks the solution I most commonly deploy for that, which is to embed the interface directly into a struct:

```
type MarshalableSumType struct {
    sumtypepkg.MySumType
}
```

and then implement marshaling methods on it, while the interface is transparently proxied to the embedded value by struct embedding's semantics.

The package that implements sum types could offer a marshaling struct like that, because a package is allowed to embed its own sum type. That essentially makes the `MarshalableSumType` a new member of the sum type that all code within the package now must deal with, which is slighty tedious but possible. This would permit a fixed set of marshalers to be defined by a package offering a sum interface type. But there would still be no way to directly embed the type as above, and so packages would have no ability to add their own marshaling that the original package may not have known about. Such a package would have to declare a struct with a named member.

Reflect-based marshaling is already only a convenient shortcut even at the best of times anyhow. There are many use cases where it breaks down and something more manual has to be implemented. If this proposal added the first thing that broke the utility of standard reflect-based marshaling, that would be a big strike against it, but it joins an already substantial list and I don't think it's a qualitative change. It is already common to have to fall back to other approaches for pieces of a marshaling process.

## All Sum Type Values Will Get Boxed Initially

As I mentioned towards the beginning, if this proposal has succeeded in its goals, it should be safe for the compiler to implement optimizations to pack a value of this interface in a way that is more efficient and unboxed in practice. 

However were this to be accepted I wouldn't expect this to be immediately implemented, so there will be a phase where all sum types would be boxed and quite likely difficult to prevent from going to the heap.

Then again that is already the case for the large amounts of code implementing sum types this way, just without the embedding guarantees provided by this proposal.

If this is a big concern it should be fixable in the future without any changes to the specification.

## No Pattern Matching

Some people think pattern matching goes with sum types. I think it's orthogonal, in that you can have pattern matching without them and sum types with no pattern matching.

Go has the most useful kind already, which is the top-level type switch using `switch val.(type)`. I believe anything further would be a separate spec. Pattern matching should work with non-sum types anyhow.

## This Won't Silence The Critics

Most of the people complaining that Go doesn't have sum types will probably not accept this as a sum type, because it doesn't look the way they expect. Especially due to the fact that the branches of the sum type continue to be specified as they are today, without any sort of syntax gloss on trying to "bundle" them together. Some of the other sum type proposals have attempted to sketch these out but I don't believe I've seen one that I would even call "good", let alone worthy of inclusion in the language specification. I wasn't able to come up with anything better in my own exploration of this proposal.

I suspect the intersection of "people who already or may someday use Go" and the very loudest of these critics is not all that large anyhow, and having a blessed mechanism will satisfy most of the Go users who have wanted a sum type.

But I think it is fair to observe that this proposal will shift those critics from "Go is lacking sum types" to "Go's sum types are weird and wrong" rather than "Go finally has sum types!". Although as I will address at the end, I'm not convinced there is any sum type proposal that Go can integrate that will not have this problem anyhow.

# Conclusion

Cards on the table, I will admit to some bias here. I believe that in Go as it is constituted today, it is almost always the correct software engineering choice to [replace conditional with polymorphism](https://refactoring.guru/replace-conditional-with-polymorphism). I believe that the vast majority of things that people think are "sum types", if you apply this principle consistently to them, end up putting everything into methods and dissolve away the entire need to switch on the type, and in many cases, also dissolve away the utility of closing the interface as well. I believe my awareness of this technique is why I don't miss them in Go very often.

However, I agree that there are rare, but definitely existing, cases where that is not a viable answer, because there are times when one absolutely, positively _needs_ the ability to add operations to a type in external packages. AST nodes are a classic case, perhaps the canonical case of this, but it isn't the only case.

There is no need to try to yank Go all the way from the side of the [expression problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expression_problem) it is currently on to the other. We can acknowledge that the need to add operations to existing types is the less usual case in a language that prioritizes adding additional types to existing operations when possible, and simply clean up/make possible handling the other side without trying to completely conquer both sides, which few, and arguably no, languages have ever done.

Other than the fact this doesn't "look like" sum types when read off the screen, and the IMHO orthogonal issue of the zero value always being included in a sum type, this:

* Covers all the bases of _functionality_ that people are looking for.
* Resolves the tension of sum types having substantial and complicated overlapping with interfaces by simply being a simple extension of interfaces.
* Minimizes the impact on the language, both in terms of analyzing this against the current language and minimizing reducing the options on any future capabilities.
* Makes it possible to do some things with "sum types" most other languages don't support, such as mixing and matching the types that implement various `sum` interfaces in a package as `ast` already does.
* Minimizes the difficulty of implementation and the probability of any other surprises discovered in the implementation.
* Breaks apart the need to nail down functionality and syntax in one proposal; future proposals can argue about how to syntax-sugar this without blocking functionality, most likely never happening.

So while this may result in a "sum type" that doesn't much _look_ like sum types in other languages, there is the compensation that they have some additional capabilities not normally associated with sum types, plus the fact that it plays with existing Go tools and future Go tools probably better than any other proposal could.

Philosophically, I think one of the reasons it has been so difficult to figure out how to put a sum type implementation into Go is that the overlap with `interface` isn't superficial. It is quite substantial. A "closed interface" today gets you 90% of the way there, and I think there's something fundamentally and profoundly true about that. I think a solid argument can be made that no other conceivable proposal for "sum types" can ever be made to work without all but breaking Go as a coherent language because the overlap is too large and there simply isn't _room_ for any other concept of sum types in Go. I'll cop to some vigorous handwaving on that point, but I think previous conversations in the previous issues can only be seen as evidence in favor of this claim.
