issue.title: No way to select virtual-host-style addressing with a custom S3 endpoint
issue.body:
## Summary

With `CUSTOM_S3_ENDPOINT` set, every value of `USE_PATH_STYLE` produces path-style requests. Providers that require virtual-host addressing (`https://<bucket>.<endpoint>/<key>`) cannot be used at all.

## Cause

`pkg/s3/s3.go` sets `BucketLookup` only when `USE_PATH_STYLE=true`, otherwise leaving minio-go's zero value `BucketLookupAuto`. But "auto" is an allowlist, not a preference — from the pinned minio-go `v7.0.84`, `pkg/s3utils/utils.go`:

```go
// Return true for all other cases
return IsAmazonEndpoint(endpointURL) || IsGoogleEndpoint(endpointURL) || IsAliyunOSSEndpoint(endpointURL)
```

Any other endpoint falls through to path-style, so: unset → path, `"false"` → path, `"true"` → path. `BucketLookupDNS` is unreachable from configuration.

This flipped silently at `0b3984d` (AWS SDK v2 → minio-go). Before it the default was virtual-host — #24 is a user hitting exactly that, `talos-backup.s3.domain.tld`.

## On #59 and #62

#59 states that minio-go defaults to virtual-host style. That is AWS SDK v2's behavior, not minio-go's. With `http://minio.storage.svc.cluster.local:9000`, `auto` already resolved to path-style, so removing `USE_PATH_STYLE` cannot have caused the DNS failure reported there. #62 therefore re-added an option whose `true` value duplicates the existing default for every endpoint outside the three-vendor allowlist — including every local-MinIO case #59 was about. The direction that is genuinely unreachable is the opposite one.

## Environment

- talos-backup: `latest` (`v0.1.0-beta.3-10-gb9fd478`)
- S3: self-hosted, virtual-host only — bucket parsed from `Host`, wildcard cert for `*.s3.example.com`; path-style requests are rejected

## Suggested fix

Add `USE_VIRTUAL_HOST_STYLE`, mirroring the existing variable rather than changing its type — the config struct is uniformly plain scalars parsed as `os.Getenv(...) == "true"`, and a `*bool` just to distinguish unset from `"false"` would be the only one of its kind:

```go
switch {
case svcConf.UseVirtualHostStyle:
	options.BucketLookup = minio.BucketLookupDNS
case svcConf.UsePathStyle:
	options.BucketLookup = minio.BucketLookupPath
}
```

Unset behavior is unchanged. If both are set to `"true"`, `USE_PATH_STYLE` winning keeps existing deployments bit-identical; failing fast with a clear message would also be reasonable, and I'll follow your preference.

Worth noting `USE_PATH_STYLE` would not become redundant: it stays the only way to force path-style on the three allowlisted vendors. Deprecating it would drop that, so I'd suggest keeping both and documenting what each does.

Happy to send the PR.

issue.title: KMS service status latches on Error after one failed health check and never recovers, while the service keeps serving

labels.name: S-reproducing
labels.description: Status: Reproducing a bug report

issue.body:
**Describe the bug**

`KmsServiceManager::health_check()` writes a failure into the shared status but never writes a success, so a single transient backend error pins `status` to `Error("Health check failed: ...")` for the lifetime of the process. The KMS service itself keeps running and keeps serving — only the reported status is wrong. `GET /rustfs/admin/v3/kms/service-status` then seals it: it performs a live health check only when the status is *already* `Running`, so a latched node can never re-evaluate its way out. The result is a node reporting a hard KMS error indefinitely while its backend has been healthy for hours.

Operationally this is a false positive that looks exactly like a real outage, and no admin API field distinguishes the two. On a 4-node cluster it presents as one node stuck at `Error` while three report `Running`, which reads as "that node's KMS is down" and invites a node restart — an expensive remedy here, since a restart discards the in-progress scanner cycle. The status is also the field monitoring and provisioning tooling naturally assert on. The triggering outage can be brief: ours was an unrelated local proxy crash; any KMS/Vault blip, network partition, or token hiccup long enough to fail one health check latches the node permanently.

**To Reproduce**

1. Configure a `VaultTransit` KMS backend and confirm `service-status` reports `Running` with `healthy: true`.
2. Make the backend unreachable (stop the Vault endpoint or block the route) and wait for one health check to fail. `service-status` now reports `Error("Health check failed: ...")` with `healthy: null`.
3. Restore the backend and confirm it is reachable from the node.
4. Poll `service-status` for any length of time. It stays `Error` with `healthy: null` permanently, while the KMS service continues to serve requests normally.

What we observed. A local HAProxy instance fronting Vault died at `08:38:59`, cutting the node off from its KMS backend; it was restarted at `10:02:07`. While the circuit was open, the deletion sweep logged this on a strict 60 s cadence:

```
{"timestamp":"2026-09-09T10:01:43.835963998+08:00","level":"WARN","message":"KMS deletion sweep could not list keys","error":"Backend error: KMS backend circuit is open; waiting for the half-open recovery probe"}
```

The last such line is `10:01:43` — the first sweep after the proxy returned produced nothing, and nothing appeared in the following 47 minutes on a log whose tail was live at `10:48:58`. The circuit had demonstrably closed, and `curl http://localhost:8200/v1/sys/health` returned `200` with `initialized:true, sealed:false, standby:false`. `service-status` on that node at `10:50`, 48 minutes after recovery:

```json
{"status": {"Error": "Health check failed: Backend error: KMS backend circuit is open; waiting for the half-open recovery probe"}, "backend_type": "VaultTransit", "healthy": null, "config_summary": {"backend_type": "VaultTransit", "default_key_id": "...", "timeout_seconds": 30, "retry_attempts": 3, "enable_cache": true, "max_cached_keys": 1000}}
```

`"healthy": null` is the fingerprint: the handler did not even attempt a live check.

**Expected behavior**

Either of these closes it; the first is the smaller change:

1. In `health_check()`, add the mirror of `mark_health_error_if_current`: on `Ok(true)`, if the checked version is still current and the stored status is `Error`, restore it to `Running`.
2. In the status handler, drop the `matches!(status, KmsServiceStatus::Running)` gate so `healthy` reflects a real check regardless of stored status — and/or report from `probe_status()`, whose doc comment says it exists for exactly this consultation.

Worth considering alongside: because `mark_health_error_if_current` keeps `current_service` alive, `Error` here means "last check failed", not "service down" — two different conditions conflated in one field. Distinguishing last-check-failed from not-running would make the status actionable.

**Environment**

- RustFS `1.0.0-rc.5` (`40a2470feb567201165a5b809b7598bb4b1f68f5`), 4 nodes, EC 12+4, KMS backend `VaultTransit` reached through a per-node local proxy.
- Code links below are pinned to current `main` (`7c85c72fd14569412a0617598989fdba8a2b19d9`); every cited function is byte-identical at rc.5.

**Additional context**

*Root cause.* [`health_check()`](https://github.com/rustfs/rustfs/blob/7c85c72fd14569412a0617598989fdba8a2b19d9/crates/kms/src/service_manager.rs#L581-L608) is asymmetric: the `Err` arm persists the failure, while the `Ok` arm — including `Ok(true)`, a fully successful check — returns the value and writes nothing. [`mark_health_error_if_current()`](https://github.com/rustfs/rustfs/blob/7c85c72fd14569412a0617598989fdba8a2b19d9/crates/kms/src/service_manager.rs#L743-L753) deliberately preserves `current_service`, so the service keeps running while the status says otherwise. The only non-test assignment of `KmsServiceStatus::Running` is inside [`publish_running()`](https://github.com/rustfs/rustfs/blob/7c85c72fd14569412a0617598989fdba8a2b19d9/crates/kms/src/service_manager.rs#L703-L716), reached from the explicit start/restart/reconfigure path. The status handler then seals the latch: [`healthy` is computed only when the status is already `Running`](https://github.com/rustfs/rustfs/blob/7c85c72fd14569412a0617598989fdba8a2b19d9/rustfs/src/admin/handlers/kms_dynamic.rs#L1212-L1219), so a node in the `Error` state never runs the check that could correct it. Together, no execution path returns a latched node to `Running` on its own, however healthy the backend becomes.

There is already a live, lock-free, I/O-free snapshot intended for this consultation — [`probe_status()`](https://github.com/rustfs/rustfs/blob/7c85c72fd14569412a0617598989fdba8a2b19d9/crates/kms/src/service_manager.rs#L567-L578), whose doc comment says it exists "so a health endpoint can consult it without turning an external KMS hiccup into probe pressure of its own".

*Workaround.* `POST /rustfs/admin/v3/kms/start` with `{"force":true}` republishes the service version and recomputes the status; we used it to clear the latched node. An unforced start does nothing: [`start_or_restart()`](https://github.com/rustfs/rustfs/blob/7c85c72fd14569412a0617598989fdba8a2b19d9/crates/kms/src/service_manager.rs#L335-L339) branches on `current_service`, which the failed health check left intact, so it returns `AlreadyRunning` and changes nothing.

issue.title: Write failures are undiagnosable at warn level: no request counters, mapped error logged, latch flips silently

labels.name: S-confirming
labels.description: Status: Awaiting confirmation for a resolved issue

issue.body:
**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**

One node of our cluster failed every write for 7.5 hours (#7361). Establishing *that* it was failing every write, and *why*, took hours of log forensics across four nodes, because at `RUST_LOG=warn` — what we run, and a reasonable setting for a cluster whose log is already ~300 MB/hour — the operator can see only failures, never successes, and only the mapped error, never the cause:

- [`log_response`](https://github.com/rustfs/rustfs/blob/40a2470feb567201165a5b809b7598bb4b1f68f5/rustfs/src/server/layer.rs#L418-L466) logs 5xx via `error!` but every non-5xx response via `info!`, so 2xx and 4xx vanish at `warn`. In the PUT path the [failure branch is `warn!`](https://github.com/rustfs/rustfs/blob/40a2470feb567201165a5b809b7598bb4b1f68f5/rustfs/src/app/object/put.rs#L1574-L1590) and the [success branch is `debug!`](https://github.com/rustfs/rustfs/blob/40a2470feb567201165a5b809b7598bb4b1f68f5/rustfs/src/app/object/put.rs#L1555-L1568). **No success/failure ratio is observable at all**: a log full of 500s is indistinguishable from a node serving 99 % of its traffic fine. The admin metrics endpoint offers no substitute — of its 550 leaf metrics none is an API request counter (425 scanner, 88 disk, 19 net, 15 rpc, 3 other). We only established the failure rate by running a controlled PUT on each node.
- The PUT failure log records `error: "We encountered an internal error, please try again."` — the already-mapped S3 text. The original error is discarded at the `ApiError::from` boundary ([error.rs:424-431](https://github.com/rustfs/rustfs/blob/40a2470feb567201165a5b809b7598bb4b1f68f5/rustfs/src/error.rs#L424-L431)), so the cause of a 500 is unavailable at any log level short of a debug build. `rustfs-err.log` is not a fallback: it did not receive any of these errors (line count unchanged across a probe that deterministically failed).
- The actual cause — the pool-metadata write latch — flips silently: [`block_writes`](https://github.com/rustfs/rustfs/blob/40a2470feb567201165a5b809b7598bb4b1f68f5/crates/ecstore/src/core/pools.rs#L4160-L4162) has no log line, nor do any of its callers. The only trace is an unrelated subsystem failing 15 minutes later: `Unable to load bucket metadata, will be retried: ... pool metadata writes remain blocked ...` ([site](https://github.com/rustfs/rustfs/blob/40a2470feb567201165a5b809b7598bb4b1f68f5/crates/ecstore/src/bucket/metadata_sys.rs#L1467)), 62 lines per tick with no `bucket` field, so even that cannot say what it failed on.
- The one line that *did* record the triggering event — `read_config_with_metadata: err: Timeout, file: pool.bin` ([site](https://github.com/rustfs/rustfs/blob/40a2470feb567201165a5b809b7598bb4b1f68f5/crates/ecstore/src/config/com.rs#L572)) — is a generic `warn!` that says nothing about the consequence, and finding it meant knowing to look for `pool.bin` in a 122 MB hour of lock-timeout noise (the storm in #7363).
- `storageinfo` reports unreachable peers' disks as `ok`/`online`. [`storage_info`](https://github.com/rustfs/rustfs/blob/40a2470feb567201165a5b809b7598bb4b1f68f5/crates/ecstore/src/services/notification_sys.rs#L1108-L1141) fans out to peers with a 5 s timeout; on timeout ([L1132-L1134](https://github.com/rustfs/rustfs/blob/40a2470feb567201165a5b809b7598bb4b1f68f5/crates/ecstore/src/services/notification_sys.rs#L1132-L1134)) it evicts the connection and calls [`handle_peer_failure`](https://github.com/rustfs/rustfs/blob/40a2470feb567201165a5b809b7598bb4b1f68f5/crates/ecstore/src/services/notification_sys.rs#L2371-L2412), which returns the peer's **last successful snapshot unchanged** while consecutive failures are below [`CONSECUTIVE_FAILURE_THRESHOLD = 3`](https://github.com/rustfs/rustfs/blob/40a2470feb567201165a5b809b7598bb4b1f68f5/crates/ecstore/src/services/notification_sys.rs#L47): no `offline` marking, no age bound (only `server_info` has [`SERVER_INFO_CACHE_MAX_AGE = 60 s`](https://github.com/rustfs/rustfs/blob/40a2470feb567201165a5b809b7598bb4b1f68f5/crates/ecstore/src/services/notification_sys.rs#L117)), and no field saying the entry is cached. This is [covered by a unit test](https://github.com/rustfs/rustfs/blob/40a2470feb567201165a5b809b7598bb4b1f68f5/crates/ecstore/src/services/notification_sys.rs#L3807), so it is by design. Observed 2026-09-07 10:35–10:48 with two peers wedged: a node up for 2.5 h answered 48/48 disks all `ok/online` while logging `peer nodeN storage_info timed out after 5s` for both peers in the same second, and a node restarted 25 min earlier (no snapshot yet) answered 24/48 for the same two peers. An operator polling `storageinfo` every ~10 min sees a healthy cluster for up to 30 min after two nodes stop answering.

The consequence for operators: a node that was rejecting 100 % of writes looked, from `/health/ready` (200), from `storageinfo` (peers' last good snapshot, presented as live), from the admin metrics (no counters), and from the logs (500s with a generic message, no denominator, no cause), exactly like a busy node. We diagnosed it by reading source.

**Describe the solution you'd like**

1. **Per-status API request counters in admin metrics** (at minimum requests by method × status class per node). Without a denominator, error-log volume is uninterpretable.
2. **Log the underlying error alongside the mapped one** on the failure path, at `warn`, before `ApiError::from` erases it — the `source` is already carried on `ApiError`; it just never reaches the log.
3. **Log state transitions that change what the node will accept**, once, at `error`: the pool-metadata write block (naming the flag and the replica error), and any similar fail-closed latch. A node that stops accepting writes should say so in one line, not be inferred from a retry message elsewhere.
4. **Include the bucket in `Unable to load bucket metadata`** so a 62-line burst is attributable.
5. **Mark cached peer entries in `storageinfo` as such** — a `cached: true` / snapshot-age field, or the same 60 s age bound `server_info` already has — so a stale `online` cannot be read as a live answer.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**

- Running at `info` — at this cluster's traffic that is multiple GB/hour of 2xx lines, and it still would not log the underlying error or the latch flip.
- External probes with a denominator (what we did: a per-node controlled PUT/GET loop, `ops/node_probe.py`). It works but is a workaround for the server not counting its own requests, and it costs a write per probe per node.
- Reading the source to map a 500 back to its cause, which is what this report is the product of.

**Additional context**

Environment: RustFS `1.0.0-rc.5` (`40a2470feb567201165a5b809b7598bb4b1f68f5`), 4 nodes, EC 12+4, `RUST_LOG=warn,...`. The incident that motivated this is filed as #7361 (the write latch) and #7363 (the lock-RPC storm that triggered it), with the full mechanism; the asks above are what would have let us find it in minutes instead of hours.

issue.title: Lock RPC timeouts against one erasure set's lock endpoints spiral into a reset/GOAWAY/reconnect loop across the cluster, with no backoff

labels.name: S-confirming
labels.description: Status: Awaiting confirmation for a resolved issue

issue.body:
**Describe the bug**

For about an hour, and again for a shorter window six hours later, every node in a 4-node cluster timed out its lock RPCs against the lock endpoints of one erasure set — overwhelmingly `node3:/mnt/rustfs11` — at the 3 s client budget, and the client-side reaction turned a slow lock server into a self-sustaining storm: each timeout cancels the gRPC stream, the accumulated `RST_STREAM`s make the server answer `GOAWAY too_many_resets`, the client evicts the cached connection and reconnects, and the next lock request re-arms the cycle. There is no backoff anywhere in the loop. Lock *releases* time out too, leaving `lock not found for release` and `distributed unlock left unreleased entries after retry` behind. The storm subsided on its own both times (07:48 the second time) with no intervention.

The storm's most expensive consequence — one node permanently latching all writes off — is reported in #7361; this report is about the storm itself, because it recurred, it hit every node, and the loop is what turns "one lock endpoint is slow" into cluster-wide lock failure.

**To Reproduce**

We cannot reproduce the server-side slowness on demand. What we can give is the shape, measured from the plain-text hourly logs on all four nodes (times local, +08:00):

- 00:07:57 first `Remote lock RPC timed out` (`timeout_ms=3000`, [`rpc_timeout`](https://github.com/rustfs/rustfs/blob/40a2470feb567201165a5b809b7598bb4b1f68f5/crates/ecstore/src/cluster/rpc/remote_locker.rs#L181), default [`DEFAULT_OBJECT_LOCK_RPC_TIMEOUT_MS = 3000`](https://github.com/rustfs/rustfs/blob/40a2470feb567201165a5b809b7598bb4b1f68f5/crates/config/src/constants/object.rs#L526)); 00:07:58 first `GoAway(b"too_many_resets", ENHANCE_YOUR_CALM)` received; 00:07:59 the first slow inbound `NodeService/Lock` on node3 (5,756 ms).
- In that first hour, lock timeouts by client node: node1 9,736 · node2 4,979 · node4 6,524 (node3's own client-side count not collected). By target, from node4's log: `node3:/mnt/rustfs11` 6,393 · `node1:/mnt/rustfs11` 106 · `node2:/mnt/rustfs11` 25 — i.e. the lock endpoints of one set, one of them very sick.
- The sick endpoint was genuinely slow to serve, not just to answer: node3 logged 3,104 slow inbound `NodeService/Lock` and 5,903 slow inbound `NodeService/ReadVersion` in the hour, versus 9 and 0 slow inbound `Lock` on node1 and node2 (which logged 6,379 and 5,145 slow inbound `ReadVersion` — the whole set was slow on reads, only node3 on locks).
- The loop, per node4's first hour: 6,671 `Evicting cached remote lock connection after RPC failure`, 64 GOAWAYs received; 1,601 evictions / 178 GOAWAYs the next hour; 3,401 / 114 when it recurred at 06:xx. The #6737 online-check ping (1 s) joins in: `remote lock client online check timed out` on all three peers' `rustfs11`, each evicting the connection again.
- Collateral on the lock table: `distributed unlock failed on client: Lock acquisition timeout for resource 'remote lock RPC release on ...' after 3s`, then `lock not found for release`, then `distributed unlock left unreleased entries after retry (remaining 1, attempts 3)` — orphaned entries of the #5939 class, created by the storm.
- Host-level: load 16-24 on all four nodes alike, no dmesg I/O errors, `rustfs11` = an NVMe at 24 % capacity. We could not identify why that endpoint's lock service was slow; the erasure set it belongs to was slow on `ReadVersion` on all three peers at the same time, so the lock service may simply have been starved behind read I/O on the same disk.

**Expected behavior**

1. **Backoff, or a circuit breaker, on lock-RPC timeouts.** Re-dialing immediately after every 3 s timeout guarantees the reset accumulation that triggers `too_many_resets`, which guarantees the eviction, which guarantees the re-dial. A slow endpoint should degrade into slower lock acquisition, not into a GOAWAY loop that also takes the healthy endpoints' streams down with it.
2. **Distinguish "slow" from "gone".** A `Cancelled`/timeout on a stream to a server that is answering other streams is load, not a dead peer; evicting the whole connection on it converts one slow request into a reconnect for every in-flight request on that connection.
3. **Lock-release timeouts should not orphan entries.** A release that times out should be retried past the 3-attempt budget (or the entry should carry a lease the server expires), rather than leaving `lock not found for release` and `unreleased entries` for a reaper to find.
4. **Lock-service latency should be observable per endpoint.** The server already knows it is slow (`http_request_inflight_slow` on `NodeService/Lock`); a per-endpoint inbound lock latency metric would let an operator find the sick endpoint in seconds instead of by log forensics across four nodes.

**Environment**

- RustFS `1.0.0-rc.5`, git `40a2470feb567201165a5b809b7598bb4b1f68f5`; 4 nodes × 12 drives, EC 12+4, TLS internode (h2); `RUSTFS_OBJECT_LOCK_ACQUIRE_TIMEOUT=30`, lock RPC timeout at the 3000 ms default.
- Workload: five JuiceFS filesystems (many small `chunks/...` objects, continuous write + delete), so lock traffic is high and every mutation also takes the pool-metadata read lock (see the companion latch report).

**Additional context**

The two windows (00:07-~01:00 and ~06:xx-07:48) ended by themselves, which argues for a load-shaped trigger rather than a fault. What did not end by itself was the write outage the first window caused on one node — that node's admission probe timed out a `pool.bin` read at 00:40:46 and latched writes off until restart; #7361 has the full chain. We mention it here because it is the cost of this loop: a storm that merely slowed writes for an hour also produced a 7.5-hour outage through a single unlucky timeout.

Happy to provide the full log windows from all four nodes for both storms.

issue.title: A single timed-out read of pool.bin permanently blocks every write on the node until restart, while /health/ready keeps returning 200

labels.name: S-reproducing
labels.description: Status: Reproducing a bug report

issue.body:
**Describe the bug**

One node of a healthy 4-node cluster (EC 12+4, 48/48 disks `ok`/`online` on every node) started failing **every** write it was given with `500 InternalError` and kept doing so for 7.5 hours — ~2.2 million 500s — until we restarted it. Reads on the same node were fine throughout, its peers were fine, and it kept answering `200` on `/health/ready`, so the load balancer kept routing writes to a node that could not accept any.

The cause is an in-process latch in the pool-metadata layer. Every object mutation runs a capacity-admission probe that reads `pool.bin` from the pool's disks under a distributed read lock; during a cluster-wide lock-RPC storm (reported separately), one of those reads timed out. The pool-metadata loader classifies a timed-out read as an *unreadable replica*, an unreadable replica sets `write_blocked`, and `write_blocked` is never cleared. From that second on, the same admission probe rejected every PUT and DELETE on the node with the (unlogged) error "pool metadata writes remain blocked after a recovery-required replica state; restart after all replicas are readable and consistent, with compatible formats". The replicas were readable and consistent again within minutes; the process never re-checked.

The chain, all on `40a2470f`:

1. Every object mutation admits itself through [`acquire_external_decommission_capacity_fence_with_active_source`](https://github.com/rustfs/rustfs/blob/40a2470feb567201165a5b809b7598bb4b1f68f5/crates/ecstore/src/core/pools.rs#L8340-L8352) — from PUT via [`run_decommission_capacity_admitted_mutation_with_capacity_lease`](https://github.com/rustfs/rustfs/blob/40a2470feb567201165a5b809b7598bb4b1f68f5/crates/ecstore/src/store/object.rs#L3738) and the [external-mutation helper](https://github.com/rustfs/rustfs/blob/40a2470feb567201165a5b809b7598bb4b1f68f5/crates/ecstore/src/store/object.rs#L2741-L2760), from DELETE via [`reconcile_decommission_capacity_before_exact_delete`](https://github.com/rustfs/rustfs/blob/40a2470feb567201165a5b809b7598bb4b1f68f5/crates/ecstore/src/store/rebalance.rs#L945). Reads do not.
2. That fence takes [`acquire_pool_meta_read_guard`](https://github.com/rustfs/rustfs/blob/40a2470feb567201165a5b809b7598bb4b1f68f5/crates/ecstore/src/core/pools.rs#L8308-L8330), which calls [`ensure_write_safe`](https://github.com/rustfs/rustfs/blob/40a2470feb567201165a5b809b7598bb4b1f68f5/crates/ecstore/src/core/pools.rs#L4260-L4266) before and after re-reading the replicas — so once the flag is set, admission fails before any data work (our failures took 9-213 ms).
3. The replica read: [`read_pool_meta_replica`](https://github.com/rustfs/rustfs/blob/40a2470feb567201165a5b809b7598bb4b1f68f5/crates/ecstore/src/core/pools.rs#L4554-L4583) turns *any* error other than not-found — including a transport `Timeout` — into `PoolMetaReplica::Unreadable`. The observing selector then [calls `block_writes()` if any replica is Unreadable](https://github.com/rustfs/rustfs/blob/40a2470feb567201165a5b809b7598bb4b1f68f5/crates/ecstore/src/core/pools.rs#L4801-L4806), before even choosing a replica, and [`select_pool_meta_replica_reads` sets `repair_write_safe = false`](https://github.com/rustfs/rustfs/blob/40a2470feb567201165a5b809b7598bb4b1f68f5/crates/ecstore/src/core/pools.rs#L4611-L4615), which [`observe_replicas` ORs into `write_blocked`](https://github.com/rustfs/rustfs/blob/40a2470feb567201165a5b809b7598bb4b1f68f5/crates/ecstore/src/core/pools.rs#L4156-L4158).
4. [`block_writes`](https://github.com/rustfs/rustfs/blob/40a2470feb567201165a5b809b7598bb4b1f68f5/crates/ecstore/src/core/pools.rs#L4160-L4162) only ever sets the flag; nothing clears it, and nothing logs the transition. A second latch of the same kind exists next to it: [`PoolMetaTransactionArm::drop`](https://github.com/rustfs/rustfs/blob/40a2470feb567201165a5b809b7598bb4b1f68f5/crates/ecstore/src/core/pools.rs#L4282-L4288) sets `aborted_transaction` whenever an armed pool-metadata save is dropped — including by an ordinary `?` error return inside `save_no_lock_armed_scoped` — and `ensure_write_safe` treats it identically.
5. The refusal surfaces as `Error::other(...)`, i.e. `StorageError::Io`, which the API layer maps to a bare `500 InternalError` with the generic text ([error.rs:424-431](https://github.com/rustfs/rustfs/blob/40a2470feb567201165a5b809b7598bb4b1f68f5/rustfs/src/error.rs#L424-L431)); the only trace at `warn` level is the bucket-metadata refresher failing every 15 minutes ([interval](https://github.com/rustfs/rustfs/blob/40a2470feb567201165a5b809b7598bb4b1f68f5/crates/ecstore/src/bucket/metadata_sys.rs#L51), [message](https://github.com/rustfs/rustfs/blob/40a2470feb567201165a5b809b7598bb4b1f68f5/crates/ecstore/src/bucket/metadata_sys.rs#L1467)) because bucket heal is gated by the same flag.
6. Readiness never consults it: [`collect_node_readiness_report`](https://github.com/rustfs/rustfs/blob/40a2470feb567201165a5b809b7598bb4b1f68f5/rustfs/src/server/readiness.rs#L721-L731) reports storage ready whenever the object-store handle exists.

**To Reproduce**

We do not have a from-scratch reproducer of the timed-out read (it needs the lock storm of the companion issue), but the state machine is deterministic and the field timeline pins each step to the second. All times local (+08:00), one node (`object04`), plain-text hourly logs:

- 23:00-23:59: zero lock timeouts, zero 500s, zero pool-metadata messages (baseline).
- 00:07:57 the lock-RPC storm begins (first `Remote lock RPC timed out` to `node3:/mnt/rustfs11`; GOAWAY `too_many_resets` one second later). For the next 33 minutes: thousands of lock timeouts, **zero** 500s.
- 00:40:27-00:40:45: six sporadic 500s whose logged cause is a lock timeout (table-catalog publication guard, `.bucket-incarnation` reads at the 5 s lock-acquire budget).
- **00:40:46.472** `read_config_with_metadata: err: Timeout, file: pool.bin` ([the warn site](https://github.com/rustfs/rustfs/blob/40a2470feb567201165a5b809b7598bb4b1f68f5/crates/ecstore/src/config/com.rs#L572)) — the only `pool.bin` read error in the hour. In the same minute the node was timing out lock *releases* on `.rustfs.sys/pool.bin@latest` and logging `lock not found for release` for it: the admission probes were holding pool.bin locks through the storm.
- 00:40:46-00:41:30: 1,994 500s (1,740 DELETE, 254 PUT), then a steady ~85/s.
- 00:41:29: first `Unable to load bucket metadata, will be retried: ... bucket heal cannot run while pool metadata requires recovery: pool metadata writes remain blocked ...` — 62 lines, repeating at :11/:26/:41/:56 for the rest of the outage, on this node only.
- Per hour, `lock timeouts / 500s`: 00h 6,524 / 83,805 · 01h 1,392 / 247,492 · 02h 34 / 423,447 · 03h 38 / 358,153 · 04h 260 / 376,913 · **05h 0 / 222,153** · 06h 3,183 / 379,208 · 07h 105 / 123,141. The 05h hour has no lock timeouts and no GOAWAYs at all and still fails every write: the storm was the trigger, not the cause.
- 08:16:23 restart; last 500 at 08:16:30; zero 500s, zero recovery-required lines since.

The storm itself was cluster-wide — this node logged 6,524 lock timeouts in the first hour and two of its peers logged 9,736 and 4,979 — but only this node's admission probe happened to time out its `pool.bin` read, so only this node latched (its three peers logged 1, 0 and 1 500s in that hour and no recovery-required lines at all). A controlled 4 MB PUT against `127.0.0.1:9000` on each node, three rounds, reproduced the node-locality exactly: `object04 put=ERR status=WEDGED_WRITE` every round, `inline`/`get` fine on the same node, all three peers `OK`; every put path and size class on the node failed, including 0-byte objects.

**Expected behavior**

1. **A timed-out replica read is not a recovery-required replica.** `Unreadable` currently conflates "the bytes are bad" with "the RPC did not answer in time"; the fail-closed block makes sense for the former and is wrong for the latter. A transport error should be retried or fail the one operation, not latch the process.
2. **Either flag must have an exit.** If the replicas become readable and consistent again — as ours were within minutes — the next successful replica read should clear the block. As it stands the error text's own remedy, "restart", is the only one, and nothing tells the operator that.
3. **A node that refuses all writes must not be ready.** This is the highest-value fix: it turns a silent 7.5-hour outage into an ordinary drain. It is the same class as #5921 — a node serving nothing while `/health/ready` stays 200 — and it is the case #5936's fix cannot catch: that watchdog withdraws readiness when an in-flight object request makes no progress for [`RUSTFS_HEALTH_OBJECT_PROGRESS_TIMEOUT_MS`](https://github.com/rustfs/rustfs/blob/40a2470feb567201165a5b809b7598bb4b1f68f5/crates/config/src/constants/health.rs#L34) (30 s), and [progress is any completion](https://github.com/rustfs/rustfs/blob/40a2470feb567201165a5b809b7598bb4b1f68f5/rustfs/src/app/object_traffic_health.rs#L149-L161) — a write rejected in 9-213 ms completes instantly and never looks stalled. Readiness needs to consult the latch directly, not infer it from timing. The latch is also the shape #6285's residual describes — a node-local fault that a restart fixes and nothing restarts — so a locally-determined liveness signal would have caught it too.
4. **Log the transition, once, at error level**, naming the flag and the replica error that set it. Today the flip is silent and the only trace is a bucket-heal retry message every 15 minutes (which also lacks the bucket name).
5. **Do not surface this as a bare `InternalError`.** It is a known, named, deterministic server state; `ServiceUnavailable` (or any distinguishable code) would let clients back off and operators recognise it.

**Environment**

- RustFS `1.0.0-rc.5`, git `40a2470feb567201165a5b809b7598bb4b1f68f5` (confirmed via `rustfs --version` on the node; every link above is pinned to it).
- 4 nodes, EC 12+4, 48 disks; Rocky Linux; `RUST_LOG=warn,rustfs_ecstore::disk=info,rustfs_ecstore::store::init=info,rustfs_scanner=info,rustfs_iam=info`; `RUSTFS_OBJECT_LOCK_ACQUIRE_TIMEOUT=30` (the 5 s figure above is the internal [`DEFAULT_OBJECT_LOCK_ACQUIRE_TIMEOUT`](https://github.com/rustfs/rustfs/blob/40a2470feb567201165a5b809b7598bb4b1f68f5/crates/config/src/constants/object.rs#L500) used by `read_config`).
- Workload: five JuiceFS filesystems, continuous write + delete traffic. Affected node had been up 4 d 17 h; no restarts on any node in that period; no decommission or rebalance ever run on this cluster.

**Additional context**

*What we ruled out.* The storage layer on the node was healthy and indistinguishable from its peers: `storageinfo` reported `('ok','online',False) -> 48` on the affected and a control node; in the affected node's logs the counts for `write quorum`, `Erasure decode failed`, `DiskNotFound`, `FaultyDisk`, `insufficient` and `quorum` were all zero; the per-minute FaultyDisk short-circuit counters were flat zero on all four nodes.

*Why every mutation touches pool.bin.* Worth a look in its own right: with no decommission or rebalance ever configured, every PUT and DELETE still reads `pool.bin` from disk and takes a distributed read lock on `.rustfs.sys/pool.bin@latest` (the "target capacity admission" probe). That is what put pool.bin's lock and read on the critical path of a lock storm in the first place, and it makes pool.bin's lock the hottest lock in the cluster under write load.

*Companion reports.* The lock-RPC storm that supplied the timed-out read is reported separately (client-side 3 s timeout → stream reset → GOAWAY `too_many_resets` → evict/reconnect loop against one erasure set's lock endpoints), as is the diagnosability gap that turned this into hours of investigation (no request counters, the mapped rather than the underlying error logged, silent latch).

Happy to provide the full log windows; the failing state is reproducible on demand for us by the companion issue's storm plus one unlucky admission probe, but we would rather not induce it on production.

issue.title: Report a session that was lost rather than ended
issue.body:
**Draft, stacked on https://github.com/USTC-vlab/sshmux/pull/45 and https://github.com/USTC-vlab/sshmux/pull/47.** Only the last commit is this one's; the five below it belong to those two. It needs `PipeError` from the first, to tell a peer that said it was done from one that vanished, and `errorAttributes` from the second, to name the error.

A session that ended because a connection went away without saying so went to standard error, where the collector holding the session's own record could not see it. The line also fired on a handshake that never reached the pipe — which the session record already reports as a failure to establish — so what it said and what a record said disagreed about what had gone wrong.

It is a record instead, at `WARN`: the session happened and `sshmux` is not the one that failed, so it is not an error of its own to answer for. It names the error by its class and text beside the connection the session's record is identified by, so a collector reads the two together by `session.id`. Only a session that was piped can be lost this way, so a handshake that failed is left to the record that already describes it.

---

**Disclaimer:** This PR is drafted by [Claude Code](https://claude.com/product/claude-code), tested and reviewed.

issue.title: Move all logging onto `slog`, critical ones reported via configured `logger`
issue.body:
Sessions went through `slog` and reached the sinks. Everything `sshmux` said about *itself* went through the standard log to standard error — a different shape, on a different path, invisible to a collector: a connection it could not accept, a Prometheus endpoint that stopped serving, an exporter that would not shut down, the deprecation warnings, a startup that failed, a session whose pipe did. `log` is no longer used outside the tests.

Those errors are records at `ERROR` now, naming one of the [error classes](https://github.com/USTC-vlab/sshmux#error-classes) as `error.type` with what the error said and what it was beside it. The metrics and the tracer are built with the logger they report through, and the logger is torn down after them, being what they report through.

None of it leaves the terminal. The logger is built on the one `sshmux` says the rest through, whose handler takes every record the sinks take and prints `WARN` and above — so these reach both, while a session that ran to its end is left to the sinks. Only what has no sink to reach stays on the terminal alone: the configuration talking before there is a logger, and a failure to shut the logger down.

**`error.type` classifies more than a session's four endings** — a refused connection, an unreachable route, a peer gone mid-stream, an address in use, descriptors run out, a file missing or unreadable, a name that will not resolve. The set stays closed, but **a failure that was `other` moves out of it**, on the session, auth and upstream-dial metrics as well as these records.

An error's text and type follow the semantic conventions as `exception.message` and `exception.type`; `ecs` keeps `error.message` and drops the type. Both are in the [conventions table](https://github.com/USTC-vlab/sshmux#attribute-conventions).

The table commit is whitespace: each README table's rows laid against the columns it already had.

---

**Disclaimer:** This PR is drafted by [Claude Code](https://claude.com/product/claude-code), tested and reviewed.
