issue.title: Cycle-budget expiry rejects the bootstrap-pending usage marker: every timeout after usage-state/reset ends in recovery-required

labels.name: S-confirming
labels.description: Status: Awaiting confirmation for a resolved issue

issue.body:
**Describe the bug**

After the supported `POST /rustfs/admin/v3/scanner/usage-state/reset` (`{"mode":"full-rebuild"}`, #6972) publishes its `bootstrap-pending` marker into `buckets/.usage.v2.json`, every expiry of the scanner cycle budget (`scanner.cycle_max_duration`, default 1800 s since rc.4) fails its post-timeout epoch fence and reports `recovery_required`. The fence re-reads the usage floor through the leadership claim with `allow_bootstrap_pending` hard-coded to `false`, so the very marker the reset just published — which the startup loader and the normal claim path accept — is rejected as "no persisted baseline identity". The result, on any cluster whose first cycle after the reset takes longer than the budget, is a `leader_usage_baseline_invalid` ERROR plus a `cycle_timeout ... generation_fenced=false recovery_required=true` WARN every budget interval until a cycle completes. With the default budget that is every 30 minutes; on our 4-node cluster (~160M objects, cycle measured in days) it would have continued for the life of the cycle.

The two code paths disagree about the same marker:

- The claim path decodes the floor via [`usage_snapshot_for_epoch_fence`](https://github.com/rustfs/rustfs/blob/40a2470feb567201165a5b809b7598bb4b1f68f5/crates/scanner/src/scanner/leadership.rs#L104-L122), which accepts a `bootstrap_pending` primary only when its `allow_bootstrap_pending` argument is true; the normal leader iteration passes the allowance it derived from the startup loader, so bootstrapping works.
- [`fence_scanner_epoch_after_cycle_timeout`](https://github.com/rustfs/rustfs/blob/40a2470feb567201165a5b809b7598bb4b1f68f5/crates/scanner/src/scanner.rs#L1435-L1470) calls [`claim_scanner_leadership`](https://github.com/rustfs/rustfs/blob/40a2470feb567201165a5b809b7598bb4b1f68f5/crates/scanner/src/scanner/leadership.rs#L369-L377) with the allowance as a literal `false` ([scanner.rs:1454](https://github.com/rustfs/rustfs/blob/40a2470feb567201165a5b809b7598bb4b1f68f5/crates/scanner/src/scanner.rs#L1454)). The claim then hits the `leader_usage_baseline_invalid` arm ([leadership.rs:432-456](https://github.com/rustfs/rustfs/blob/40a2470feb567201165a5b809b7598bb4b1f68f5/crates/scanner/src/scanner/leadership.rs#L432-L456)), returns false, and [`cycle_timeout_requires_recovery`](https://github.com/rustfs/rustfs/blob/40a2470feb567201165a5b809b7598bb4b1f68f5/crates/scanner/src/scanner.rs#L1478) turns `generation_fenced == false` into `recovery_required` at the [`cycle_timeout` warn](https://github.com/rustfs/rustfs/blob/40a2470feb567201165a5b809b7598bb4b1f68f5/crates/scanner/src/scanner.rs#L1490-L1515).

**To Reproduce**

From scratch, single node, ~2 minutes — a deliberately tiny budget so every cycle expires:

```
$ docker run -d -p 127.0.0.1:19000:9000 -p 127.0.0.1:19001:9001 -e RUSTFS_ACCESS_KEY=repro -e RUSTFS_SECRET_KEY=repro-secret-1 \
    -e RUSTFS_SCANNER_CYCLE_MAX_DURATION_SECS=3 -e RUSTFS_SCANNER_CYCLE=5 -e RUSTFS_SCANNER_START_DELAY_SECS=5 rustfs/rustfs:1.0.0-rc.5
$ rc bucket create repro/budget-repro && rc put -r ./objs repro/budget-repro/      # 2400 small objects in 40 prefixes
```

1. Control — with a normal, complete usage floor, budget expiries are clean. In two independent runs, every pre-reset `cycle_timeout` line (7 in one run, 5 in the other) reads `cycle_state_persisted=true generation_fenced=true recovery_required=false`, no ERRORs (`scanner/status`: `timeouts=7, recovery_req=0, recovery=healthy`; `datausageinfo`: `usage_snapshot_complete=true, objects_total_count=2400`):

```
{"timestamp":"2026-09-02T10:50:12.623552131Z","level":"WARN","message":"Scanner cycle deadline expired; durable cursor/generation fencing completed when possible","event":"scanner_cycle_state","component":"scanner","subsystem":"runtime","state":"cycle_timeout","worker_stopped":true,"cycle_state_persisted":true,"generation_fenced":true,"recovery_required":false}
```

2. Publish the bootstrap marker with the supported reset (this needs the leader lease to be free — it lands between budget attempts):

```
POST /rustfs/admin/v3/scanner/usage-state/reset  {"mode":"full-rebuild"}
200 {"status":"reset","mode":"full-rebuild","usage_state":"bootstrap-pending","leader_epoch":15,"next_cycle":17,"reset_paths":["buckets/.usage.v2.json","buckets/.usage.v2.json.bkp"]}
```

3. From the very next expiry, every timeout fails its fence, paired in the same millisecond with the ERROR:

```
{"timestamp":"2026-09-02T10:51:05.751659114Z","level":"ERROR","message":"Scanner leadership claim deferred because the usage baseline is invalid","event":"scanner_persist_state","component":"scanner","subsystem":"runtime","path":"buckets/.usage.v2.json","state":"leader_usage_baseline_invalid","error":"Scanner error: scanner usage epoch fence from buckets/.usage.v2.json has no persisted baseline identity"}
{"timestamp":"2026-09-02T10:51:05.751741406Z","level":"WARN","message":"Scanner cycle deadline expired; durable cursor/generation fencing completed when possible","event":"scanner_cycle_state","component":"scanner","subsystem":"runtime","state":"cycle_timeout","worker_stopped":true,"cycle_state_persisted":true,"generation_fenced":false,"recovery_required":true}
```

Over the following two to three minutes: every subsequent expiry fails the same way — 16 of 16 in one run, 23 of 23 in the other, each paired with its ERROR (the first failure 3 s after the reset, then one every 8 s) — with `scanner/status` `cycle_recovery_required_total` climbing in step, `cycles_completed_at` empty, and `usage_snapshot_complete` still false. The scanner log lines live in `/logs/rustfs.log` inside the container (`RUSTFS_OBS_LOGGER_LEVEL=warn`); they do not appear on `docker logs`.

4. On our production cluster (rc.5, 4 nodes × 12 drives, EC 12+4, ~160M objects) the same pair appeared, to the second, at each of the four 30-minute expiries after we ran the reset — 16:35:02 and 17:35:23 on one leader, 17:05:04 and 18:06:18 on another — with the one difference that the fleet also reported `cycle_state_persisted=false` on every expiry (the rig reports `true`). We stopped it by setting `scanner.cycle_max_duration=0`, after which the attempt ran past 50 minutes with no further timeout or recovery.

**Expected behavior**

1. The post-timeout epoch fence should accept exactly what the normal claim path accepts: pass the bootstrap-pending allowance derived from the current floor state (or re-derive it from the primary) instead of a literal `false`. A marker the system itself published moments earlier should never be classified as an invalid baseline by another path of the same system.
2. A budget expiry during bootstrap should be an ordinary deferred attempt (`generation_fenced=true, recovery_required=false`), exactly as it is with a complete floor — the control above shows that path already works.
3. The `leader_usage_baseline_invalid` ERROR should not fire for a valid bootstrap marker; today it is indistinguishable from the genuine trap in #6969/#6907.
4. A regression test: publish the bootstrap marker (via `reset_scanner_usage_state_for_full_rebuild`), expire a cycle budget, assert the fence succeeds.

**Environment**

- 1.0.0-rc.5 (`40a2470f`), both on the 4-node production cluster and the single-node Docker rig above.
- The budget itself arrived in rc.4 via #6352, which also changed `DEFAULT_SCANNER_CYCLE_MAX_DURATION_SECS` from [`0` in rc.3](https://github.com/rustfs/rustfs/blob/1aae6803739a5bac67e0d702ac46d43f09fb06dd/crates/config/src/constants/scanner.rs#L148) to [`30 * 60`](https://github.com/rustfs/rustfs/blob/40a2470feb567201165a5b809b7598bb4b1f68f5/crates/config/src/constants/scanner.rs#L151); the reset endpoint arrived in rc.5 via #6972. The two have not met before rc.5.

**Additional context**

*Open question, unconfirmed — can a bootstrapping cluster ever leave bootstrap while the budget cuts every cycle?* On the rig, no cycle completed and the marker never resolved across 16 and 23 consecutive cut attempts in the two runs (each attempt scanning ~340 of the bucket's 2400 objects before the 3 s cut — enough visits, in aggregate, to cover the bucket several times over), on a bucket whose usage floor was complete before the reset. On the fleet, four 30-minute attempts made forward progress but completed no bucket. We could not separate two candidate causes and are not claiming either: (a) the fence failure above forces recovery on every attempt, so an attempt may never be allowed to finish; (b) the resume checkpoint [rotates a bucket's folder list to the checkpoint rather than skipping folders already walked](https://github.com/rustfs/rustfs/blob/40a2470feb567201165a5b809b7598bb4b1f68f5/crates/scanner/src/scanner_folder.rs#L423-L452), and the per-folder cache refresh is [keyed to the cycle number](https://github.com/rustfs/rustfs/blob/40a2470feb567201165a5b809b7598bb4b1f68f5/crates/scanner/src/scanner_folder.rs#L1792-L1794), which is constant across attempts — so a bucket whose full walk exceeds the budget might never be *completed* within any single attempt regardless of the fence. If (b) holds, the rc.4 default of 1800 s changes cycle semantics on large namespaces (our rc.3 cycles ran for days uninterrupted), and that change was not release-noted; a note pointing operators of large clusters at `cycle_max_duration=0` (the [documented off switch](https://github.com/rustfs/rustfs/blob/40a2470feb567201165a5b809b7598bb4b1f68f5/docs/operations/scanner-runtime-controls.md#L55)) would have saved us an afternoon. If (a) is the whole story, fixing the fence closes this too. We are happy to test either hypothesis on the fleet once the fence is fixed.

*Two smaller observations from the same session.* The fleet reported `cycle_state_persisted=false` on every expiry while the rig reports `true`; the docs say the cursor is confirmed durable when the worker stops cooperatively (`worker_stopped=true` in both), so this may be a second, cluster-only defect — logs available. And `usage-state/reset` on a healthy single node returned `500 InternalError: scanner leader lock is busy: Lock acquisition timeout ... after 5s` on eight consecutive tries, because a healthy leader holds its lease continuously; harmless (a healthy node does not need the reset) but a 409-style "scanner is leading, nothing to reset" would read better than a 500.

issue.title: Scanner permanently stops on rc.4 when the persisted usage floor is an epoch-bearing incomplete snapshot inherited from rc.2/rc.3 (usage_floor_load_failed, no recovery path)

labels.name: S-confirming
labels.description: Status: Awaiting confirmation for a resolved issue

issue.body:
> **Rewritten 2026-08-30.** The original report blamed `RUSTFS_SCANNER_CYCLE`; that was wrong (I closed the issue while we investigated). A/B testing falsified the env-var theory, clean-room installs ruled out rc.4 itself, and the file logs plus the rc.4 source revealed the actual root cause below. Same clusters, same symptom — corrected diagnosis.

## Summary

On rc.4, `data_usage_info_has_persisted_baseline_identity()` (crates/scanner/src/scanner.rs:388) accepts a persisted `buckets/.usage.v2.json` only if it is (a) a complete snapshot, or (b) a pre-marker legacy snapshot with **no** `scanner_epoch`. A snapshot that carries `scanner_epoch` but has `usage_snapshot_complete:false` fails both branches, and cycle-state loading (crates/scanner/src/scanner/cycle_state.rs:1357) turns that into a hard error:

```
ERROR Scanner stopped because the persisted usage floor could not be loaded
      event=scanner_persist_state path="buckets/.usage.v2.json"
      state=usage_floor_load_failed
      error="Scanner error: scanner usage floor from buckets/.usage.v2.json has no persisted baseline identity"
      (crates/scanner/src/scanner.rs:2195)
```

Because the scanner stops **before** it would ever rewrite the floor, the state is a deadlock: every scheduled attempt fails identically, forever. Both our production clusters (the same ones from #6218/#6219/#6804/#6313 — 3 nodes × 2 drives, EC 4+2) have been in this state since upgrading rc.3 → rc.4, on every node. The scheduler itself is fine: attempts fire on cadence (hourly with `RUSTFS_SCANNER_CYCLE=3600`, every ~60 s at defaults — which is what misled the original report), each one dying on the same load error.

Where the poisoned snapshot came from: our persisted `.usage.v2.json` has `scanner_epoch:9`, `usage_snapshot_complete:false`, zeroed totals, and a `last_update` frozen ~10 days before the upgrade — i.e. it was left behind by the usage-census collapse era we reported in #6804 (fixed by #6811, which is not in rc.4). rc.2/rc.3 tolerated that file indefinitely; rc.4's new strict check refuses it with no way out.

## Why it looks like a silent scheduler stall

- `scanner/status` shows nothing wrong except `effective_interval_available:false`, `current_cycle:0`, freshness "no completed cycle recorded". The load error is not surfaced there.
- The ERROR line only appears in the file logs, once per scheduled attempt.
- Leader metrics are misleading in this state: on both clusters **every node** reports `execution_role:"leader", leader_lock_state:"acquired", held_by_this_process:true`. Our reading: each node acquires the lease, dies on the floor load, the lease lapses and rotates; the status endpoint keeps showing the last successful acquisition. On healthy clusters we see the expected 1 leader + N followers ("contended").

## Verification matrix (rc.4 = digest `a9fbb5e5…`, rc.3 = `800cf3f3…`)

| setup | scanner |
|---|---|
| fresh rc.4 single node (4 dirs) | ✅ cycles within ~2 min |
| fresh rc.4 3-node cluster, HTTP | ✅ 1 leader, cycles fine |
| fresh rc.4 3-node cluster, TLS (self-signed, same file layout as prod) | ✅ |
| rc.4 3-node TLS cluster through our production rolling-restart pattern (restart node3, node2, stop leader 180 s, start) | ✅ converges back to 1 leader |
| fresh rc.3 single node → stop → rc.4 on the same dirs | ✅ (rc.3 had written `usage_snapshot_complete:true`, so the baseline check passes; `scanner_epoch` bumped and cycles continue) |
| production clusters upgraded rc.2→rc.3→rc.4 carrying an incomplete epoch-bearing snapshot | ❌ permanent `usage_floor_load_failed` loop on every node |

So a clean install — and even a clean rc.3→rc.4 upgrade — is fine; the trap needs a snapshot in exactly the state that the rc.2/rc.3 census bug (#6804) left behind: `scanner_epoch` present, `usage_snapshot_complete:false`. Also falsified along the way: `RUSTFS_SCANNER_CYCLE` removed on one whole production cluster (full rolling restart, defaults everywhere) — the stall was unchanged.

## Impact

- usage census and ILM processing fully stalled since the rc.4 upgrade (lifecycle deletions no longer issued);
- background heal proper unaffected (observed a version-stack reconciliation completing during the stall, see #6218);
- silent from the admin API; only the file logs tell the truth.

## Workaround (verified in production — two traps, not one)

Removing the poisoned floor alone is **not** sufficient on a long-lived cluster. After we did that in production, the scanner scheduled again but every cycle ended within milliseconds as `last_cycle_result:"deferred"` — no walk, no ops, adaptive interval backing off forever, and once more nothing wrong visible in `scanner/status`. The file logs showed a second leftover-state trap:

```
WARN Scanner rejected a set cache cycle regression
     event=scanner_cache_persist_state cache_name=".usage-cache.bin"
     requested_cycle=0 cached_cycle=17118 state="stale_cycle_rejected"
     (crates/scanner/src/scanner_io/io_cache.rs:297)
```

The surviving `.usage-cache.bin` objects (top-level **and per-bucket**) carry the old cycle counter (17118 after months of rc.1/rc.2 60-second walks); the freshly bootstrapped floor restarts numbering at 0, so the cycle-regression guard rejects every new cycle. A young test cluster never trips this (its counters are small), which is why our clean-room validation missed it.

**Complete workaround**: with the whole cluster stopped (all nodes — otherwise heal resurrects the objects from the remaining copies), move aside on **every drive** under `.rustfs.sys/buckets/`:

- `.usage.v2.json`, `.usage.v2.json.bkp`, `.usage.json`, `.usage.json.bkp` (the floor),
- `.usage-cache.bin`, `.usage-cache.bin.bkp`, `.usage.observed.json` (top level),
- `<bucket>/.usage-cache.bin`, `<bucket>/.usage-cache.bin.bkp` (per bucket),

then start all nodes. Verified on our first production cluster: healthy leadership (1 leader + followers "contended"), real scanning within a minute (life_time_ops going 964 → 72k while rebuilding the census, per-bucket caches regenerated), zero `usage_floor_load_failed` / `stale_cycle_rejected` afterwards.

## Suggestions

1. Treat an identity-less (epoch-bearing, incomplete) snapshot as *recoverable*: log, quarantine the object (as `DATA_USAGE_BLOOM_RECOVERY_PATH` already does for undecodable cycle state), and fall back to the bootstrap path — instead of a permanent hard error. Any cluster that lived through the #6804 era and upgrades to rc.4 will otherwise stall silently.
2. Surface `usage_floor_load_failed` in `scanner/status` (e.g. in `cycle_recovery.state` or `freshness.reason`) so the condition is visible without file-log access.
3. Make the cycle-regression guard recoverable too: when the persisted floor legitimately restarts at cycle 0 (bootstrap after recovery), stale caches with a higher `cached_cycle` should be quarantined/adopted rather than deferring every cycle forever — and a permanently-deferred cycle deserves a visible status reason as well.

Happy to test a patch/nightly on the affected clusters and report back within a day, as usual. Raw snapshots (sanitized) and full logs available on request.

comment.body: Same guard, same provenance, one step further along: our rc.3 → rc.5 cluster hit `usage_floor_load_failed` on an epoch-bearing incomplete snapshot exactly as described here, except ours carried real bucket totals rather than zeroed ones — so it falls outside the byte-exact empty shape #6914 accepts and is still fail-closed on rc.5 and `main`. Full trace (why the rc.1-rc.3 leadership fence produces this shape on every claim, why a small control cluster cannot reproduce it, and confirmation that #6972's `usage-state/reset` recovers it on the failing cluster) is in https://github.com/rustfs/rustfs/issues/6969#issuecomment-5506825015. The residual ask is the one you made in (1): treat a pre-marker floor with data but no completed cycle as recoverable rather than terminal.

issue.title: Scanner refuses to run after rolling upgrade on a 40-node cluster: usage floor has no persisted baseline identity (1.0.0-rc.4); preceded by scanner_cycle_mismatch fence deadlock (rc.2/rc.3)

labels.name: S-confirming
labels.description: Status: Awaiting confirmation for a resolved issue

issue.body:
## Environment

- RustFS `1.0.0-rc.2` → `rc.3` → `rc.4`, musl static builds (hosts run glibc 2.38)
- 40 nodes × 10 HDDs = 400 drives, single pool, EC parity 4, ~45 buckets, ~64k objects
- Upgrades done as rolling restarts (4 nodes per batch), systemd managed
- A 4-node test cluster went through the exact same version chain (control group)

## Timeline

### 1) On rc.2 and rc.3: ns_scanner fence deadlock

After every full-cluster rolling restart, all nodes continuously reject internode scanner RPCs:

```json
{"message":"internode rpc request rejected","reason":"scanner_cycle_mismatch","rpc_path":"/rustfs/rpc/ns_scanner","method":"POST","status_code":409,"error":"Scanner error: remote namespace scanner fence does not match persisted state: requested_cycle=60925, persisted_cycle=60924, requested_epoch=10, persisted_epoch=10"}
```

- Persistent off-by-one between `requested_cycle` and `persisted_cycle`; epochs match on both sides
- Uniform on all 40 nodes, ~260 rejects/hour/node; observed continuously for days, never converges
- Effects: data usage never rebuilds (`Objects: 0` in `admin info`), `mc du` times out, auto-heal and ILM effectively stalled; the S3 data plane is fully unaffected
- The state survived full-cluster restarts and the rc.2→rc.3 upgrade unchanged

### 2) On rc.4: fence deadlock is gone, but the scanner now refuses to start

With rc.4 (containing #6624, which fixes #6135) the `scanner_cycle_mismatch` rejections are gone — 0 for 24h+, where rc.2/rc.3 re-deadlocked within ~2h after every restart. Thank you for that fix.

New blocker, exactly once per minute on every node:

```json
{"level":"ERROR","message":"Scanner stopped because the persisted usage floor could not be loaded","event":"scanner_persist_state","component":"scanner","subsystem":"runtime","path":"buckets/.usage.v2.json","state":"usage_floor_load_failed","error":"Scanner error: scanner usage floor from buckets/.usage.v2.json has no persisted baseline identity"}
```

## What we tried (usage still not rebuilt)

1. **Full rolling restarts (twice)** — no change.
2. **Removed the persisted floor objects from all disks** (raw filesystem level: `.rustfs.sys/buckets/.usage.v2.json` and `.usage.v2.json.bkp`, 16 shards each, forensic copies kept), then performed a full rolling restart. rc.4's bootstrap path wrote a NEW floor object (xl.meta present, ~27 KB inline payload) — and the scanner STILL reports `has no persisted baseline identity` against the freshly bootstrapped floor, so no scan ever starts.

This looks like a chicken-and-egg state: the bootstrap floor carries no baseline identity → the loader refuses to run the scanner → no completed scan ever publishes an identified/authoritative floor.

## Control group

A 4-node cluster upgraded through the exact same version chain has fully working usage (correct object counts, no floor errors, scanner quiet). Only the 40-node cluster with rc.2/rc.3 deadlock history triggers the refusal — consistent with the "larger clusters after upgrade" pattern of the #6135 family.

## Additional notes

- The `.rustfs.sys` system namespace is not addressable through the S3 API (server returns `InvalidBucketName` for `.rustfs.sys` / `.minio.sys`), and `mc` rejects those bucket names client-side — so there is currently no supported admin surface to reset usage state; we had to operate on raw disk shards. An admin command to reset/rebuild usage state would be very helpful for this class of failures.
- We enumerated the `RUSTFS_SCANNER_*` environment knobs present in the rc.4 binary; none appear to bypass the floor identity check.
- Auto-heal and ILM remain stalled for the whole duration (data plane unaffected), which is the main operational risk for us.

## Questions

1. Is there a supported procedure to force a usage-floor rebuild on a large upgraded cluster?
2. Should the bootstrap path produce a floor the loader accepts as non-authoritative (per #6624's description) so the first scan can complete and later publish an authoritative floor?

Happy to provide full logs, forensic copies of the floor objects, and any further reproduction details.

comment.body:
We hit the same guard on a 4-node cluster upgrading 1.0.0-rc.3 → 1.0.0-rc.5 (~150M objects, bare metal), and since we could read the persisted state off the drives and trace it through the source, here is what we found — including why a small control cluster does not reproduce it, and confirmation that #6972 recovers it.

**Symptom.** Identical to your phase 2, with rc.5's rewording of the same check: every node takes the scanner leader lock, fails to load the usage floor with `persisted scanner usage floor from buckets/.usage.v2.json has no authoritative baseline or newer valid backup` (`state=usage_floor_load_failed`), releases the lock, and the next node repeats — every 5-10 s, on all four nodes, from the moment the roll completed. No cycle ever starts, and nothing a restart does can change that. Your rc.4 string `scanner usage floor from ... has no persisted baseline identity` is the same rejection from the same function; the message was reworded in rc.5.

**What is being rejected.** All four usage slots were intact. Decoded, the v2 primary carried real data — `buckets_count = 2` (two entries), `objects_total_count = 156382067`, `last_update = 2026-08-27` — with `usage_snapshot_complete = false`, `scanner_epoch = 13`, and `scanner_cycle` absent. The legacy `buckets/.usage.json` beside it had the same data with both `scanner_epoch` and `scanner_cycle` absent.

**Why the guard rejects it.** [`data_usage_info_has_persisted_baseline_identity`](https://github.com/rustfs/rustfs/blob/40a2470feb567201165a5b809b7598bb4b1f68f5/crates/scanner/src/scanner.rs#L536-L552) accepts a snapshot either because [`is_complete_bucket_usage_snapshot`](https://github.com/rustfs/rustfs/blob/40a2470feb567201165a5b809b7598bb4b1f68f5/crates/data-usage/src/data_usage.rs#L1968-L1973) holds (`usage_snapshot_complete == true`), or via the pre-marker legacy identity, which requires among other things `scanner_epoch.is_none() && scanner_cycle.is_some()`. Only a completed cycle sets `usage_snapshot_complete`. And the previous release writes the exact inverse of the legacy clause as a matter of routine: rc.3's [`fence_scanner_usage_epoch`](https://github.com/rustfs/rustfs/blob/1aae6803739a5bac67e0d702ac46d43f09fb06dd/crates/scanner/src/scanner/leadership.rs#L98-L122) runs on every leadership claim, decodes the persisted primary as-is, sets `scanner_epoch = Some(claimed_epoch)`, and writes the whole snapshot back with `scanner_cycle` untouched (the same fence exists in rc.1 and rc.2). So any cluster whose scanner produced usage data but did not finish a cycle before the upgrade arrives at rc.4/rc.5 with a floor that has `scanner_epoch` set, no `scanner_cycle`, and `complete = false` — which fails both routes. Our `scanner_epoch = 13` is just the number of leadership claims since the last completed cycle (2026-07-24 for us), not corruption.

**This is why scale appears to matter.** It is not cluster size as such; it is whether a cycle completed before the upgrade. A small control cluster finishes a cycle every few seconds, so its floor always has `complete = true` and is accepted — we confirmed that with a two-phase Docker rig (rc.3 write → rc.5 on the same volume), which does *not* reproduce. A 40-node or 150M-object cluster that could not finish a cycle has `complete = false`, and the fence has stamped an epoch on it, so it is rejected. That matches your 40-node vs 4-node observation exactly.

**Why #6914 does not cover it.** [`legacy_empty_usage_fence_epoch`](https://github.com/rustfs/rustfs/blob/40a2470feb567201165a5b809b7598bb4b1f68f5/crates/scanner/src/scanner/cycle_state.rs#L1717-L1762) accepts only a snapshot that is byte-for-byte the *empty* rc.2/rc.3 fence (`last_update` and optionally `scanner_epoch`, exactly the fourteen listed JSON fields) — the #6907 case. A snapshot with bucket data is marked `unrecoverable_baseline_path`, which also disables the auto-recovery branch ([cycle_state.rs:2293-2309](https://github.com/rustfs/rustfs/blob/40a2470feb567201165a5b809b7598bb4b1f68f5/crates/scanner/src/scanner/cycle_state.rs#L2293-L2309)), and the loader returns the error at [cycle_state.rs:2318-2321](https://github.com/rustfs/rustfs/blob/40a2470feb567201165a5b809b7598bb4b1f68f5/crates/scanner/src/scanner/cycle_state.rs#L2318-L2321) before the missing-state bootstrap is reached. That is the #6907 shape (zeroed totals, `scanner_epoch` set, `complete = false`); ours differs only in carrying real totals and bucket entries, which is what puts it outside the fourteen-field exact match. So the empty case was fixed; the non-empty case — arguably the common one for any real cluster whose scanner had run — is still open.

**#6972 recovers it (confirmed on the failing cluster).** We ran `POST /rustfs/admin/v3/scanner/usage-state/reset` `{"mode":"full-rebuild"}` once ([handler](https://github.com/rustfs/rustfs/blob/40a2470feb567201165a5b809b7598bb4b1f68f5/rustfs/src/admin/handlers/scanner.rs#L349-L380), [doc](https://github.com/rustfs/rustfs/blob/40a2470feb567201165a5b809b7598bb4b1f68f5/docs/operations/scanner-runtime-controls.md#L190-L240)). Response: `{"status":"reset","usage_state":"bootstrap-pending","leader_epoch":14,"next_cycle":9846,"reset_paths":[all four slots]}`; two seconds later a node held `leader.lock` and started cycle 9846 (~80k objects/min, set scans and heals active), `scanner/status` went from `usage_floor_load_failed` to `healthy`, and the ERROR stopped on all four nodes (5 per node in the ten minutes before, 0 after). It works because [`reset_scanner_usage_state_for_full_rebuild`](https://github.com/rustfs/rustfs/blob/40a2470feb567201165a5b809b7598bb4b1f68f5/crates/scanner/src/scanner/cycle_state.rs#L1498) only decodes the slots to take the max epoch — it never applies the identity check that trapped the loader. So for your ask 1, on rc.5 that endpoint is the supported procedure; on rc.4 there is none — neither #6914 nor #6972 is in rc.4 — and the only route is deleting all four slots by hand.

**On your ask 2 (fresh floors rejected after bootstrap).** A hypothesis worth checking against your logs rather than a finding: rc.4's own bootstrap marker *is* accepted (both the fence and the loader special-case `bootstrap_pending`), but any snapshot that an rc.3 node's leadership fence touches gets `scanner_epoch` stamped without `scanner_cycle` — the trapping shape. In a 40-node *rolling* upgrade there is a window in which an rc.3 node can win leadership and re-stamp a floor that rc.4 nodes then reject; a small cluster rolls too fast for that to happen. If the rejected fresh floors had `scanner_epoch` set and `usage_snapshot_bootstrap_pending` cleared, that would be it.

**What we would suggest.** (1) A pre-marker floor that carries bucket data but no completed cycle should be treated as *missing* (bootstrap) rather than fatal — or the #6914 hatch widened to accept it; our legacy slot fails the pre-marker identity on the single clause `scanner_cycle.is_some()`, and `scanner_epoch.is_none()` is unsatisfiable for any floor the rc.1-rc.3 fence has touched, which is all of them. (2) The `usage_floor_load_failed` error and `scanner/status` should name `usage-state/reset` — we found it only by reading the source, and the message currently names a path and stops. (3) A regression test that loads the fence-written shape (`last_update`, `scanner_epoch: Some(n)`, `scanner_cycle: None`, `complete: false`, `buckets_count == buckets_usage.len()`) against `persisted_usage_floor_for_startup(store, true)`, since that shape is what the released code produced. (4) Whether rc.4 remains a supported upgrade source — if so, its users need (1).

issue.title: rc.5 refuses to start with RUSTFS_SERVER_DOMAINS set

labels.name: S-confirming
labels.description: Status: Awaiting confirmation for a resolved issue

issue.body:
**Describe the bug**

A node running 1.0.0-rc.5 refuses to start whenever `RUSTFS_SERVER_DOMAINS` is set to anything other than `<domain>:<listening port>`, exiting fatally about half a second in:

```
[FATAL] Server runtime failed: Some subdomains overlap with each other
```

```json
{"timestamp":"2026-09-02T11:00:44.094397304+08:00","level":"ERROR","message":"Server runtime failed","event":"server_runtime_failed","component":"main","subsystem":"startup","error":"Some subdomains overlap with each other","target":"rustfs::main","filename":"rustfs/src/startup_entrypoint.rs","line_number":125}
```

We hit this rolling a 4-node cluster from rc.3 to rc.5: the first node crash-looped through three restarts and was rolled back. The same configuration starts fine on rc.3 and rc.4. The console setting is irrelevant (see root cause), and a single configured domain is enough.

Our deployment is the typical production shape, which is exactly the one that fails: RustFS sits behind a reverse proxy (HAProxy on every node, proxying to the local RustFS backend on `:9000` over TLS), clients address `oss.example.com` on the proxy's port, and the proxy forwards the Host header unchanged. The listening port therefore never appears in any Host header RustFS sees, so `RUSTFS_SERVER_DOMAINS=oss.example.com` — the bare form — is the natural and correct configuration, and it is the form rc.5 rejects. The only value that survives, `oss.example.com:9000`, names a port no client ever sends.

**To Reproduce**

Standalone in Docker, no cluster needed:

```bash
docker run --rm --user 0:0 --tmpfs /data:rw,size=256m,mode=1777 \
  -e RUSTFS_ACCESS_KEY=testkey -e RUSTFS_SECRET_KEY=testsecret123 \
  -e RUSTFS_VOLUMES=/data -e RUSTFS_ADDRESS=:9000 -e RUSTFS_CONSOLE_ADDRESS=:9001 \
  -e RUSTFS_SERVER_DOMAINS=oss.example.com \
  rustfs/rustfs:1.0.0-rc.5
```

Matrix against `rustfs/rustfs:1.0.0-rc.5` (binary `git commit 40a2470feb567201165a5b809b7598bb4b1f68f5`, `git tag 1.0.0-rc.5`), listening on `:9000`:

| `RUSTFS_SERVER_DOMAINS` | `RUSTFS_CONSOLE_ENABLE` | result |
|---|---|---|
| `oss.example.com` | `true` | **fatal: subdomains overlap** |
| `oss.example.com` | `false` | **fatal: subdomains overlap** |
| `oss.example.com` | unset (default) | **fatal: subdomains overlap** |
| `oss.example.com:9000` (listening port) | `true` | starts normally |
| `oss.example.com:1234` (any other port) | `true` | **fatal: subdomains overlap** |
| `a.example.com:9000,b.example.com:9000` | `true` | starts normally |
| unset | `false` | starts normally |

**Expected behavior**

1. A node with `RUSTFS_SERVER_DOMAINS` set should start. The safe fix is to deduplicate the expanded domain set by port-stripped host before constructing `MultiDomain` — see root cause for why simply deleting the port-variant expansion is *not* safe on its own: the rate-limit layer's bucket extraction still exact-matches that expanded set, so dropping it would silently stop attributing port-carrying virtual-hosted requests to their bucket. Dropping the expansion is fine if `request_bucket` is made port-agnostic in the same change (mirroring s3s's `strip_port_suffix`).
2. The error should name the offending entries. `Some subdomains overlap with each other` gives an operator nothing to act on — and here the two "overlapping" entries were generated by the server itself from one configured value.
3. Worth raising in s3s as well: two entries that are equal after stripping the port are the same domain written twice, not an ambiguity, and could be deduplicated instead of rejected (the genuine `example.com` vs `s3.example.com` overlap should of course stay rejected).
4. A CI boot with `RUSTFS_SERVER_DOMAINS` set. No workflow currently starts a node with it configured — the only touchpoint is [`scripts/test/site_replication_smoke.py`](https://github.com/rustfs/rustfs/blob/40a2470feb567201165a5b809b7598bb4b1f68f5/scripts/test/site_replication_smoke.py#L241), which is not wired into any workflow and which happens to use the `127.0.0.1:<listening port>` form — the one form immune to this bug. An E2E case that boots with a bare domain (the form every proxy-fronted deployment uses) and a `domain:<other port>` form, asserts readiness, and issues one virtual-hosted-style request to confirm bucket resolution would have caught this; this class of change — a dependency bump altering host-matching semantics — is exactly what unit tests do not see.

**Environment**

- 1.0.0-rc.5 (`40a2470f`), both `rustfs/rustfs:1.0.0-rc.5` and a distribution binary of the same commit; reproduced on a 4-node erasure-coded bare-metal cluster and standalone in Docker.
- rc.3 (`1aae6803`) and rc.4 (`44f3f0e7`) with the identical configuration are unaffected.
- Current `main` (`b422d1fe`, 2026-09-02) still carries the identical expansion block ([`http.rs:1207-1217`](https://github.com/rustfs/rustfs/blob/b422d1fea973cb9d09001e36b7ebeab214d711b0/rustfs/src/server/http.rs#L1207-L1217)) and the same s3s pin, so it is affected too.

**Additional context**

*Root cause.* [`start_http_server`](https://github.com/rustfs/rustfs/blob/40a2470feb567201165a5b809b7598bb4b1f68f5/rustfs/src/server/http.rs#L883-L902) expands every configured domain into two entries, the value as given and a variant carrying the listening port:

```rust
for domain in &config.server_domains {
    domain_sets.insert(domain.to_string());
    if let Some((host, _)) = domain.split_once(':') {
        domain_sets.insert(format!("{host}:{local_port}"));
    } else {
        domain_sets.insert(format!("{domain}:{local_port}"));
    }
}
```

The validate-only call on the raw list ([`http.rs:886`](https://github.com/rustfs/rustfs/blob/40a2470feb567201165a5b809b7598bb4b1f68f5/rustfs/src/server/http.rs#L886)) passes — one entry. The failure is the first `MultiDomain::new` built from the *expanded* set, the metadata-route host at [`http.rs:916-920`](https://github.com/rustfs/rustfs/blob/40a2470feb567201165a5b809b7598bb4b1f68f5/rustfs/src/server/http.rs#L916-L920) (the `set_host` call at [`http.rs:937-949`](https://github.com/rustfs/rustfs/blob/40a2470feb567201165a5b809b7598bb4b1f68f5/rustfs/src/server/http.rs#L937-L949) would fail identically but is never reached).

Whether that set is self-overlapping depends on s3s. At rc.3's pin (`ed70cb04`, 0.15.0-alpha.1) the overlap check was exact-string — [`is_overlapping`](https://github.com/rustfs/s3s/blob/ed70cb048cc4be168419d461cb9ac3c2c7fa6d5a/crates/s3s/src/host.rs#L220-L222) is `a == b || is_subdomain_of(a, b) || is_subdomain_of(b, a)` — and request matching retained the port ([`parse_host_header`](https://github.com/rustfs/s3s/blob/ed70cb048cc4be168419d461cb9ac3c2c7fa6d5a/crates/s3s/src/host.rs#L229)). Under those semantics the port variant was load-bearing: it is what made `Host: oss.example.com:9000` match at all. s3s commit [`794e4940`](https://github.com/rustfs/s3s/commit/794e49406e6e612d01fe49ad5df697164724d08a) (rustfs/s3s#764, 2026-08-29, marked breaking with `!`: "ignore explicit ports when matching virtual-hosted base domains") added [`strip_port_suffix`](https://github.com/rustfs/s3s/blob/28e9ebb23dd2fb7d667084f34121b4aa4807a5c6/crates/s3s/src/host.rs#L206) and applied it both in [`parse_host_header`](https://github.com/rustfs/s3s/blob/28e9ebb23dd2fb7d667084f34121b4aa4807a5c6/crates/s3s/src/host.rs#L265) and in [`is_overlapping`](https://github.com/rustfs/s3s/blob/28e9ebb23dd2fb7d667084f34121b4aa4807a5c6/crates/s3s/src/host.rs#L254-L258), so [`MultiDomain::new`](https://github.com/rustfs/s3s/blob/28e9ebb23dd2fb7d667084f34121b4aa4807a5c6/crates/s3s/src/host.rs#L398-L414) now returns `OverlappingSubdomains` for exactly the shape rustfs generates. The commit message is explicit about it — "`["example.com", "example.com:8080"]` is now rejected as overlapping instead of producing iteration-order-dependent routing" — it adds the test `multi_domain_new_overlap_ignores_ports` for that list, and in the same commit s3s deleted the `--domain localhost:8014` duplicate from its own four e2e scripts, keeping only `--domain localhost`. The matrix follows directly: `oss.example.com:9000` makes the two inserts identical (the `HashSet` collapses them, one entry, no overlap); any other value yields two entries that strip to the same host.

*Which rustfs change shipped it.* rustfs's own domain code is unchanged between rc.3 ([`http.rs:876-886`](https://github.com/rustfs/rustfs/blob/1aae6803739a5bac67e0d702ac46d43f09fb06dd/rustfs/src/server/http.rs#L876-L886)) and rc.5. The s3s pin moved from `ed70cb04` (rc.3) through #6545, #6665 and #6795 (`6e7b4125`, 2026-08-28 — still 23 commits *before* 794e4940) and rc.4's `0f6f83d9` (2026-08-27, also before it), to #6981 (`c8f575e3`, 2026-09-01 — the first pin that contains 794e4940, in an object-metadata DTO adaptation that crossed the breaking commit incidentally) and #6990 (`28e9ebb2`, [rc.5's pin](https://github.com/rustfs/rustfs/blob/40a2470feb567201165a5b809b7598bb4b1f68f5/Cargo.toml#L310)). So the regression entered with #6981 and first shipped in rc.5; rc.4 is clean.

*Why the console setting does not matter.* The expansion block is guarded by `!config.console_enable`, which looks like it should skip the whole thing when the console is on. It never does for the S3 listener: [`s3_http_server_config`](https://github.com/rustfs/rustfs/blob/40a2470feb567201165a5b809b7598bb4b1f68f5/rustfs/src/startup_server.rs#L329-L333) clones the config and forces `console_enable = false` before `start_http_server` is called for the S3 port, with the console served by a [second listener](https://github.com/rustfs/rustfs/blob/40a2470feb567201165a5b809b7598bb4b1f68f5/rustfs/src/startup_server.rs#L335-L349). The guard is effectively "is this the S3 listener", and the comment above `set_host` ("only ... when server domains are configured and console is disabled") is stale. This split already exists in rc.3, so it is not part of the regression — it is just why every console setting in the matrix behaves the same.

*Why the fix must account for the rate limiter.* The expanded set is also handed to the API rate-limit layer ([`http.rs:903`](https://github.com/rustfs/rustfs/blob/40a2470feb567201165a5b809b7598bb4b1f68f5/rustfs/src/server/http.rs#L903)), whose [`request_bucket`](https://github.com/rustfs/rustfs/blob/40a2470feb567201165a5b809b7598bb4b1f68f5/rustfs/src/server/rate_limit.rs#L348-L371) matches the request Host against those entries with exact, [explicitly port-inclusive](https://github.com/rustfs/rustfs/blob/40a2470feb567201165a5b809b7598bb4b1f68f5/rustfs/src/server/rate_limit.rs#L321-L334) string comparison — its doc comment says it "mirrors s3s host routing", which stopped being true at 794e4940. With the port variants removed and no other change, a request with `Host: bucket.oss.example.com:9000` would still route correctly (s3s strips the port) but would no longer be attributed to `bucket` for per-bucket rate limiting. Hence the recommendation above: dedupe by stripped host for the `MultiDomain` construction, or make `request_bucket` port-agnostic and then drop the expansion.

*Workaround for operators.* Configure the domain with the node's listening port:

```
RUSTFS_SERVER_DOMAINS="oss.example.com:9000"
```

Behind a reverse proxy this looks wrong — `9000` is the internal backend port, invisible to clients — but it works because s3s now strips ports on both sides before matching, so the entry matches a forwarded `Host: bucket.oss.example.com` (or `:443`) all the same. It is not merely a startup dodge — we verified virtual-hosted routing end to end on rc.5 with that setting: after a path-style `PUT /vhbucket`, a SigV4 `GET /?list-type=2` sent with `Host: vhbucket.oss.example.com` (no port) returned that bucket's `ListBucketResult`, while the same request against the bare endpoint returned `ListAllMyBucketsResult`. Clearing the variable also avoids the crash but disables virtual-hosted-style resolution, so it is not equivalent.

issue.body:
**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**
RustFS console now displays scanner status in `/rustfs/console/status` from the local node. This doesn't reflect the cluster status, where normally should have a single scanner running and others idle. 

**Describe the solution you'd like**
The console should display the working scanner status instead, making it a cluster-wide probe, matching the other statuses on the page.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**
N/A

**Additional context**
We've encountered many of scanner failures and reported some of them as issues. To get the scanner status, we now have to maintain a script to scrape scanner info from each node's `localhost`. Giving RustFS console cluster-wide information while keeping the admin API / metrics local should provide a clean split and more convenient debugging experience.

issue.title: fix(ecstore): reclaim stale object prefixes
issue.body:
## Related Issues

Fixes #6898.

## Summary of Changes

Reclaim stale directory prefixes after an exact empty recursive `max-keys=1` listing proves that a prefix has no live objects. Cleanup is limited to authoritative never-versioned buckets, preserves the bounded non-recursive listing fast path from #6174, and removes only empty directories or individually classified files in UUID data directories carrying a valid committed delete marker.

## Verification

- `cargo fmt --all --check`
- `git diff --check`
- `./scripts/check_logging_guardrails.sh`
- `cargo +1.97.1 clippy -p rustfs-ecstore --lib --ignore-rust-version -- -D warnings`
- `cargo +1.97.1 test -p rustfs-ecstore orphan_dir_entries_must_be_single_relative_components --lib --ignore-rust-version`
- `cargo +1.97.1 test -p rustfs-ecstore orphan_cleanup_preserves_object_published_after_scan --lib --ignore-rust-version`
- `cargo +1.97.1 test -p rustfs-ecstore orphan_cleanup_keeps_commit_marker_when_residue_delete_fails --lib --ignore-rust-version`
- `cargo +1.97.1 test -p rustfs-ecstore purge_orphan_dir_object_ --lib --ignore-rust-version`
- `cargo +1.97.1 test -p rustfs-ecstore empty_directory_listing_purge_requires_complete_exact_recursive_request --lib --ignore-rust-version`
- `cargo +1.97.1 test -p rustfs-ecstore empty_recursive_listing_purges_committed_delete_residue --lib --ignore-rust-version`
- `cargo +1.97.1 test -p rustfs-ecstore test_scan_dir_nonrecursive_fast_path_preserves_probe_bound --lib --ignore-rust-version`
- `make pre-pr` completed every pre-test gate before the rebase; the test phase hit an unrelated host-capacity failure in the rebalance test.
- `cargo nextest run --all --exclude e2e_test --no-fail-fast`: 15,742 passed, 3 failed before the rebase. Both non-capacity failures passed in isolation; the rebalance test consistently requires about 12.3 TB while the host has about 1.81 TB available.
- `cargo test -p rustfs-ecstore --features test-util prepared_snapshot_transition_duplicate_and_late_get_use_committed_remote_generation --lib -- --nocapture`
- `cargo nextest run -p rustfs-ecstore --features test-util decommission_entry_rejects_subquorum_free_version_conflict_and_retains_source --no-capture`

## Impact

Users can remove stale prefixes left by interrupted delete cleanup without reintroducing the large metadata-probe regression from #6174. Versioned, ambiguous, malformed, non-authoritative, or path-escaping disk state fails closed and retains the conservative behavior.

## Additional Notes

- Correctness: cleanup requires a complete empty exact-prefix result and rescans every online disk before deletion.
- Security: malformed markers, `xl.meta`, uncommitted data, and disk/RPC entries that are not single relative path components veto cleanup.
- Concurrency and durability: only files classified during the scan are removed, committed markers are deleted last so failures remain retryable, and every directory removal is non-recursive so a concurrent object publication survives.
- Compatibility: versioned and legacy-ambiguous buckets keep conservative prefix verification, with no on-disk or wire-format change.
- Performance: top-level delimiter listings retain zero recursive visibility probes; cleanup is restricted to the `max-keys=1` request shape used by recursive removal.
- Tests: request gating, committed and malformed residue, concurrent publication, partial-delete retryability, path-component validation, nested metadata, physical probe bounds, and the end-to-end listing cleanup path are covered.
- Rollback: reverting this commit restores the previous listing behavior but also restores the stale-prefix failure.

issue.title: Scanner cycle completed without a durable data usage snapshot

labels.name: S-reproducing
labels.description: Status: Reproducing a bug report

comment.body:
Adding a field report from another cluster, because it confirms the one hypothesis in @mauritz-envo's excellent analysis above that was left unconfirmed — the "temporarily offline" peer marking — and because it puts a number on what the pre-#6859 behavior costs. Full credit to the analysis in this thread and to the fix; we verified from source that #6859 addresses exactly what we hit.

On 1.0.0-rc.3 (four nodes, EC, TLS internode), a scanner cycle that had been running for **eight days** and had walked **264 million objects** was discarded **18 milliseconds** after a single end-of-cycle activity probe failure, with the peer named in the error up and serving throughout (no restarts in eight days, ~390k log lines written in the surrounding four-minute window):

```
WARN  Scanner cycle activity verification failed  state=cycle_activity_probe_failed  error="Io error: peer https://node3.<redacted>:9000 is temporarily offline"  (scanner_io.rs:296)
ERROR Scanner cycle completed without a durable data usage snapshot  cycle=9846  outcome=NoUpdate  state=usage_not_durable  (scanner.rs:1304)
```

```
before:  cycle=9846  objects_scanned=264,194,178  cycle_started=2026-08-24T08:19:42Z
after:   cycle=9846  objects_scanned=     72,521  cycle_started=2026-09-01T07:29:31Z
```

**The "temporarily offline" marking is aggressive independently of load, as suspected.** That error string is produced only by the fast-fail gate at the top of `PeerRestClient::get_client` ([peer_rest_client.rs#L649-L653](https://github.com/rustfs/rustfs/blob/a41134eb8a25258cfbe49a618ed36d20a5f6ec46/crates/ecstore/src/cluster/rpc/peer_rest_client.rs#L649-L653)), so the probe never sent an RPC at all: any earlier network-like blip on the shared client — from any subsystem — sets the `offline` flag, and until the background recovery monitor's first TCP check clears it (first attempt after the drive-active-check interval, default 15s, backing off to 30s), every call fast-fails against a healthy peer. On rc.3 an end-of-cycle probe landing in that window costs the entire scan; on rc.4 it produces the silent `deferred` re-walk loop documented above. This also explains the idle-cluster reproductions: no CPU throttling is needed, only one transient blip in the wrong 15–45 seconds.

**We verified #6859 covers this trigger.** `scanner_activity_with_retry` ([notification_sys.rs#L1979-L2008](https://github.com/rustfs/rustfs/blob/a41134eb8a25258cfbe49a618ed36d20a5f6ec46/crates/ecstore/src/services/notification_sys.rs#L1979-L2008)) treats the gate error as retryable and calls `prepare_retry()`, which clears the offline gate before re-dialing — so the second attempt actually reaches the peer instead of fast-failing identically. And if both attempts fail, the completed walk is now retained as a non-converged observational snapshot with a `Partial` outcome instead of being discarded ([scanner.rs#L1692-L1705](https://github.com/rustfs/rustfs/blob/a41134eb8a25258cfbe49a618ed36d20a5f6ec46/crates/scanner/src/scanner.rs#L1692-L1705)). Both halves are what this incident needed.

release.name: v0.4.13 — one tool, current context, quiet reconnects
release.body:
Tylina now contributes one current, session-scoped Harness context instead of appending connection notices on every editor reconnect. The current contract supersedes historical tool descriptions after upgrading, and Harness restores it after compaction. Both editions expose only the single `tylina` command tool, with progressive Skills and commands such as `editor.state` for the live selection.

## Update

```sh
dsh plugin --profile web update dsh-tylina@0.4.13
# Or, for the native edition:
dsh plugin --profile web update dsh-tylina-native@0.4.13
```

Install only one edition per profile. Restart the running Harness after updating. Verify the installed version with `dsh plugin --profile web list dsh-tylina --depth 0` (substitute the native name when applicable). pnpm's release-age policy can keep `@latest` on an older eligible release; these exact commands select this release without disabling the policy globally.

Existing historical connection messages remain in chat; new connections no longer append them. No changes to the native compiler or Web assets are required.

## Verified

- Typechecking and 26 tests passed; 5 optional SDK CLI/stdio tests were not enabled.
- Six reconnects preserve one scoped contract, without injecting chat messages; switching projects updates it and disconnecting removes it.
- Packed WASM and macOS native bundles passed the actual installed Harness/browser suites: one Tylina tool in model requests, context restoration after compaction, live editing, compilation, PDF/PNG/SVG exports, reconnection cancellation, and detached window recovery.

release.name: Tylina for Harness 0.4.2
release.body:
Tylina for DeepSeek Harness: edit typeset documents beside your conversation, with a shared workspace, templates, Skills, and MCP tools.

![Tylina inside Harness](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/tylina/dsh-tylina/main/docs/media/harness-slides.png)

- Better Sidebar tabs when installed; a resizable document sidebar otherwise. Expand, collapse, or open a separate window.
- Templates for résumés, posters, academic slides, charts, papers, notes, and reports; fonts load on demand.
- Slides Mode, presenter view, document history, PDF export, and Agent document tools.
- **WASM 0.4.1** compiles in the browser. **Native 0.4.2** compiles on the Harness host and fixes installation with pnpm's default dependency checks.
- Native runtimes cover macOS, Windows, and Linux on x64/arm64; Linux requires glibc.

### Install one edition

```sh
# Browser WASM
dsh plugin --profile web add dsh-tylina@0.4.1

# Or native compilation
dsh plugin --profile web add dsh-tylina-native@0.4.2
```

Use one edition per profile. Run `dsh web`, open Tylina, and choose the conversation's document project.

### Update your installed edition

```sh
dsh plugin --profile web update dsh-tylina@latest
# Or:
dsh plugin --profile web update dsh-tylina-native@latest
```

Restart Harness after updating. Native 0.4.1 is deprecated; use 0.4.2 or newer.
Attached archives are the exact npm packages, accompanied by SHA-256 checksums. No Tylina source checkout or Rust toolchain is required.

### 中文

本次包含 **WASM 0.4.1** 与 **Native 0.4.2**。文档默认显示在对话右侧，与当前会话共享工作区；支持 Better Sidebar、独立窗口、模板、Slides、演讲者模式、PDF 导出，以及提供给 Agent 的 Skills 和 MCP 工具。

Native 0.4.2 修复了 pnpm 默认依赖校验下的安装问题，0.4.1 已弃用。请按上方命令选择一种版本安装或更新，完成后重启 Harness。

issue.title: DP write errors are discarded and failed writes are marked as sent
issue.body:
### Description

DP writes can report success even when TinyTuya returns an explicit transport error. In `TuyaLocalDevice._set_values()`, the return value of `set_multiple_values(..., nowait=True)` is discarded and each pending property is unconditionally marked `sent=True`. The retry wrapper receives `None`, so it cannot see the error and marks the protocol as working.

`nowait=True` skips waiting for a device response; it does not prevent TinyTuya from returning connection/handshake/write errors. Separately, exhausting the wrapper's exception retries also returns normally to the write caller.

### Steps to reproduce

Offline, with the device API mocked:

1. Add a pending property with `sent=False`.
2. Make `set_multiple_values` return `{"Error": "Network Error: Device Unreachable", "Err": "905", "Payload": null}`.
3. Call `_set_values()` for that property.

Observed: `_set_values()` returns `None` and the pending property has `sent=True`. Error `914` reproduces the same behavior. No hardware connection is needed.

### Expected behaviour

Explicit write failures should not be recorded as sent, and final write failures should reach the service caller. Read/status polling should retain its existing tolerant behavior. This is not a request to add retries or treat a successful socket write as proof of physical execution.

### Additional context

Reproduced on 2026.7.2 with TinyTuya 1.20.0; the affected code is unchanged in 2026.9.0 and current `main` (`9786abd9`). Both remote and infrared entities use this shared write path. This was found during IR troubleshooting, but is not claimed to explain the appliance's physical failure.

A focused fix and regression tests will follow in a separate PR.

comment.body:
Thanks for explaining. I agree with updating the UI optimistically. My concern is separate: when TinyTuya already returns an error, `_set_values()` discards it, so the retry wrapper treats the write as successful. Handling that error wouldn't require delaying the UI update or waiting for an acknowledgement.
You're right that I haven't demonstrated a real-world impact yet.
English isn't my first language, and I used AI to help with the English wording. Sorry if it came across badly.

issue.title: Infrared commands silently discard the requested carrier frequency
issue.body:
### Description

The generic infrared sender ignores `InfraredCommand.modulation`. It only uses `get_raw_timings()`, encodes the durations as raw Base64, and sends an empty `head`. Consequently, commands requesting different carrier frequencies are indistinguishable to the device.

### Steps to reproduce

Offline, capture the DP value with the device send method mocked. Send identical timings `[2400, -600, 600, -1200]` first with `modulation=38000`, then with `modulation=56000`.

Both calls produce:

```json
{"control": "send_ir", "type": 0, "head": "", "key1": "1YAlYAlgCsAQ="}
```

### Expected behaviour

Where the blaster/encoding supports a requested carrier, preserve it in the outgoing command. If the requested carrier cannot be expressed, report that limitation rather than silently discarding it.

### Additional context

Reproduced on 2026.7.2; the implementation is unchanged in 2026.9.0 and current `main` (`9786abd9`). No physical transmission is required to reproduce the information loss. This is not a claim that the small carrier difference in one particular AC codebook caused its hardware failure.

TinyTuya already provides `pulses_to_head_key(..., freq=...)`, so a custom codec should not be necessary. However, switching every blaster to compressed output without checking compatibility would be unsafe. A future fix should define the supported device paths, preserve learned-code behavior and validate generated signals on hardware.

This concerns encoding generic HA infrared commands; accepting an already-existing native `head/key` pair through the remote action is a separate enhancement.

issue.title: Support sending native Tuya IR head/key pairs through the remote action
issue.body:
### Description

Enhancement request: allow an existing Tuya native IR `head/key` pair to be sent locally without first converting it to raw pulses.

The single-DP paths in `remote.py` and `infrared.py` currently always emit an empty `head` and `key1 = "1" + raw_base64`. There is no existing input that expresses a nonempty `head` and the native compressed `"0" + key` form. `b64:` and `TuyaRemoteCommand` represent uncompressed learned codes.

### Evidence

With an externally powered DP 201/202 blaster using `basic_ir_remote`, protocol 3.5 and TinyTuya 1.20.0:

- Sending converted Pronto through HAIR/Tuya Local did not operate the AC.
- Sending the decompressed pulses through `remote.send_command` also did not operate it.
- Sending the following original-format DP 201 value through a standalone TinyTuya client on a reachable network path received an authenticated success response and physically turned the AC off:

```json
{
  "control": "send_ir",
  "head": "010f060000000000040015003f00ac07d0",
  "key1": "001$$0030B24D7B84E01F@$$$0030B24D7B84E01F@%",
  "type": 0,
  "delay": 300
}
```

These comparisons also changed the sending implementation, so they do **not** prove that the blaster cannot support raw playback.

### Proposed scope

An explicit native-code input for the existing remote send action, preserving `head/key` and validating it before transmission. Keep `b64:`, RF and existing learned codes backward compatible. No cloud codebook retrieval, virtual AC subdevice connection, arbitrary DP service, or bundled code library is requested.

Before implementing a PR, I would like maintainer feedback on whether extending the existing inline command formats is the preferred interface.

### Versions

Physical tests: Home Assistant 2026.9.0 / Tuya Local 2026.7.2. The relevant packaging code is unchanged in 2026.9.0 and current `main` (`9786abd9`). An integration-level implementation has not yet been hardware-tested. Carrier preservation is a separate issue.

issue.title: Infrared long-gap splitting breaks mark/space boundaries
issue.body:
### Description

`TuyaLocalInfrared.async_send_command()` splits timings longer than 50000 us at the timing's index, but leaves the replacement 5000 us value at the start of the next block. When the split timing is a space, this turns a space into the first mark of the next Tuya pulse block.

### Steps to reproduce

Call `async_send_command()` with an `InfraredCommand` returning the following signed timings, replacing `_ir_send` and `asyncio.sleep` with mocks. Decode the captured Base64 with TinyTuya's `base64_to_pulses`.

```text
Input:  [9000, -4500, 560, -60000, 560, -560]
Output: [9000, 4500, 560], [5000, 560, 560]
```

Both blocks have an odd number of timings. The original space has become a mark in the second block.

A trailing space also produces a spurious extra command:

```text
Input:  [9000, -4500, 560, -52002]
Output: [9000, 4500, 560], [5000]
```

### Expected behaviour

Split blocks should preserve mark/space boundaries and end with a space. A trailing gap should not produce another IR mark. Long marks must not be treated as idle time.

### Additional context

Offline reproduction on 2026.7.2; the implementation is unchanged in 2026.9.0 and current `main` (`9786abd9`). This affects the generic infrared timing path, not the legacy learned-code fast path. It is independent of native compressed-code support and carrier handling, and is not claimed to explain commands that do not trigger the split.

A focused fix and boundary tests will follow in a separate PR. No physical transmission was used for this reproduction.

issue.title: Fix order local refit copies after source updates

labels.name: Approved
labels.description: All necessary approvals have been made

issue.body:
- [X] I, the PR author, have personally reviewed every line of this PR.

# What does this PR do?

Local same-rank refit copies can silently read stale model weights when the source update is still queued on the caller's CUDA stream. NCCL, Gloo, NIXL, and NVSHMEM all run the local copy on a dedicated stream, but only order the caller stream after that copy; they do not order the copy stream after the producer before it reads the source tensor.

This change makes each local copy stream wait for the caller's current stream before copying. It preserves the existing copy-to-caller join and does not change the public API or remote-rank transport.

## Tests

```bash
python -m torch.distributed.run --nproc-per-node 8 -m pytest -q \
  tests/unit_tests/resharding/test_copy_services.py::test_local_copy_waits_for_current_stream \
  tests/unit_tests/resharding/test_copy_services.py::test_optional_backend_local_copy_waits_for_current_stream
```

With the fix, every rank passes all four backend cases (`4 passed` per rank). Removing only the corresponding `wait_stream` calls makes every affected case fail with the destination retaining the stale value (maximum absolute difference `1.0`). The NIXL/NVSHMEM test uses real CUDA streams and tensors while mocking only the optional remote transport, so it does not require those optional runtime dependencies in the unit-test environment.

As supplemental validation, I also exercised the public `swap_model_weights()` path after fused AdamW updates on a 20-layer, hidden-size 4096 GPT model. The source/destination logits were the oracle:

| Backend | Current code | Fixed | Exact revert |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| NCCL | max diff `3.0010` | `0` | max diff `3.3286` |
| Gloo | max diff `2.8388` | `0` | max diff `2.8373` |
| NIXL | max diff `0.9583` | `0` | max diff `7.2628` |
| NVSHMEM | max diff `0.9849` | `0` | max diff `0.9629` |

### NCCL/Gloo refit latency

I measured the cost of the added dependency with the repository's `examples/rl/benchmark_refit.py` on one H200. Both variants used collocated TP1/PP1/EP1, BF16, a 20-layer/4096-hidden/32-head GPT model (4.23B parameters per model), sequence length 8, batch size 1, five warmup iterations, and 30 timed iterations. Each timed iteration synchronizes CUDA before refit, so this comparison measures the dependency overhead when source work is already complete.

The fixed tree differed from the current tree only by this PR. The same temporary current-main API compatibility adjustment and statistics output were applied to both trees and are not part of the PR. All values below are milliseconds; `mean / median / stddev / min-max` summarizes all 30 samples.

| Backend |                                Current |                                  Fixed |           Median delta |             Mean delta |
| ------- | -------------------------------------: | -------------------------------------: | ---------------------: | ---------------------: |
| NCCL    |     `7.39 / 7.38 / 0.05 / 7.33-7.52` |     `7.51 / 7.45 / 0.24 / 7.40-8.67` | `+0.07` (`+0.95%`) | `+0.12` (`+1.62%`) |
| Gloo    | `16.34 / 8.28 / 44.07 / 8.24-249.67` | `16.21 / 8.27 / 43.47 / 8.24-246.39` | `-0.01` (`-0.12%`) | `-0.13` (`-0.80%`) |

Each Gloo arm contained one approximately 250 ms outlier, which inflates its mean and standard deviation; the median shows no measurable regression at the reported precision. If source work is still pending, the new dependency intentionally includes the time required before those weights are valid rather than allowing a stale copy to return early.

## Contribution process

### Pre-checks

- [X] I have added relevant unit tests
- [ ] I have added relevant functional tests
- [ ] I have added proper typing to my code [Typing guidelines](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html)
- [ ] I have added relevant documentation
- [X] I have run the [autoformatter.sh](https://github.com/NVIDIA/Megatron-LM/blob/main/tools/autoformat.sh) on my PR

@YangFei1990 Sure. 

First, thanks for flagging NIXL and NVSHMEM. I reproduced the same bug in both backends through the public `swap_model_weights()` path after fused AdamW updates on a 4.23B GPT model. At the current PR head, the destination logits were stale, with maximum differences of `0.9583` for NIXL and `0.9849` for NVSHMEM. Adding one producer-to-copy stream dependency to each backend made all three iterations exact. Removing just those two lines brought the stale results back.

I extended the patch and CUDA ordering test to both optional backends. The test uses real CUDA streams and tensors and mocks only the remote transport, so it does not require the optional NIXL or NVSHMEM runtime. Under the repository's 8-GPU `torchrun` topology, all four backend cases pass on every rank. Reverting only the NIXL and NVSHMEM waits makes both cases fail on every rank, with the destination retaining `0` and a maximum difference of `1.0`. The gate now uses `get_cycles_per_ms()`, and the expected all-ones tensor is independent of the source.

Each wait remains at its backend's local-copy site, one line next to the stream it orders. A shared helper would add indirection while all four backends would still need separate calls. I did not add a Gloo cleanup fixture because `GlooCopyService` inherits the no-op `CopyService.close()`, so the fixture would not release the process group. The test creates the group collectively on every rank in the same `torchrun` invocation.

issue.title: Fix fused MLA Q-RoPE in-place load/store races

labels.name: Final Review
labels.description: PR is in the "final review" stage

labels.name: waiting-on-maintainers
labels.description: Waiting on maintainers to respond

issue.body:
- [X] I, the PR author, have personally reviewed every line of this PR.

# What does this PR do?

Issue #4640 reports intermittent BF16 gradient mismatches from `fused_apply_mla_rope_for_q` with packed THD input. The investigation found the same in-place load/store race in both Q-RoPE kernels. Forward converts interleaved values to split layout, while backward converts split-layout gradients back to interleaved layout. With multiple warps in one Triton program, one warp can overwrite a source element before another warp has loaded it.

This change adds one unconditional `tl.debug_barrier()` after the source loads and before the first overlapping store in each kernel. It restores the original upstream multi-warp autotune space and keeps the existing `flaky_in_dev` marker. THD scan and autotune-key changes remain separate performance work.

## Issue tracking

Fixes #4640

## Reproduction and regression

Run the fusion test file in the standard Megatron Core development environment with one CUDA GPU.

```bash
uv run python -m torch.distributed.run \
  --nproc-per-node 1 \
  -m pytest -q \
  --experimental \
  tests/unit_tests/fusions/test_mla_yarn_rope_apply.py
```

The new regression first checks a `BLOCK_H=1, num_warps=1` control against an independent PyTorch RoPE oracle for the tested configuration. It then compares known failing multi-warp configurations with that control using exact equality.

- Forward uses `BLOCK_H=1` with 8 warps and 200 replays for each layout.
- Backward uses `BLOCK_H=2` with 4 warps and 100 replays for each layout.

Removing only the forward barrier makes both forward layout cases fail. Removing only the backward barrier makes both backward layout cases fail. All four cases pass with both barriers present. Their test bodies take about 2.4 seconds combined on H200, and the slowest takes 1.43 seconds.

The same test file exercises the normal `fused_apply_mla_rope_for_q` entry point with both SBHD and packed THD input and runs autograd backward. The full file passed on the same H200 with two adjacent Triton versions.

- Triton 3.5.1 completed 11 tests in 23.86 seconds.
- Triton 3.5.0 completed 11 tests in 23.52 seconds.

### Supplemental public-entry stress

A separate BF16 packed THD stress run covered Q projection, `fused_apply_mla_rope_for_q`, and autograd backward from a scalar loss. It used 32 local heads and `cu_seqlens=[0,27,54,99,128]` on one H200. The runtime was Python 3.12.3, PyTorch `2.11.0a0+eb65b36914.nv26.02`, CUDA 13.1, driver 590.48.01, and Triton 3.5.1.

A single-warp control was validated against the PyTorch oracle before each forced multi-warp candidate was replayed 1,000 times.

| Observable                                 | Multi-warp configuration |        Before |       Fixed | Remove only its barrier |
| ------------------------------------------ | ------------------------ | ------------: | ----------: | ----------------------: |
| forward output                             | `BLOCK_H=1`, 8 warps   | 749 incorrect | 0 incorrect |           719 incorrect |
| backward Q and projection-weight gradients | `BLOCK_H=2`, 4 warps   |   8 incorrect | 0 incorrect |             4 incorrect |

The fixed candidates also completed 1,000 replays per direction without a mismatch on Triton 3.5.0. This stress run supplements the checked-in regression and is not required to execute it.

## Performance impact

The barrier-only benchmark forced identical block sizes and warp counts before and after the fix. Six rounds ran in alternating order on one H200. Each variant used 200 warmup launches and 2,000 timed samples per round. The table reports the pooled median across 12,000 timed samples per variant.

SBHD shapes are ordered as sequence length, batch size, local heads, and head dimension. THD shapes are ordered as token count, local heads, and head dimension.

| Kernel / layout | Input               | Before median | Fixed median |  Delta |
| --------------- | ------------------- | ------------: | -----------: | -----: |
| forward / SBHD  | `[4096,8,32,256]` |   868.032 µs |  852.960 µs | -1.74% |
| forward / THD   | `[32768,32,256]`  |  1606.688 µs | 1605.632 µs | -0.07% |
| backward / SBHD | `[4096,8,32,192]` |   322.624 µs |  322.624 µs |  0.00% |
| backward / THD  | `[32768,32,192]`  |   421.344 µs |  423.200 µs | +0.44% |

No material regression was observed. The negative forward deltas are not treated as a speedup claim.

## Contribution process

- [ ] I have added relevant functional tests
- [ ] I have added proper typing to my code [Typing guidelines](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html)

Black, isort, Pylint, Python compilation, and `git diff --check` pass for both changed files.

issue.title: [Bugfix][Structured Output] Let terminal grammars stop under min_tokens

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: mrv2
labels.description: Model Runner V2 specific

issue.body:
## Purpose

`min_tokens` can force structured-output requests to sample outside the grammar after a short schema reaches its terminal state. For schemas such as `{"type":"boolean"}`, `{"enum":["a"]}`, or `{"type":"null"}`, the grammar's only legal continuation after the value is EOS. `min_tokens` then masks EOS because the request has not reached the requested minimum length, leaving no legal token.

On xgrammar this returns `finish_reason="error"` with a trailing `!`, for example `true!`. On guidance the same conflict silently emits `!` until `min_tokens` is satisfied. This PR lets stop/EOS survive only when the `min_tokens` mask would otherwise empty the row, then finishes the request once the structured grammar accepts its terminal token. Normal `min_tokens` behavior is unchanged when any non-stop token remains available, and the same guard is forwarded through the V2 spec-decode sampler path.

This is not covered by the existing FSM-adjacent work I found: #45015 is pipeline-parallel stale FSM state, #44297 and #44993 are spec-decode reasoning-boundary masking, #37506 is `ignore_eos` plus extra speculative tokens, and #42619 is an already-terminated matcher being advanced later. I re-ran current `main` after #44297 and it still fails the `min_tokens` terminal-schema case below; none of the adjacent fixes handles `min_tokens` masking the only grammar-legal EOS token.

## Test Plan

Run a real `LLM.generate` A/B on Qwen3-0.6B with xgrammar structured output. The before case uses the PR diff against upstream `main` reversed.

Also run the focused V1 regression test, the logits-processor correctness suite, a CUDA smoke for the GPU all-masked fallback, ruff on changed files, and `git diff --check`.

## Test Result

Qwen3-0.6B A/B flips the bug on current `main` after #44297: with the patch, boolean/enum/null terminal schemas stop cleanly at EOS; with the patch reversed, the same requests emit `!` and finish with `error`. Guidance shows the same boolean conflict: before it emits `true!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!`, after it returns `true` and stops at EOS.

Focused tests and checks passed:

```text
GPU all-masked fallback smoke

ruff check changed files
All checks passed!

git diff --check
PASS
```
